" THE WAY WE DO AT SCHOOL." Young Tom, home for the holidays, A hero seemed to Nell, Who opened wide her sweet blue eyes AS, the tales he had to tell. Of how he fought in battles, And had broken every rule; Of what the "fellows" said and did, And "the way we do at school." "The languages, he knew them all, " Ich bin," "tres bon," oui, oui," And girls were silly little things ; Why, he knew Rule of Three. And when a hail:Mess cow they passed Ile showed, too, he could run, Leaving his sister Nellie To face the cow alone. "I don't know French, or Rule of Three, Or any other rule; But, still, to ran and leave me so Was very, very cool. • I see," Nell slyly whispered, the way we do at school.'" "‘ Little Folks" Magazine for January. •

That scientitic empedition round the world may perhaps be able to 'tell us when it returns why a man always takes 011 his boots first when undressing, while a woman begins at her hair-pins. "Lenny," said her maiden aunt, "you should eat the barley that is in your soup, or you will never get a hus- band." Lenny, looking up with an innocent but comical smile, replies, "is that what you eat it for, aunty ?" A. lady, who was very modest and submissive before mar- riage, was observed by her friend to use her tongue pretty freely after, whereupon the observing friend remarked, "There was a time when I almost imagined she had none," a Yes," said her husband with a sigh," but it is very long

since. • A vigilant sentinel is posted at the door of a picture gallery, with strict orders of the customary character. A sightseer lounges in, and is promptly halted. "Here, sir, you must leave your cane at the door." "But, my friend," I haven't got any cane." "Then go back and get one; no one is allowed to pass ia here unless he leaves his cane at the door.' Orders is °niers !" Vratuk ITS OWN RSWAILD.—A Dog on a warm summer day lay down In the shade and soon fell asleep. Be was awakened by the Noise of a huge Ball approaching his shady resting-place. "Gee up," said the Ball," and let use Lie Clown there." "No,' replied the Dog, "you have no Bight to the place; I was here First." "Well," said the Bull, looking Innocently at the Dog, but with a ferocious Twinkle in his left Eye, which made the Dog's spinal Column ran cold and his lower Jaw give way," let us Toss up for it." "Thank you," said the Dog Politely, "I never Gamble," and he walked away. Moral—Virtue has its own -

, reward.—Life. DEBILITY AND ITS CURE,—Sea-sickness is very easy with those who possess stamina and nerve. You come on board with this; then perhaps mat de mer attacks you. Well, if you keep below you have merely your own strength to defend you; if you go on deck, and keep on deck, you find allies, most valuable, in thepure bracing air of the sea, and in the sunshine, and in the walking exercise yon take, to say nothing of the good mental effects that accrue from seeing everything that is taking place around you, and from exchanging ideas with your fellow-passengers. In this Way debility flies; you get stronger instead of weaker every day, and as you gain more and more strength, farther and farther flies away the danger of becoming a victim to sea-sickness. Debility must be fought by passengers going first to sea; and my advice to all is to prepare for the voyage for three weeks or a fortnight beforehand by regular living, temper- ance in everything, 'good diet, exercise, and fresh air. Do not take stimulants at sea, or the liver is bound to go wrong, and your last state will be worse than your first.—"Cassell's Family Magazine" for January. ' A LASTING REPCTATION.—Withont great abilitieo, yith- out large means nnenetained by rank or fortune, Mshop Wilson achieved' a work which remains, and won an influ- ence which spread beyoA the narrow confines of his small diocese; his writings ate read to-day ;devout communicants, as they feed on the bread of life, still take his words with them to fix their thoughts =cleanse their spiritual affec- tions. Simple and unaffected, almost meagre as his sermons are, the churches filled when he used to preach ; nay more— we are told that when these divine discourses were preached in Manx after his death, crowds began to flock again to the churches which Methodism was beginning to empty. . What men wanted from Bieholp Wilson was not so much his teaching or his oratory. They desired most of all his blessing. At the Isle of Man, after the service, the people would wait in the churchyard and kneel, uncovered, to •reoeive his blessing. In 'England, too, at Warrington and in London, the people crowded round•hica with the cry, "Bleee me too, my lord." And when became to court simply attired, the King stepped forth from among his courtiers, and taking him by the hand, said, "My lord, I desire your prayere.—Caiten Boyd Carpenter in The QuirJr" for January. TEE FIRST JEWS IN Roan--Julius Carar—who, as Philo informs us, felt an undisguised admiration for the manly independence with which the Jews held themselves aloof from that all but idolatrous adulation into which the degenerate Romans were so ready to plunge—allowed them to settle in a large district beyond the Tiber, and yearly to send deputies and temple-tribute to their holy city. From that time forward they were the incessant butt for the half-scornful, half-alarmed wit and wrath of the Roman writers. The district assigned to them, being in theleigh- bourhood of the wharfs where the barges from Ostia were accustomed to unlade, was partecularly suitable for the retail trade in which they were mainly occupied. They increased with almost incredible rapidity. Their wisp of hey and the basket, which were their sole belongings, and were adopted to secure them from the danger of unclean meats, were known in every quarter. Martial describes how Jewish hawkers broke his morning slumbers with their bawling, and Juvenal complains of the way in which their gipey-like women got themselves smuggled into the bou- doirs of rich and silly ladies to interpret their dreams. Others of them, with a stipple versatility which would have dene credit to the Greeks themselves, thrust them- selves into every house and every profession, flung them- selves with perfect shamelessness into the heathen vices, and became the useful tools of wealthy rascality, and the unscrupulous confidants of the "gilded youth." Some be- came the favourites of the palace, and made nominal prose, lytes of noble ladies, who, like Poppcca, had every gift ex- cept that of virtue. Bat whatever their condition, they were equally detested by the mess of the population. If they were false to their religion they were flouted as rene- gades; if they were tree to it, their Sabbaths, and their .circonciaion, and their hatred of pork, their form of oath, their lamp-lightings, and their solemn festivals, were held up to angry ridicule, as signs of the most abject supersti- tion, If a Roman saw a knot of Jew beggars, he turned from them with a 'shudder of disgust; if he noticed the statue of a Jewish king or Alabarch, he frowned at it as a proof of the degradation of the age. Whether successful or unsuccessful—whether he was an Herodian prince or a match-selling pedlar—the Jew was to the Latin races an object of abhorrence and disdain. They were regarded with the same feelings as those with which a citizen of San Francisco looks on the Chinese immigrant—as intruders, whose competition was dangerous—as aliens whose cus- toms were offensive.—" The Life and Work of St. Paul" for January. 191E,REPORTEE'S Farmens.—We read in a Paris journal the interesting piece of news of the death of the "oldest rag-picker," Daddy Moreau, who died at the age of 100 years all but theee days, in a garret of the Rue de Monlinet. The return of that periodical paragraph—for it reappears every year—filled us with pleasure. We like to see old ac- quaintances, and we have known Daddy Moreau since 1867. He was then invented by a penny-a-liner in the Cloche. Other journals, to heighten the interest of the death of the oldest rag-picker, have since added that he was formerly a colonel in the Grand Armee, or that he was born a marquis, or that he was once a page of Charles X., &c., Lee. Our con- temperary, which has once more put the piece of sews in circulation, states that Moreau died of starvation on a mat- tress filled with gold. That variation is rather used up, for we have heard so many stories of Paupers rolling in wealth and blind beggars who were capitalists, ..kc. But no matter; we will accept the mattress filled with gold in consideration of the pleasure we have derived from seeing that excellent Daddy Moreau once more make the round Of the jour- nals. We carnot say whether the tour will be an ex- tended one this time, but two years ago it had a very wide range, fetr we read the "Death of the oldest Paris • rag-picker" in the 31e/bourne Times, one of the principal journals in Australia. Daddy Moreau is by no means the only creation of the kind, and has a certain number of companions who are trotted out from time to time. There is the last survivor of the Battle of Trafalgar, a venerable relic named Tiron, who dies every year at the age of 104. He has always lost a leg and an arm shot off by English CAWS balls. Some details of the life of this hero follow. After being for thirty years at pensioner at the Hotel des Invalides, he came into a &all fortune, and went into honsekeepin. He was sensible to the last, and his dying words were " Viva la France V' • There is also Briot, the last survivor :of the shipwreck of the M6duse, who has died regularly once a year since 1861 Of course he never existed any more then any of the others, and he was always a hun- dred years old. A curious fact reladt;vdacyosncseurnffeinrgedhifmromwaas that since the shipwreck he had nervous trembling, and he could never see a black man without feeling qealras of the stomach, because he fed on one on the raft. Gericanit was also said to have introduced him in his famous picture, and sometimes an account of the wreck of the Manse was brought in which made another, sixty lives. We pass over "the last of Charles X.'s pages, ' the "cripple who suffered ampntatten at Wagram," Lee. We could name a dozen more types of the kind, iventions of the penny-a-liner, but we have said enough to prove that the excellent "oldest raepicker " is not the only one of his kind, and has many imitators.—Paris Lanterne. A La umors Lutern.--Lieut. Diek, of the Russian Army, has discovered a new luminous powder which has three colours —green, yellow, and violet, the last-named giving the moit powerful light. Mixed with wiser in a glass vessel, an illuminating liquid is produced which may prove very useful in mining and military operations. The Mar:ai- -1 slating power lasts for eight hours, when fresh powder must _ _

, be added. THE RESSAREMILE Smisirrs have been seen in Tarkey, as well as elsewhere, and have been interpreted as a portent of coming war and bloodshed, as the following extract from an Adrianople correspondent of the Eastern Express shows : Aman Yarabbiln! Merciful Lord !", I heard yesterday a devout neighbour of mine exclaim, "are we, then, des- tined to Bee more blood spilt? Is the wrath of heaven still upon us, and have we not yet drained the cup of our mis- fortunes? May the Lord and the Prophet avert so dire a

calamity. SNAKE BITES—We take the following from a Brazilian paper :—Relative to the alleged failure of permanganate of potash as an antidote against the bite of rattlesnakes, Dr. Lacerda says that the poison of snakes seems to be iden- tical in all and to act in the same manner. He considers that cases of failure arise from three causes :—The poison having been injected directly into a vein; too late applica- tion of remedy and its injectipn in insufficient quantity; and the employment of an old solution. The last he be- lieves to be the most frequent cause of failure. He recom- mends, therefore, the use of freshly made solutions of the salt and careful avoidance of contact with organic matters, which rapidly deoxygenise it, and frequent injections in different parts of the limb until the poisonous effects begin

to disappear. CONVERSION OF LIGHT INTO ELECTENCITI.—The conver- sion a electricity into light is now a fact of every-day utility, but the reverse process ha' been very slow of an.' complishment. It has, however, been effected by Herr Sauer, whose sunlight battery has been described in the Electrotechnische Zeitschrift. The chemical rays furnish the power, and the battery will only act in sunlight. It consists of a glass vessel, containing a solution of 15 parts of table salt and seven parts of sulphate of copper, in 106 parts of water. In this is placed a porous cell containing mercury. One electrode is made of platinum,and the other of sulphide of silver, and both are connected with a gal- vanometer. When not in use the whole is enclosed in a box. When in use, the platinum electrode is immersed in the mercury, and the other in the salt solution; the battery is placed in the sunlight, and the galvanometer needle is then found to be deflected, the sulphide of silver being the negative pole. If the sun is clouded, or any other change in the intensity of the light occurs, it is indicated by the needle. The exact effect produced by the light rays does not as yet appear very clear, but their presence distinctly produces electrical action, and their absence suspends it.—

-Engineering. Tux CONVEYANCE OF DIPETYIERIA.—The Wiener Allge- meine lfedicinische Zeitung states that Professor Gerhardt, of Warzburg, has carried oaf a series of observattons for the purpose of determining whether diphtheria may be corn- nannicated by pheasants,kpigeons and domestic fowls, and has come to the affirmative conclusion. In September, 1881, 2,600 fowls were sent from the neighbourhood of Verona to Neleelhansen, in Baden, where there is a great fowl-rearing establishment. Some of them must have been affected with diptheritis before they started, and in the end 1,400 fowls died of it. In the summer of last year 1,000 chickens were hatched from eggs collected from many different places. Six weeks after their birth diptheritis manifested itself among the young chickens, and so badly that in a short time they all died. Five eats that were kept in the estab- lishment also became ill of the same malady, and died. A parrot that hung in a cage in the house was also attacked, but recovered. Last November an Italian hen, while being " painted " about the jaws with carbolic acid by the chief keeper, bit the man's wrist and foot. Presently he became ill with a smart fever, considerable swelling at the wounded parts, and all the symptoms of traumatic diphtheritis. His recovery was very tedious. This was not the only case of the transmissim of the disease to men. Two•thirds of all the laboaving persons employed about the establishment be- came ill with.ordinary diphtheritis, and one man conveyed the infection to his three children. A NEW MODS OF JOINING TRANCIES.—The fatal acci- dents which have occurred at Birkenhead,.Blackburn, Hud- dersfield, and elsewhere, through the overturning of tram- cars, have led the Board of Trade to recommend that steam tramway companies be not licensed to.c irry bof-passengers on eteepgrade lines having sharp curves on the inclines. In turning corners there is always a certain amount of what is called" overhang" of the cars; and if the passenger-load happen to be unequally distributed, so that it preponderates on the overhanging side, there is a great tendency to turn over—especially if the curve be on an incline, and the car be travelling at a quick rate of speed. To obviate this risk, and also to provide a superior mode of connecting tram engines with their Mrs an invention has been patented by i Mr. E. C. Wickes and 'Colonel Beaumont, R.E , by which the car is divided into two parts—one portion containing the engine and part of the passengers, and the other carry- ing the remainder, inside and outside, altogether fifty-six 1 persons. The length of the whole is less than 30 feet, or about 5 feet shorter than the space occupied by two horses and car carrying forty-six persons. The car is jointed about the middle. eV held by a perch pia in the floor and roof, which enables the car to move freely in a lateral direction, and to take the sharpest carves with ease, each portion tending to keep the other on the line.' The passage between the two is about a foot in length, and could be dispensed with entirely. It is protected from the weather by cylin- drical shells moving within each other, in such manner that in the sharpest curves no portion of the passage is exposed to wind or rain. The overhang being, so to speak, cut in two, is. deprived of all danger—the latter portion of the vehicle following the former round the curve with the greatest freedom; and thus the valuable roof•space for carrying purposes is not sacrificed, whilst safety from up- setting is practically insured. Where mechanical power is I employed, the advantage of this is obvious, as every pas- I senger carried tells in the receipts; and however great the load, there is no "cruelty to animals." The cars are of handsome appearance; and being used with compressed-air engines, nothing is seen of the latter, which occupy about 6 or 7 feet of the front portion of the car, and are of course I free from the heat, smoke, steam, or fumes of the ordinary steam-locomotive. The mode of junction is said to be equally spplicable to connecting steam engines with their cars, or for connecting a series of ordinary railway carriages. Cars according to this patent have been constructed for use on one of the suburban tramway lines of the Metropolis, land are shortly expected to be in daily operation.—Cossell's ' Magazine. EXPERIMENTS WITH MINERS' SAFETY LAMPS.— ADOPTION OF A NEW LA.MP AT THE ALTHAM • COLLIERIES. . Recently a paper on the new Marsaut Safety Lamp for .Mines was read before the Manchester Geological Society by Mr. Joseph Dickinson, her Majesty's Chief Inspector of Mines. Since then a number of experimental tests with the lamp have been carried oat. by Mr. Dickinson, with the re- suit that certain modifications have been introduced, and ail., improved " Marsaut," made in accordance with these tests, was a few days ago introduced into the Altham Colliery, near Accrington, the scene of the recent disastrous explo- sion. The tests were carried out at the Celvnen Colliery, Monmouthshire, and by the kindness of Mr. J: T. Green, the manager, the special apparatus there being made available for the 'purpose. The lamp was tested by being put into a tube or pipe, and exposed to quick and varying currents of an explosive mixture of lighting gas, nearly all the series , of tests being made three times, with the following results: —lst Tests: The Marsaut lamp, as sent by M. Marsaut, and as described in the paper read by Mr. Dickinson, vont out, but gas continued burning under the gauze. A Celynea Mueseler lamp tested at the same time went out entirely. 2nd Tests: The Marsant, with the addition of a strip of tin plate, about iin. in width, placed from the top to the bottom against the inner side of the inner gauze cylinder the lamp went out as before, bat gas continued burning under the gauze. The Celynen Mueseler went out entirely. 3rd Tests: The Marsaut, with the addition of a strip of safety lamp gauze dividing entirely the inner gauze cylinder from top to bottom; the lamp went out, but gas continued burning under the gauze as before. The Celynen Mueseler went out entirely. 4th Tests: The Marsaut, with the addi- tion of a third glaze cylinder place& outside the two other gauzes; the lamp went out, but gas continued burning under the gauze as before. The Celynen Mueseler divested of its gauze cylinder, but in other respects as before, went out en- tirely. sth Tests: The Marsaut, with the outlet apertures at the top of the outer casing so covered as only to admit of the lamp burning freely, went out, but gas continued burning under the gauze as before. The Celynen Mueseler and an Evan Thomas lamp went out entirely. 6th tests: The Marsaut, with the outlet apertures covered as in No. 5; with all the side inlet holes covered, and also with about one half of the inlet space at the tap of the crown or inner rim covered—all the air having to pass up the vertical holes, and just enough allowed for the Wan to burn brightly—the lamp went out, and then without flash of gas under the gauze it went out entirely. The Celynen and the Evan Thomas also went out entirely. This was repeated three times with the same results. About 20 tests were made. In none of them did gas fire outside the Marsaut, but in those tests where gas continued burning underneath the gauze, and where it so burned for about half a minute without go- ing out, Mr. Dickinson observes that it seems probable that it would have fired through if the test had been continued long enough. These tests, Mr. Dickinson adds, show indis- putably that if the Marsant lamp is to be used where it may be exposed to a current of explosive gas, a change in the I construction will be required. M. Marsaut has tried a movable ring for closing the air apertures, so as to ex- tinguish the lamp. In our report to-day of the Blackburn Town Council meet- ing is n important discussion on ensilage. , It is announced in the Field that a movement has been set on foot to form a society to promote and encourage the breeding of Cleveland bays, and publish a stud book. WASTE PRODUCTS lITILISED.—TO a few remarks respect- ing sulphate of ammonia (a new source of nitrogen), which is so extensively used as a top-dressing for grass and cereal crops, attention is desired. Twelve months since, gray of 24 Or cent, strength was worth £lB 10s.•, it is now £l3 108. The, mportant decline is to be attributed to the re- duced price of nitrate of soda, and, in a greater degree, to a new source of production. Appliances have been erected for the saving of the ammonia from the blast furnaces; and, without giving elaborate details, it is stated that one firm have ben blowing £30,000 per annum, for some years past,

into tke' air. The past year nas been agriculturally an improvement upon its immediate predecessors. This is probably true of it as a whole, notwithstanding the great disaster in the enor- mous extension of the foot-and-month disease which it has witnessed, and notwithstanding the carious diversity of ex- perience which a comparison of different districts reveals. On the whole it is probable that rents have this year been generally paid out of produce, not out of pocket as they have of late years generally been paid. The yield of oats and potatoes, which are the crops rattier of the poorer than of the richer districts of the country, is this year remark- ably good, and thus Ireland has had a good year. From the western counties, too, we have good eports ; from the easterecoanties, and especially from the fen districts, we have poor accounts. 1M course, the great misfortune of the year, affecting all districts more or less, but especially affecting, those which had a late and unfortunate harvest, has been the low prices obtainable in the market. Nothing can make up for a loss of £3 per acre ea the value of a corn crop; and that has been experienced this year in all dis- tricts where the barley harvest has been spoiled by the weather. The rent over, the whole farm goes at one swoop in the corn market, in such a case as this, excepting only produce of the finest quality.—The interest shown in ensi- lage is one of the features of 1883. Under good manage- ment, the silo promises to be an aid, especially in districts where plough land is the exception, and where root crops cannot be economically grown or consumed.—Among the illustrations of zig-zag experience of which every agricul- tural year is full, nothing, probably, ever exceeded the effect of the great hurricane which raged during the first days of September among the hop grounds of the country. One of the finest promises of yield ever witnessed was at once nearly half destroyed.—Agncultural Gazette. PROFESSOR TANNER ON AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION.— Lecturing recently at Bedford, Professor Tanner said it was often asked—What is the use of all these efforts to teach this subject, for shrely the practice of farming can be learnt as it was before? This clearly showed a misconception of what was aimed at in the science classes. The object was to make people more generally intelligent upon the circum- stances which surrounded the operations of the farm, in order that they might thereby be better enabled to learn the work of the farm. He never heard any objection to im- parting a good "commercial" education, and no one dreamt that by this it was meant to teach the busiwe of any par- ticular trade. " Agricultural " education anlbunted to much the same thing, as by it was simply meant a course of in- struction which should put voting men and women into the best position for learning the practice and business of agri- culture. Most people, including many farmers, had in former times fallen under the impression that it needed very little preparation to learn farming, and on that account everybody thought himself qualified to give advice to the farmer. Since then, however, a change had taken place.— (The Chairman: I beg your pardon. We have it every day.)—Professor Tanner said it only illustrated what he was i say log—that, owing to an idea having' got abroad that farming work needed very little reparation. everybody felt competent to give advice. The lecturer then proceeded to point out the importance of pr iminary Instruction in all matters pertaining to the farm, and said it would be Valu- able to all classes engaged in agriculture—the labourers, the tenant-farmers, and the landlords. If a skilled artisan was of greater service to his employer than an unskilled one, a farm labourer who understood the nature of his occupa- tion must also be of great value to the farmer. And if it were important to have an intelligent labourer, it was much more important that the farmer himself should understand

nothing.— REAM CaLvas.—ln some districts where cows are timed to calve very early in the year they will soon be dropping, and while some farmers will decide to rear the calves, others will do as of old aad either sell them or fatten them for the butcher. No one can for a moment desire to dictate what the butcher shall kill or the consumer eat; but I would suggest with all earnestness that the farmer should rear rather than do anything else, and more especially in the case of heifers. Rearing beasts pays well; if it does not the system is greatly at fault. There appears to me to be far too much stress laid upon high feeding, and it is forgot- ten that it is possible to overfeed just as it is to overstock. The formula given by breeders who breed for Smithfield should never be accepted by the practical farmer, and it should be his aim to do the best he can in order to reap a profit. It is folly for a man to take his stand upon the argument that he must feed high. I have seen repeatedly experiments made in growing beasts up to two or two. and a half years, which.beasts were bought in for fattening by butchers or farmers who made a practice of fattening and which paid very well. If, however, a calf is allowed, for instance, to remain with a Cow until it is eight weeks old, consuming milk worth 12s. a week, it piles up a bill of costs at the very beginning of its career which will at all times be a load against it as a profitable investment. There is no doubt that it is a mistake to allow calves to suck at all, and I think that any person who has given the system of artifi- cial feeding by means of pails fitted with indiarabber teats , a trial will bear this out. The calf must never be allowed to suck its dam if this practice is to be adopted, inasmuch as it is most difficult to teach it afterwards, and the longer the delay the more difficult it becomes. Cowmen generally oppose anything of this kind because of the additional trouble it gives them, for the calves have to be patiently taught, the milk has to be heated and mixed with meal, and the vessels have to be thoroughly cleaned. All this is of course superseded by putting the calf to the cow morning and night, for it should never be allowed to remain with the cow, or her miking property may be materially damaged. If cows must be used it is a good plan to put two calves to ' each cow, supplementing their feed after the first fortnight with a little oilcake dust, and then a slice or two of mangel or turnip, hay having been given them from the first week. There are few old farmers who have any faith in condimental foods. These ingredients have their virtues, but any farmer can mix them to suit his own case. It should not be for- gotten that spices and condiments are not beds, but tasty morsels intended to whet the appetite and stimulate the digestive organs. If the farmer desires to do this, he can readily manage it for himself, remembering that there is no food know even to manufacturers' which will put on flesh quicker and better than the grain and pulse he grows upon his farm. Farmers, it is to be hoped, will think over the question of calf rearing—that they will always retain the heifers, and as far as is their power, rear them for the dairy or breeding herd. Cows are far too few in England. The farmers alone can bring them back to their normal number.

COTTAGE GARDENING. GARDENING AND TRU Poort— trader this heading, the Gardener's Chronicle has a leader, in which it makes allu- sion to the all-absorbing topic—the over-crowding of the masses in our large towns—and suggests the following as remedial measures:—" If anything is to be done, in the first place we must endeavour to check this constant migration,. and in the second place to re-attract many of the crowded, and starving denizens of our large towns back into rural life and happiness," The allurements offered by the Chronicle are the breaking up of large farms into small holdings, and fields into gardens." Whether the bait would be suffi- ciently tempting to restrain the one and entice the other we are not prepared to say. We, however, should like to see every working man in possession of as much land, attached to his house or as garden plot, as he and his family could attend to. We do not mean possession on the levelling system, but at a reasonable rent. The possession of a garden is calculated to have a beneficial influence on their social and moral welfare. The man who attends well to his garden is usually a sober man, and he must necessarily be indus- trious. In the garden there is always some light employ- ment for the boys, who would be otherwise idle or engaged in mischief. Owners of land near towns and villages should emulate Lord Carrington and one or two others. His lord- ship allots land to all conaws on his estate near the town of High Wycombe, for a number of years (we think four), or, in other words, the land is re-let every few years, and those who may not have done justice to their plot will have it taken from them. The tenant is at libetty to give his ground up at any time, the four years net being binding upon him, and the option of depriving him of it at a fixed time must be an advantage to the other tenants; for the neg- lected plot would soon be a source of mischief to these adjoining by propagating weeds, whose seeds are readily disseminated by the wind over a much greater area than one would imagine, and ultimatejy require much labour to eradicate. Residents in towns, and those engaged in sedentary occupation make better gardeners than those who have always been employed on the land, and for that reason they ought to be encouraged. Land let in this way should realise as much more rent as when let for or- dinary farming, and the system of cultivation secures such results that those produced after the erasures of a plough are mere phantoms in comparison. To set apart land for the cultivation of fruit and vegetables means more employment. Some of the market gardeners in the neighbourhood of Lon- don employ over one man to the acre, and his pay will be from 18s. to 21s. per week, a sum that the nearest farmers Gannet afford. We fear the want of small holdings and plots is not so much felt as the absence of fixity of tenure. The planting of fruit trees and the establishing of per- manent crops involves much labour and expense for any one to attempt on a yearly tenancy. Those acquainted with gardening know too well the truth of the old proverb," He that plants pears plants for his heirs." The labour and ex- penditure demanded to produce temporary crops is not re- turned within the limits of a twelve month. A man trench- him and manuring a piece of ground should continue to reap the benefit of it for four years. Uncertainty of tenure must stand sponsor for bad gardening as well as bad farm- ing. Does any one believe for a moment that any man in I taking a farm from year to year makes it produce half of , what it might? Business men do not spend sums of money I to improve or repair premises that do not belong to them, and which in twelve months they may be told to quit. We presume that those engaged in tilling the soil are not less sagacious, and are to be excused for doing as little as they can to the soil. In conclusion, we would state (though foreign to cottage gardening) that any farmer who has his land for a term need not hesitate to combine fruit and vege- table cultivation with the production of milk and butter; the one assists the other, and both will assist the farmer. Tax FRONT GARDEN.—If any ground in the beds or border remains unmoved, it should be either dug or forked forthwith, so that the weather may act upon it and prepare it for the reception of the plants, and whatever their nature may be they will prove how they appreciate friable, sweet soil. Many bulbous plants are making their appearance above ground, but where the position of the most backward ones is not indicated by a label or stick, disturbing the ground will be a dangerous proceeding, and had better be delayed till such time that they are all visible. Bulbs, like other plants, have sundry enemies, for no sooner is that harbinger of spring, the snowdrop, above ground, than it is assailed by birds, and the mice are always diligent in search of the roots of these as well as other bulbs. Some of our fresh-planted tulips haye become their victims; though planted din. deep, their whereabouts had been so accurately hit upon that every hole was as perpendicular and directly over each bulb as if they had had a plummet in use. To destroy them, in addition to trapping, place a few scraps of , bloaters or a red herring somewhere near the spot. This will attract cats in their nocturnal perambulations, and if I the mice have been about they will smell them also and lay in wait for them. THE WINDOW.—The soil most suitable for a fern case is a mixture of peat and loam, in proportion of two of the former to one of the latter, with about one-eighth of the' whole of coarse silver sand. The best substitute for peat is half-decayed oak leaves, and pieces of sandstone, broken fine, will serve instead of sand. Some of the most delicate rooting ones should have nothing but peat and sand. The New Year will soon bring round the season for potting various plants, and the cottager should make preparations by collecting at various times nice pieces of turf, also leaves or leaf mould. All Boil intended for potting should now have some boards placed over them to throw off the rain, or it will be unfit for use when wanted. The medical profession are now ordering Cadbury's Cocoa Essence in thousands of cases, because it contains more nutri- tious and flesh-fe rming elements than any other beverage and is preferable to the thick starchy cocoa ordinarily sold. When you talk for Cadbury's Cocoa Essence be sure that you get it, as shopkeepers often push imitations for the sake of extra Prouts. Makers to the Queen. Faris Depot, 90, Faubourg Bt. Efonore.—Adrt. Turner, the painter, was a ready wit. Once at it dinner of artists and literary men a minor poet, by way of being facetious, proposed as a toast, "The health of the painters and glaziers of Great Britain." The toast was drunk, and Turner. after returning thanks for it, proposed "The health of the British paper•stainers." The laugh was loud against the poet. FUT YOURSELF IN ars PLACE.—" Did you ever hear anything like that ?" said a robin to a blackbird, as they were picking up crumbs on the ledge of a window where a captive thrush was wailing out its melancholy notes. "I shouldn't have known it for a thrush. • I'd hold my tongue if I couldn't sing better than that." " Wait awhile, friend," said the blackbird, "till you are caught and caged, and see what sort of a song you'll give us then. I'm very glad he's, able to sing at all, poor fellow; there are very few of us that would have spirit enough left for it, in his place, I fancy." KAI'S Comeottnn, for Couzhs and Colds, is equally service able for Horses and Cattle. Bold everywhe-e.—Adst.

what he was about. THE SEASON.-11 correspondent writes to a contemporary: —We have had a long spell of open weather, and advantage has been taken of it to keep the plough very active. . I hear compluints of the close weather having been inlarious to the preservation of potatoes which were dug in the showery weather that prevailed in the early part of the lifting time, and some of the tubers have suffered very much from the rot. Where they were dug up and covered without rain reaching them they are keeping very welt. Some farmers who are large growers, and were lucky enough to get their potatoes " hoggea" without rain, assure me they never knew them freer from disease at this time of the year. Wheat root generally is looking well if it has not shot too for- ward. There is much manure out_aspon the meadow land unspread. The good quality of last season's hay crop has so far done well for the farmer, and will to some extent make up for the deficiency in height. The animals eat it closer, and they are in better condition than usual at this time of the year. A correspondent from the dairying dis- tricts of North Lancashire informs sue that he has not known cattle eat up their hay so close for many years past. Instead of a considerable proportion of the foddering being left in the "boost," as was the rule during the wet seasons,i they eat some of the seeds as well. He has only discovered one or two instances of ergot, and has not heard of a single case of abortion amongst the cattle in his district. In his opinion, it is many years since farm stock was in such good condition for the time of the year. I have a favourable re- port of the quality of horses to be shown at the great horse fair at Preston, and this is 411 the snore satisfactory when we consider the number of buyers who now scour the Fylde district after horses. I find a better tone of feeling amongst farmers generally than for many years past, and it seems that we may at last look with confidence to a more hopeful future. It is to be feared, however, that foreign competi- tion will keep the home farmers on the alert for years to come. TNE FIRST OF ENGLAND'S GRRAT BREEDERS.—The year 1780 is usually considered to mark the beginning of a new era in the history of Shorthorns. At this period, as it would seem, a fresh impetus was given, and a new interest added, to the pursuit of breeding these alreaiy famous cat- tle. Many causes, no doubt, contributed to this, some of which are more or lees obscure. The country was advancing in prosperity, and population was increasing; Shorthorn interests, previously more or less scattered, were becoming numerous and important enough to command a sort of sys- tematic unity and recognition. The celebrated Robert Bakesvell, of Dishley, in his management of Leicester sheep, had reduced the art of breeding to a system in which the results coald.be predicted with moderate certainty, and his genius was attracting many followers and admirers. His principles, so far as he allowed them to be known, were ap- plied not to sheep only, but to horses and cattle, and in each case with marked 'success. It was evident that man had secured the secret of moulding and improving domestic animals almost at will, as a potter moulds his clay. They improved visibly in each successive generation, until, in a comparatively short space of time, animal forms were built up possessing such beauty, symmetry, and general excel- lence, that they have not 'easily been surpassed in more modern times. Bakewell's system was the creation of his own genius, and differed widely from the usual practice of English stock-breeders of his day. He dissected some of the carcases of his cattle and sheep, minutely examined the flesh, bones, and sinews, and so obtained a sound and prac- tical knowledge of animal physiology. He put his anatomi- cal specimens in pickle, and afterwards hung them up in his hall for subsequent reference. From this scientific in- vestigation he deduced a system of laws of animal nutri- tion and economy at once sound, accurate, and practical. His method in breeding was to select animals, wherever he could find them, of the best blood, and possessing as nearly as possible the form he needed for the objects he had in view; he then bred them strictly in their own family alone, only going out of it when he found specimens elsewhere which he considered would still further improve his stock. His judgment was sound, clear, accurate, and penetrating ; and he was at once a profound scholar and master of the principles which, far more than any other man, he had • studied and formulated into a system. In the strictest sense of the word he was a man of "genius ;" and more than to any other man, England owes to him the marvel- lous improvements in her cattle and sheep which have been made in the past hundred years.—From Cassel l's "Dairy- Farming," for January. MOLES.—In the course of my lecturing tours, I sometimes find myself at Hull, and on one occasion met several large landowners at dinner. The conversation turned on moles and their iniquitous depredations. Of course I took up the cudgel for the mole, and with a fair amount of success. Someone mentioned that within a few miles there was a well-known field which had once swarmed with moles, and was notable for the steady crops which it produced an- nually. It had nassed into the hands of another proprietor, who had the moles destroyed, and the field was ever after- wards as barren as it had been prolific. I need not say that at the first opportunity I visited the field in question, and a more hopelessly ragged and forlorn piece of ground can hardly be imagined. Finding that there was a resident far- mer who knew all the circurnstances,and who never allowed moles to be killed on his own land, I lost no time in making his acquaintance. He was very kind in giving the requisite information, which was so valuable that I asked him to put it on paper for the benefit of the British farmer. So I here present it to the reader t—" North Ferriby, September 7, 1882.—Dear Sir,—l have much pleasure in writing what I know of the uses of the mole, and the loss sustained by killing it. .To kill moles is to leave the corn and turnip crop, especially upon light soils, such as sand and deep- soiled wold land, to the ravages of the wire-worm, the grub (viz., the cockchafer larva), and other insects. I have farmed and still farm from 1,000 to 1,500 acres of land in different parishes, and have noticed that when you kill and try to exterminate moles, rooks, sparrows, &a., you have pr6portionate destruction from the creatures which they feed upon. An old mole-catcher once came to me and asked if I would have the moles killed on my land. I said to him, 'No; it I had no moles I should have no crops.' He replied, Sir, you axe the first I have heard say that, but you are right.' He then Went on to say, ' I once killed for a gentle- man who had a field with a large hill in it. The soil was sandy and full of moles, and:yet it used to grow nice crops. I killed the moles and it never grew anything to speak of afterwards. The wireworm, grub, &c., used to eat the roots %of everything that was sown, and the young plants died off.'

Mr. Langbane held an inquest upon the bc;cly of Emily Novell, an unfeetuetate, who WAS found dead at -7, Artillery- square, VVestrninetere on December 30th, at half-part one o'clock in the morning. The jury found a verdict of " Wilful murder "against some person or persons unkewn. Mr. Richard Bredin, a Liverpool corn mierchant, and also, a justice of the peace for the borough of Bootle, was on Tuesday committed for trial by the Liverpool stipendiary magistrate on a charge of wrongfully appropriating the pro- ceeds of a quantity of Indian corn purchased for Messrs. Sever and Tunnicliffe. The defendant was admitted to bai. SENTENCE CO' DElTH.—Sestence of death was yesterday passed at the Central Criminal Court, London, upon Henry Job Billing, stevedore, who was found guilty of the murder of his wife, by shooting her, at Plaistow, on the let De- cember last. The jury recommended the prisoner to mercy on account of the provocation he had received from his wife. THE EXPLOSION AT A PAPER MILL.—The inquest on three of the victims of the boiler explosion at Messrs. Spicers' paper mills, near Godalming, was concluded at Guildford on Monday. The jury found that the accident was caused by the pipe leading to the safety valve being plugged, and recommended that such boilers should be vs- tematicallv inspected after charging. At Nottingham, on Tuesday, Mr. W. H. Trumon, a wine and spirit merchant, was summoned by the postmaster for cutting telegraph wires attached to a chimney stack on the roof of his premises. The defendant pleaded that the recent gales had interfered with the chimney stack to the danger of the public walking in the street, and for that reason he cut the wires. He was tined £5 and costs. AGRICULTURISTS AND THE tiOVERNMENT.—At a meeting of agriculturists, held at Norwich on Saturday, a resolution was passed demanding the prohibition of the importation of live stock from places abroad where foot and mouth disease is known to exist, and the withdrawal of the present restric- tions on the removal of live stock in England till effect is given to the resolution of Parliament of July last. Mr. Asher, Solicitor-General for Scotland, was present on Saturday night at a meeting of the Elgin Burghs Liberal Association, and spoke on the present state of political affairs. With regard to the Corrupt Practices Bill, he said it was necessary that such associations as those should be organised everywhere. He also referred to the state of Ire- land, and commended the present Government for the man- ner it had dealt with Ireland. SUPPOSED MURDER.—A married woman named Lilly Easedale, or Smart, was on Saturday morning found lying dead beside her husband, at 21, Pleasance, Edinburgh. Her face was covered with bruises, end on each side of her eyes was a deep stab. Her husband, John Smart, was appre- hended on a charge of suspected murder. Some time ago a considerable property was left him, and since then he has not followed his ordinary occupatien as a plumber. I THE FLYING SCOTCHMIN ON FIRE.—As this train was psssing Bedford on Saturday afternoon, George Ord, a post- man, observed that a second class compartment was on tire. He immediately reported the circumstance to the stationmaster, who telegraphed without delay to Smeafield,' the next station, where the train was pulled up. A plenti- ful supply of water being available the fire was quickly extinguished, and the Flying Scotchman proceeded on its way. SHOCKING ACCIDENTS—TWO shocking accidents were re- ported in Birmingham, on Tuesday morning. A boy, named Jordan, while in a swing boat, fell from the extreme end just as it had reached a great height, and sustained such severe injuries to the head that he is not expected to live. Another boy was watching the swing boats when he was struck by one of them a terrible blow on the head, and hurled a considerable distance. He, too, lies in a critical condition. AN Isomerous SWINDLE.—Some of the leading gentle- ' men in Leicestershire and Northamptonshire have just been the victims of an ingenious swindle. Several "swell " photographers giving false addresses in Nottingham called asking permission to photograph the gentlemen's residecces for artistic purposes. Consent being given various views Were taken, and subsequently orders got for private photea graphs of the family, dec., for which payment was made, and nothing sent in return. Are ECCENTRIC Wonarrorsa MASTER —John Owen, who until lately held the position of master of the Carnarvon Workhouse, is in custody charged with causing a number of incendiary fires in the island of Anglesey. The out- breaks have produced considerable uneasiness amongst farmers, several valuable stacks of produce having been destroyed. A reward was offered for the capture of the incendiary, but Owen anticipated arrest by giving himself up to the police. He is supposed to be of unsound mind. Gaoss CRUELTY.—A case of abominable cruelty came be- fore the Staffordshire magistrates on Saturday. A youth named Silvester, while employed in boiling turnips at a farm Pear Stafford, picked up a fox terrier and threw it into the boiler, where it struggled in frightful agony till dead. When taken out, the flesh dropped from off the animal's body. Silvester said he did it because his master had struck him.l He was sentenced to one month's hard labour, the ' bench expressing regret that they could not order him to be flogged. Tice GLOSSOP SUFFOCATION Casas.—The adjourned in- quest on the bodies of Richard Townend, Dorothy Stafford, and two daughters of the latter, who were anti mated in the house in which they lived, at Glossop, on the 29th Deem- her, was resumed on Tuesday. The evidence clearly indi- cated suffocation by coal gas, and a verdict to that effect was returned, the jury not attaching blame to anyone. Gas had found its way into the house from a service pipe in front of the house, which had been broken, it was thought, by the tipping ef a load of coal. THE MINERS' STRIKE.—A meeting of Yorkshire and North Derbyshire coalowners, held on Monday at Sheffield, declined to grant the interview requested on behalf of the miners, who are asking a 10 per cent advance in their wages. The proprietors, in conveying this intimation to the men, remarked that in view of the general depression of trade a reduction of wages appeared to them more necessary than an increase. The Yorkshire Miners' Association, Which also held a meeting. determined to renew their demand for the advance, and directed a vote to be taken at all the col- lieries with regard to their course of action in case the re- quest should be refused. DISAPPEARANCE OF A CURATE—The clerical world of Sheffield is ruffled, owing to the conduct of a curate. In March last one Of the city vicars obtained a ve,y superior man as a curate. He was good and rich, and had, accord- ing to himself, many friends among the ar stocracy. This good young man became engaged to a young lady who Was one of the flock over which he exercised sway as a deputy shepherd. Under these circumstances he announced that a ducal friend had offered him a wealthy living; but he allowed himself to be persuaded not to leave Sheffield. The time came for his being licensed to his curacy. The archbishop made the usual inquiries. The curate on this disappeared, and nothing has since been as- certained as to,his whereabouts. TILE STORE NEWINGTON MURDER.—Sir John Hum- phreys, the Coroner for East Middlesex, on Monday, resumed his inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of John B. Tower, underwriters' clerk, whose body was found is a reservoir at Stoae-Newington, on the previous Wednesday. After the evidence of several witnesses had been taken, the Coroner said there was no doubt that the deceased bad been murdered. The most likely theory was that be was attacked on the vacant ground and that he broke through the hedge and ran up the embankment to escape, but was pulled back by someone. Notwithstanding this, the deceased had apparently reached the top before he was thrown down and strangled. The jury returned a verdict of "Wilful murder" against some person or persons unknown. THE FATAL TRAMCAR ACCIDENT AT FEMEERTON.—The Government inquiry into the tramcar accident at Pember- ton, which resulted in the death of Mr. T. W. Barker, county coroner, was concluded on Tuesday. A number of experi- ments were made by Major-General Hutchinson in order to test the truth of the driver's statement that his engine ran away after he jumped off to save a child, and that he could not overtake it. The driver of the engine drawing the car which was run into. whe had been under medical treatment, said be was only driving for 15 days before the accident. When he saw the runaway engine approaching he took off the brake and put on steam in order to move forward, sad so lessen the expected shock, but the collision took place before he could move the engine. He afterwards ran after the retreating engine and shut off steam, or it would have dashed into a second tramcar. During his experience as a driver his engine was not controlled by "governors," which had been broken. The Inspector did not call the tramway manager or officials, whose evidence he thought might be reserved until the adjourned inquest. A JOURNALIST IN BEGGAR'S DISGUISE.—Mr. Maclauch- lan, who is understood to be a member of the staff on a Lon- don evening paper, has come sadly to grief in an attempt to imitate the once famous "amateur casual." It occirred to Mr. Maclauchlan and his employer that an article might be written on "the profits of begging in London," and forth- with the reporter was "got up " in costume and turned out into the streets in the character of a professional beggar. Another member of the staff, with a proper sonse of the fit- ness of things, carefully tore Mr. Maclauchian's clothes in several places. But once in the streets, it soon appeared that Mr. Maclauchlan was a very poor beggar indeed. In- stead of exhibitlng any of the adroitness with which the professional beggar contrives to elude the police, he man- aged to encounter one particular policeman several times; and on being challenged, at last, had nothing better to say for himself than that he was "a journalist." The officer "at once arrested him," as though he had said he was a dynamitard, and the amateur found that among the "profits" of begging must be reckoned a night in the .lock-up, MEDICINES, ELASTIC STOCKINGS, CHEMICALS, AC.. by Parcel Poet. under tile. 3&—Tay Bros., etockport.—eldea,

THRNATENING A RAN& MANAGER:A telegram from Tip' perary states that a notice was posted on one of the wialnWO of the Munster Batik, in the centre of the town, on Monde'', warning the manager, Mr. Samuel Heuston, J.P., that if he did not mend his harsh manners as land agent the aveng3r would be pot on his path, and the death that was given tt" Carey would be given him. TREYFLYAN ON TNE PODISCOMING IRISH DEGISLA' lON.—In reply to a deputation which waited upon him at Dublin Castle, on Tuesday, Mr. Trevelyan promised that the Governmeat would introduce a bill amending the Irish Pharmacy Act. The Government, he further remarked, were pledged to introduce two Irish measures next session, one of which was the Irish Sunday Closing Bill, which would probably meet with great opposition. Mn; DAY= ON PAYMENT Or MEMBERS OF PARMA' MENT.—Mr. Michael Devitt arrived in Limerick, on Tues- day, er;route for London. Previous to his departure a de' putation from the Limerick branch of the National Leagne waited on Mr. Davitt, who in reply to questions put to hitt by indlYidual members, said that after the next general election it would be necessary that the Irish people should pay their representatives in the Howe of Commons. MINERS STRIKE 11RELA-ND.—The miners; 400 in nurn- ber, at the Slieveardagh Colliery, Kilkenny, reaently struck against a reduction of wages. The agent of the Mining Company of Ireland, the owners, informed the men that if they did not resume work operations wonle.‘ be pernaanentli discontinued. This prospect failed to make the colliers yield, and now, it is stated, the pumps, whica- had to be constantly at work to prevent flooding, have beea stopped. Mn. HEALY AND THE ULSTER DANDLORD3.—Mr. Maly/ M.P., on Wednesday, attended a meeting of the National League in Dublin, and moved a resolution condemning "the reckless and criminal " conduct of Ulster landlords in porting Orange labourers from distant towns to assail the liberty of public meeting. The hon. gentleman asserted that the result of Sir Stafford Northcote's late visit to ~iflater had been to excite the Nationalists to opposition, and now 3 Whig Solicitor-General was being returned unopposed for County Derry. RESIGNATION OF Mn. DALY, M.P —Mr. John Daly, the senior member for Cork city, issued on Monday his valedie' tory address, in which he states that pressure of bnsiness , will prevent him from giving that attention to Parliamew tary duties which is required, and as Parliament is within month of assemblage he does not wish to further delay the resignation of his seat. Commandatore Delany, the recentlf defeated candidate for the mayoralty, is spoken of as a 'aro* bable candidate. It was pretty generally believed that Alderman Daly would not seek re-election, but kis resigns' tion was quite unlooked for. ALLEGED CONFESSION OF O'DONNELL—United .TrEICACI of Which Mr. William O'Brien, member for Mallow, 13 editor, and Mr. Parnell, proprietor' contains an account of the tragedy on board the Melrose Cistle, stated to be fron3 the pen of a gentleman who received the statement from I O'Donnell. It was not to be told so long as a shadow of chance remained to save O'Donnell from the gallows. A 3. cording to this 'statement O'Donnell did deliberately kill ) Carey, and because he was James Carey. "There was no, struggle, Carey made no attack on O'Donnell, and O'Donflell. never pet up a plea of self-defence. Had Judge Denman permitted him to speak before pronouncing sentesa3 O'Donnell would then have told the whole truth, and vill‘ dicated himself. O'Donnell did not know Carey cn the voyage from England to the Cape. He was not a member of any society; he could not read or write, but he knew of Carey. He had no picion, however, that the man with whom he played cattle and thank an occasional glass of beer was this monster. He, however, recognised him by a woodcut which he saw at Capetown, and instantly resolved to kill Carey, and on the, impulse of the moment he said to Cubbitt, I'll kill hint - From the moment he formed his purpose he never wavered in it. O'Donnell determined to ship with him to Port Elizabeth, go with him to the farm Oarey had told him he was going to take, and then, without concealment of pur- pose or motive, show that there was no spot on which an Irish informer would be safe. Finding himself sudden'," alone with Carey and his travelling companion, he cauld not resist the desire to kill him at once. Carey, with light' fling quickness, perceived his danger, and the two me°, glowered at each other. Carey hissed, Do you know me? O'Donnell hissed back, I do; you are Carey the informer ; to hell with you.' The bullet sped with the words, and the deed was done. Carey clutched his own revolver, hut it was too late. O'Donnell discharged a second shot and a third to make sure of his work, and Carey rolled to the deck."

The Very Rev. B. M. Cowie (late Dean of Mancheeter) wry on Thursday formally installed as Dean of Exeter. At the conclusion of the ceremony a" reception" took place at the Bishop's Palace, at which most of the leading resi- dents of the county were present. SHOCX.ING DISCOVERY. The Birmingham parochial authorities on Wednesday found in the house of a pauper, named Owen, at Aston, the corpse of his sister, who died at Islington 20 years ago. The body was enclosed, coffined, in a large box, and Owen's story is that, baying no money to bury his sister when she died, he had kept the corpse ever since in the room which he occupied. POLITICS AND SPlTE—Speaking at Loughborough, on Wednesday evening, Lord John Manners, M.P., stated that there had never been a Government which had promised so much and performed so little as the present Administration, and that in now pushing on the subject of reform the ob- ject of the Government was solely to hide from the people, when a general election should come, their miedoings and mistakes. A FATAL SHOT—At Haslington, Crewe, on Wednesday night, Jaohn Tomkinson, a farm servantewas shot dead while looking down the barrel of a gun which ;vas in the hands of a fellow-servant. The gun had been tanen in a haphazard manner freen a rack, and it appears to have been only by accident that Tomkinson did not kill somebody else, for he is s eid to have "playfully pointed" the weapon at two of his companions before performing the silly freak which cost him his life. DESTRUCTIV`Y Firm—The lace factory of Messrs. Austin and Sons, at Low Eaton, near Nottingham, was destroyed by fire early en Wednesday morning. Efforts were made to check the flames with appliances at hand, but proved fruit- less, and before aseistance could be procured from Notting- ham and Derby the factory was gutted. Seventy lace-making machines were destroyed, and the total damage is estimated at £lOO,OOO. The neighbouring houses were with difficulty prevented from being destroyed. The cause of the fire is unknown. FRIENDLY SOCIETIES' GRIEVANCES:—A deputation re- presenting friendly societies ,vaited upon the Chancellor of the Exchequer on Thursday to ask for relief from the trouble and inconvenience arising from the practice in refer- ence to income tax. By the Act of Parliament friendly societies are exempt from the tax, but the existing custom is to charge them and compel them, at the cost of great trouble and annoyance, to apply for a return of the pay-- ment. The interview was private, but it is understood that Mr. Childers expressed his desire to assist the societies in the matter, and promised that the subject should receive his careful attention. SINGULAR ACTION FOIL FALSE IMPRISONMENT.—On. Thursday, an action for false imprisonment and malicious prosecution was brought in the Court of the Lord hlayor of London against the Great Eastern Railway Company by a Mr. Langford and wife, who were arrested at a railway station by detectivee, taken to the superintendent's office, charged with loitering and stealing a parcel, and then taken through the streets to a police stition. They were locked up all night, and on the following day the magistrate dis- charged them owing to the evidence against them being insufficient. The jury awarded £5O damages to Mr. Lange ford, and £75 to his wife. DRIVEN TO MURDER AND SUICIDE:A CASS of supposed murder and suicide was investigated by the coroner for Cam- berwell, London, on Thursday. On the 16th December a woman, named Mitchell, aged 41, left her husband, an iron- founder, living at 126, Alderminster-road, Bermondsey, taking the youngest of her five children, aged two years. The body of the child was found in the Grand Surrey Canal, last week, with a handkerchief tied around the neck. On Sunday the body of the woman was found in the same canal. The evidence showed that the husband and wife lived unhappily, and that she had previously threatened to commit suicide. The jury returned a verdict ,of " Suicide whilst of unsound mind." ALLEGED ATTEMPTED MURDERS NEAR BATH—On Tuesday night, at Corston village, near Bath, a young man of respeetable position, named Henry Lock Upham, attempted, it is alleged, to murder his father and brother by attacking them with a razor. It is stated that upon Upham ' returning from a walk his father admitted him, and.the former immediately cut his throat. A struggle followed, and the father who is 50 and had lost much blood, was just falling exhausted, when another son arrived and beat down the assailant, who, however, succeeded in inflicting a throat wound upon him also. Both the injured men lie in a serious condition, and Henry Upham has been arrested. He is stated to be suffering from overstudy. MR. SAMUEL SMITH, M.P., ON COMMUNISTIC TEACHING —Mr. Samuel Smith, M.P., took the occasion of a meeting of the Liverpool Penny Ranks Association, on Thursday, to utter some words of warning against the Communistic teaching of the present time. He said some of the thinking part of the people seemed to be impressed by the schemes for the plunder of the landlords ; but in a short time they would find that such schemes would not stop short at land- lords, but weuld be taught as openly against all who pos- sessed other forms of property. He felt that in increasing the number of the saying class they were building up bul- warks against the day of battle, which was sure to come, when the thriftless, improvident, anarchial, and atheistical , classes should band themselves together and do their best to reduce the country to a general dead level of ruin and devastation. ENGLISH PATENTS. The following patents amongst others, published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal, were sealed during the week ending January sth, 1884:— Charles Anthony Burghardt, of Manchester, for improve- ments in apparatus for the collection and condensation of 'vapours evolved in the manufacture of india-rubber goods; 'Thomas Fox, of Sheffield, improvements in the manufacture lof plain and ornamental felloes or tyres; Joseph Woodcock, Huddersfield, and James Coulter, Batley, im- provements in the construction of vessels employed for dyeing, milling, scouring, washing, and brewing purposes; Richard Loiagden Hattersley and James Hill, Keighley, im- provements in looms for weaving; Thomas Hirst, Man- chester, improvements in or applicable to smallware looms, partly applicable to other looms; Thomas Fletcher, of War- rington, improvements in or applicable to gas burners for , boiling, grilling, toasting, and similar uses; Samuel Edwards, of Salford, improvements in chaff-cutters.— List supplied by Mr. George Davies, CE., Fel. Inst., Patent Solicitor, 4, St. Ann's-square, Manchester. EXTRAORDINARY CASE OF TRANCE.—A singular circum- stance of the inability øf medical men to distinguish be- tween a trance and actual death has just occurred at Leeds. Emma Whittaker, 16 years old, has for a long time been suffering from consumption, and the disease, it was believed, terminated fatally on Thursday last. She apparently breathed her last early in the afternoon, and the body was Accordingly washed and laid out in the usual manner. An. undertaker was called in and took the measurement for the coffin, and other preparations for the funeral were in course. Late at night the mother and a neighbour were sitting in the kitchen, when they were startled by hearing a noise up- stairs, followed by a cry of "mother." Much startled they went to ascertain what it all meant, when they found the poor girl still wrapped in her grave clothes, standing on the top of the stairs complaining that she was very cold. She was put to bed and medical aid summoned. She soon be- came quite rational, though, of coarse, she has not been told how far the arrangements had progressed towards her burial. This sine'ular case of trance is exciting a good deal of interest both among medical men and the public generally.

On reaching what is known as Friarage Bridge, the dog suddenly sprang into the water and brought to the surface a dead bodi, which proved to be that of the missing young woman. ARMENIAN CIIRISTIANS.—The Armenians are Christi of a pronounced type, with a native alphabet, and a canon containing several books pronounced apocryphal by the Western Church. Their ritual is more Greek than Latino and their s'stem of monasteries approximates to that of the Tibetan Buddhists. Though at times the Armenians 113_11 been independent, and even powerful, their political rale tions have been usually with Persia, which at present divides the sovereignty over them with Turkey and Bugle' There is also a colony of Armenians in Persia, near IsPe' han, many in India, thousands in Constantinople, and 00 the .1 Island of St. Lazarus, in Venice' there is an important settlement of Armenian monks, with a monastery rich ill published and unpublished manuscripts. The number European Russia is under 40,000. In Armenia they ate agriculturists; in Persia, &c., they are merchants; and ill , India they divide with the Jews and Parsees the almost erY tire monopoly of banking and money-lending. Before he' 1 coming Christians the Armenians were fire-worshippers, lil° the ancient Persians and the modern ° Parsee& some are, Nestorians—that schism having spread widely amon,; 'them in the eighth or ninth centuries—and a few are Boras', Catholics, Gregorians, and Protestants. There are patiefi archs over all these sections of the Armenians, the he'; patriarch being only recognised by the orthodox, who nul. ber about 4,000,000. Some of the oldest works on th` Christian doctrines are in the Armenian language, and 000 of the oldest known translations of the Scriptures is in °1....0 same tongue, which is one of the oldest of the Aryan tii.'"" —" The Peoples of the World" for January. MR. GLADSTONE ON BRITISH FARMING.—Mr. Gladstone was present on Wednesday night at the annual rent audit at flawarden, and spoke on the position and prospects a British farming. After expressing fhe hope that agricultural prospects would brighten, he referred to the great openings afforded to farmers by the milk trade, and proceeded to urge greater attention to the large cultivation of fruit and eggs, and the more extended rearing of poultry. He said they might depend upon it that the capacity of the human stomach was enormous, and no consumer did more justice to the producer e of food than the consumer born and bred in this country. With regard to the increased prices now I charged for butter, he understood that these had brought about a large development of the jam trade. The supplies of jam came, mainly, from America and the Continent, but if British butter was to be undersold by jam, he would rather see It undersold by British than by foreign jam, especially as our climate was not more unfavourable than that of other countries, and we had larger supplies of cheap sugar. In conclusion, Mr. Gladstone referred to the pros- pective improvement in the communication by the Mersey tunnel and the local railway projects. THE SOLICITOR-GENERAL AT GATESHBAD.—Sir F. Hers- chell on Thursday visited Gateshead, and opened a new building erected to accommodate the local Liberal Associa- tion. In his address the Solicitor-General depicted the utility of organisation, no matter in what cause it was per- formed. He denied that there was any important difference of opinion existing within the Liberal party. They had candid friends amongst them, but he was content to let each member of the party state his points of divergence and then see wlether they did not lead to a common end. He con- sidered that no Liberal ought to break loose from the party until he had arrived at the 1 conscientious conclusion that the Government which that party supported ought in the interest of the country to be replaced by another. Speaking at a public meeting in the evening, Sir F. Herschell said he could quite reconcile his utterances of a year ago in regard to Egypt with the later policy of the Government. There Was no doubt that a great improvement had taken place in the condition of the fellaheen since European control was established. The Government were confronted with the Malide who was an utter barbarian, occupying a most in- accessible, arid, and difficult district. If the Soudan were reconquered it would have to be occupied permanently by an immense force, far beyond the power of Egypt to main- tain, and he thought the course her Majesty's advisers had taken was the wisest within their choice. On the subject of reform he had no doubt as to the genuineness of the de- mand for an extended franchise, which, as usual, the Tories ; were ascribing to the wirepullers. A resolution of confi- dence in the Government was unanimously adopted. SOLVED AT LAST !—What Mr. Bradlaugh was always doing at the "bar" of the House.—Drinking CAMMACK'S SODA WATER.—. 4 dot.
