Bach action and 'concurrence will be held in the higtuset esteem by this cora- Inittee, 3.3 d tise sulacribers generally, and it is hoped that as l'jas beoefits arising from the construction of the Canal will be liberally distributed over the whole district, the corporate 'Bodies genera' wtay see their way to give eundertaking '3l.lbatantial sumsart in some loran. I itua, dear Air. Mayor, Yours faithfully. DANIEL AD/IE6CE. Chairman of the Provi- biOtal Committee." Councillor Dr. MAcpn strongly recommended that the course the Mayor haft hinted at should be followed, especially as the Town Clerk and Mr. Lengdin had been aPPOiettedeo draw up a report. He thorght it would be : only the ordinary exercise of judicious economy if they Were to refrain Irons pledging theanselves in any way what- ever to subscribe to the carrying out of the scheme so far as itS expensee were concerned until they-knew whether they as a town were to be met fin a proper epirit. He hoped they • Would not think for one moment that he meant to .suggest there would be anything wrong; in Lae., he was glad to take that opportunity of saying that he knew officially there was not Itkely to be anything wrong—certainly net as regarded the landowners in the neighbourhood. Alderman Heassfets expressed the opinion that it was very undesirable to subscribe to any undertaking of that sort. Councillor CA.EDWELL asked if the Council could authorize the amount themselves, or would they have to appeal to the ratepayers at large? The MAYOR: We shall have to appeal to the ratepayers, certainly. Councillor CALDWELL thought they would have to be 'careful iu the matter, and they should not venture on a decision without further consideration. The MAYOR: There need be no anxiety on that score. 'Ate letter was subsequently referred to the General Pur- Poses Committee. THE PHOPOSED RESTRICTION OF FAIRS!. The MAYOR: I have an interesting communication from our old friend, Mr. Beament, the first Mayor of \Varrirsgton, and to whom we are mainly indebted for the incorporation of the borough. It IS a letter with reference to the holding of Warrington fairs and I read it with very great pleasure. hope it will find its way not only into the newspapers, but also into our large year-book. The letter is as follows: "Os ford Hall, Warrington, January 2nd, 1884.—Dear Mr. IraYer.--it has occurred to use to send you an ace amt of the charters of which I spoke to you respecting the Warrington fairs. I hope you will not think this an intrusion, or, if you do, you will account it as one of the troubles which the chief magistrate of this borough haste pay for, being the first marl of 41,000 persons. The first of these charters whieh was ob- tained for this borough is more than GOO years old. 1555 lug been granted by King Henry IU, 20th October (30th Henry III.), 1254, and by it the King granted permission to his faittilm and beloved William Butylier to have a yearly fair of three days, at his manor of Warrington. namely, on the eve, the day, and the morrow of the Translation of St. Thomas the Marty r, at that time a saint In the very zenith of hispopularity, and whose translation was held on the Bth of July, until the alts ration of the style in the last century, when the people who believed there was virtue in the old day, insisted on adhering to the original day, and the fair has ever Mace begun on the 18th July. The next charter is dated Nov. 7. in the 10th Edward 1., 1282. It is also more than 600 years old, and by it the king granted to his faithful and.Voved William Butyaer to keep a weekly market on Friday, and a Yearly fair at his manor of Warrington for eight days, namely, on the eve, the day, and the morrow of St. Andrew the Apostle and five following days, and this fair still continues to be kept Oil St. Andrew's Day, the 30th November. The next and only remaining charter bears date May 26, in the 13th Ed. 1., 1255, and by it the king grants to his beloved and faithful William Butyller to hold a weekly market on Wednesday at Ms manor of Warrington and also to hold a yearly fair of eignt days; these, that is 'to say on the eve, the day, and the mor- row of the Translation of St. Thomas the Martyr, and aye following days. This charter. except granting a weekly market on Wednesday. is little more than an enlargement of the summer fair from three days to eight. There is no char- ter for the weekly market on Saturday, and that was probably a market by prescrip ion, and before a charter, while the Friday's market was found to be unneces ary, ana was, there- fore, never held. My design however, Air. Mayor, in bringing these details before you, is en ex proas my earnest hope, a hope Mug entertained, that the Town Council might be induced to shorten the duration of two fairs ist July sod November to three da a each. When these Salts originated, so many cm- Ludes ago, there was a necessity tor having a cootnuation of eight days; our local tradesmen had not suffi,deot capaal to lay in a sufficient stock of articles ef clothing and of household use, and the inaoufaciurers from York-hire and the West of Bug and, from Wales and Ireland resorted to wares of all sorts, such as the neighbourhood required. In these days the male were founderous and bad, public conveyances were unknown, highwaymen were abroad, and the policeman was unknown. It was safer for the great manufacturers to seek the customer than for the latter to ven- ture Irons home to supply himself, and more especially was this the case with the rustle population, who had neither money nor time to spare for it. The resort ef the great manufac- turers, or indeed of any large manufacturers, to our fairs has long been a thing of the past; a new state of things requires new conditions to meet it. No place is better or more numerously supplied with good shop. and fair tradesmen than Wartmgton—(iear, hear)—ad nobody need wait for the fairs to supply whatever he wants. He will find cutlery, hardware, woollen. and cotton goods at home at all times. This beiog so. I venture very respectfully to ask your Worship te bring under the notice of the Council the unnecessarily long con- Lb:mantas of the two annual fairs. These fairs bring to the town a large class of exhibitions, many of which are of the " Baraurn " kind, consisting of mermaids, dead and stuffed, and of seals that talk, and of low practitioners ot legerdemain, Which Shakespeare In " The Tempest" makes Trineule ray, that if he had but Caliban in England, there is not a holiday fool there but would give a piece of silver to see hlrn. Curl sity attroats numbers who like to be deceived, and one of the most learned of our monerns, Lord Stowell. the brother of Lord Eldon, set an example in paying his sixpence ore shilling to scrawl:at was not worth seeing. My own im- Preesioa is that morals are not benefited by the indiscriminate throng the fairs draw into the lawn, while the schools are thinned by their music and uproar, and th.: frequenters of the hospital can bear witness to the number of accidents sustained there by young people, one of whom was under treatment there more than 12 months, owing to a hurt received from a swing boat. fain aware that some money is received from the tolls of the fairground, but the amount is small in conearison with the harm that is done. Bartholomew Fair" produced a inlet m money to the Corporation of London, but they did . net think the gain was sufficient reason fore iitinuing such an evil; an' I believe the good example set by the metropolis has been followed in many boroughs like your own —I have tte honour to be, dear Mr. Mayor, yours very faithfully, WILLIAM 'DEA:MONT. The Maxon (continuing) : Well, gentlemen, I think there is a great deal worthy of consideration in this letter. You see Mr. Beamont does not propose to maim a radical Change in the matter, he only proposes to modify, not abolish, and I venture to suggest that the proper way to deal with this—and the Town Clerk thinks it is—is to sub- rnit it to the Markets Committee. No doubt these gentle- men will deal with this letter in the respectful manner I submit it is entitled to be dealt with. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Jolts PIERPOINT asked if the Town Clerk could tell them whether they could reduce the number of days on which the fairs were held. The MAYOR: It is by charter. Councillor dons PIERPOINT : The cuestion is whether a charter would not stand in the absence of an Act of Parlia- ment to alter it. The TOWN CLERK: The Conceit can deal with it. • Councillor CALDWELL : I suppose it cannot be altered without the sanction of this Council ? The Tows CLERK Oh, no. COnLeillor CALD WELL : I hope I shall never live to see the day that it is altered. The Mayon: When a motion came before the Connell some time ago to abolish it entirely I was one who voted against it. But there is a great diffcreEce between abolishing it altogether anti redecing the period it should continue. I canaot help thinking if it was reduced to three days instead of eight it would be an advantage to us in many ways. However, it is for the Markets Committee to consider, and no doubt they will report their views, and the Council will then deal with it when the proper time arrives. No`..hin will be done without allowing you full opportunity of ex- , Preelsing your views meta it. Alderman HoLwEs had heard the letter read with great pleasure, but would refiain from expressing his views upon it until it again came before the Council. Conuesillor.Dr.Memetu was glad Mr.Beemont had not gone the leregth of wanting to abolieh the fairs altogether. (Rear, hear.) No doubt so far as the ,ques- lion of trade was concerned tee fair was no longer a necessity, as trade was carried on differently now to what it was in the reigns of the great ' men Mr. Beantont had neared, and none of whom showed such great interest in IVarringtnn as to give it the right to send a member to Parliament—which they by virtue of their own kingship might have dame, and very often did. Rat in the interests of those who were not traders—thoee who found pleasure and mirth on the occasions of the fair —4lle hoped the coaniaittee would deal very geutiy with any proposal to alter matters. Councillor Szerros said he bad listened with pleasure to the interesting letter from Mr. Bearnont, and he thorrght it e9ataiced very good suggestione, well worthy of consiciera-

tioa. Alderman CUANDLEY remarked that the subject was con- sidered by the Markets Committee some years ago, and they decided that the fair should be discontinued. Of course there was no necessity for fairs; it was only a question

whether or not they were a moral evil or whetb there were evil influences attending them. As to the, "- neteeetty for trading purposes, that had been exploded i,n no The question was decided by the Markets ' eg . joetemaittee that the I fairs should be discontinued, but wb It was brought be- fore the Council the Council negy.efefeed that opinion, and decided that the fairs should 'cie centinued as before. As fan as his own feelings we.'-eth etrd'agly advocated the con- tinuance of the fairs but be thieught the first question for the committee s'aouid be Whether or not they had an evil, immoral, or b ..eid tendency on the populace and youth of the town• r-.l"cat point woufel decide the principal Question. Tig.;.S.IAYOR: I weuld. remark, in order to save time, that Viers is nothing 'really before the Council for discussion. The only queselon is, shall it of shall it not be referred to the Markets 'Cionamittee. Afterwards we shall have op- portunities Iter discussing all these details. Councilleer r'LA.T.T quite agreed with the advantage that would am ue from referring it to the Markets Committee, but SOFZE gentlemen had expressed opinions on one side, and he (Councillor Platt) did not see why every other member of the Council should not express his opinion as well. He. thought Mr. Beament had given them very strong and rnwerful arguments why the fair should be limited to three days—(hear, hear)—and there was no doubt the time would 'nine with the spread of education and when people found more rational pleasures with some benefit to them that the fairs would be discontinued. At the same time he scarcely thought it would be advisable to discontinue them at present. The MANOR then put the motion that the letter be re- ferred to the Markets Committee, and it was carried. INTERNATIONAL HEALTH EXHIBITION AT LONDON. The MAYOE observed that an luternational Health Ex- hibition was about to take place in London, and if they could do anything to forward so good a movement he tholight they would be glad to do so. He did not see how they could do it themselves, but a letter which he had re- ceived on the subject might be referred to the Sanitary Com- mittee, in order to cave the trouble of discussing it at that ' meeting. He begged to move that it be referred to the Sanitary Committee. Councillor FRANCOMB seconded the motion. Alderman CHANDLEY did not want the letter reading, but would like to know the nature of its contents. The MAYOR said it was simply to the effect that they were establishing an exhibition—similar perhaps to the Fisheries Exhibition—for the exhibition of sanitary ap- pliances, and for eliciting all the information that could be obtained with reference to sanitary matters generally. If they could help them by contributing anything in the shape of appliances they would be happy to receive them. Councillor PLATT : May I suggest that they send the ,Longford machinery there? (Laughter.) Alderman lacer: I hope if they do so Councillor Platt will have to pay the carriage. (Hear, hear.) THE TRAFFIC IN SANKEY-STREET. COMICIBOT DIXON drew the attention of the Watch Cotit- mittee to the necessity fer the regulation of the traffic in Sankey-street on Sunday nights. Some time ago he asked for something to be dotes, tut up to the present it had re- mained very uncomfortable and very unpleasint for anyone to walk along the street on Sunday nights from half-past six to half-past nine. fEe thought some regulation should be made whereby people walking along.the footpaths should not be compelled to leace them owing to the bands of young men who were walk*: along hand in hand. 41lerman linate would recommend that foot passengers should be requested te keep to the right. Councillor DIXON found in all other towns there was a regulation of the traffic, and he thought the time had come when it should be done in Warrington. Alderman Cneeenunv humonroasly observed thet Coun- cillor Dixon was on the wrong side of the read when he was pushed off the footpath. He should have 'kept to the right. (Laughter.) Councillor HUTCHINSON could bear out what Councillor Dixon had said in relation to the traffic in Sankey- street on Sunday night. There was a lot of 'reckless law- lessness on the part of youths going about the streets arm in arm, not for the sake of a pleasant walk, but strolling out and rallying round each other on the 'footpath. He thought if there was an extra officer in the neighbourhood there would not be the pushing off the footpath there was at present. Alderman BURGESS said there was no doubt Sankey- street was uncomfortable on a Sunday egght but they had no power to prevent youths or other people'rambling round the streets. It was very difficult to walk along at times, but he did not really see what could be done. He had seen the widest street in Liverpool within the last month more crowded and more .difficult to go along than Sankey-street was—even on Sunday nights. The MAYOR: Mr. Councillor Dixon may rest assured that Mr. Hunt's attention shall be called to his complaint, and if anything can be done to minimise the evil it will be done.

THE THEATRE OF VAREOTIES. Councillor PLATT, in moving the minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee, said they mostly related to the wooden building known as the Circus, and he only hoped that the suggestions which hid been made by the in,rough surveyor would be carried out in their entirety. The committee still thought that the building was not free from danger, but he hoped that nothing serious would hap.

pen. Councillor BARKER seconded the motion, and the minutes were passed. THE CONDITION OF SANZEY-ETHEET. Alderman REAR moved the contirmatioa of the proceed- ings of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, and Councillor WOOLFALL seconded. Councillor Dr. MActLIE said he would like to call attention to the state of Sankey-street, between the park gate and the top of Bold-street. The macadam was frequently being taken up, and it was up again. Ile understood that it was their poverty and not their will that they consented to the condition of that short length of macadam. If the members of the Council would just look at it when they went out they would see that it was in such a condition as to make it upleasant for the young men and maidensto step off the , pavement on to the street. The length that was left unpaved was exceedingly short, and it was almost an advertisement of how poor the town was. The MAYOR said he fully sympathised with the remarks of Dr. Mackie. He supposed it was a question of expense, and yet if it was they were told on such authority as Alder- man Kean and Alderman Burgess that macadam was the most eYpensilre in, the long run. He thought that there should not be a vestige of macadam left in the borough. Alderman KEAN said that as chairman of that committee he had advocated the borrowing of money to sweep away all macadamised roads in the town, and the sooner that was done the better. Sankey-street was now in a very bad state. They were simply waiting favourable weather, in order to put down the wood pavement and after that the sets. Sankey-street would have been paved long ago, but certain gentlemen in the town opposed it. The next step to be taken would be to go in for borrowing powers to sweep away these dis- creditable streets altogether. The rainutee were carried. HALF-TIMERS AND SCHOOL MANAGERS. Councillor WALLINGTON moved, and Councillor BovroN seconded, the passing of the School Attendance Committee's minutes. Councillor PLATT said he was-sorry the chairman of the School Attendance Committee was not present that night, because he wished to call his attention to the difficulty ex- perienced by parents of half-timers in getting their childrea admitted into schools. Half-timers were turned out and had to find fresh places, any school being nearly full would not admit them. Coneequently the parents of these children ex- perienced much difficulty. In his opinion the employment, of half-timers ought not to be discouraged by the school managers, for the reason that the authority of the School Attendance Committee ceased when a child was of the age of 13 yeas, and there were a great many children.at that moment of tbat age who had not had a common school education. If they were employed as half-timers they were compelled to go to school until they were 14 years of age. If they dd not work half-time they could leave school at 13. He thought that the employment of half-timers ought to be encouraged rather than otherwiee, because half-timers were obliged to attend school regdlarly, or else they were prosecuted. Councillor CALDWELL : I think Councillor Platt has been wrongly informed. Councillor PLATT, continuing, said he did not think he bad. He knew case where a schoolmistress said that orders had come from the committee to turn out half-timers. It must 41:tavo put parents to considerable difficulty. In many cases children working from 13 to le were a great help in large fatuities, although they might earn only 5s or Gs per week. Councillor FRANcoene thought •that Counciller Platt should furnish the Chairman of the School Attendance Committee with the names of those teachers who refused to admit half-timers. ge happened to be the manager of a branch school of the parish church, and be was one for recommending that some of the children be turned out of that school. They had also an adult school, where every requisite was provided for a good edueation, nut the other was a kind of mushroom school with a poor staff, and the object in turning the children out of that school was not that they should not go to school but that they should go to the adult school, where better facilities were provided for education. He believed that the People's College and the Catholic School in Buttermarket-street were examined in exactly the same fashion. When they considered that the People's College had got certificated teachers to every standard and that they had got the cream of the town as echolars, whose parents were willing to pro- vide them with every requisite for advancing their educa- tion; and then, on the other baud, if they would go down to the Catholic school and see the children there clothed in rags and bare feet, they would see that the examinations , ought not to be similar. It was exactly the same with the Crossley-street school. They had there an excellent mistress, who worked like a slave, and at the end of it all she gota bad report. The teaching power was simply com- plete Of one case and simply miserable ia the other. In turning the children out of the Crossley-street school it was only intended that they should be removed to the other , in Church-s'reet. Councillor BOLTON disapp, •yed of half-timers being turned away from school, but thought that Councillor Platt was entirely wrong in blaming the committee. Councillor PLATT explained that he blamed the managers of the schools, and said that the attention of the committee ought io be drawn to it. Councillor Dixox said that it was a difficult question, •nd one which had engaged the attention of the chairman .e well as the School Attendance Committee from time to ...me hefeere, He was, however, willing to leave it in the
hands of the cotnruittee, by whom he was sure it would be

properly dealt with. Councillor BURGESS felt confident that the managers of schools would not turn half-timers away so long as theyhad room for them. But half-tlmers would not be permitted in schools of a higher class than those spoken of, and be did not think the committee would be justified in saying any- thing on the matter to the managers of the schools they had been referring to. Councillor Dr. Me.cmn was afraid Councillor Burgess had not used his usual discrimination in what he had just said. Those schools were supported by public money. Something like a Million a year was paid to schools such as those which had been named, and he could only say that if they absolutely turned away half-timers to make room for others they were acting against the spirit of the Education Act, and for which that support was given. Councillor CALDWELL said that if they believed all the complaints they heard they would not know what to do to please. He did not think that the state of things mention:A by Councillor Platt existed. Alderman KEAN remarked that the School Attendance Committee had done wonders its Warringten, and he hoped that the dissatisfaction which now existed would be swept I away. If they•had a school board they would remember it. I In Birmingham they were paying 911 in the X, and at the time people were contending for a scnool board in Warring- ton, Widnes was paying is. 21. in the X. Councillor PLATT: Mr. Caldwell says that the state of things I mentioned does not exist. I expressly said that I was dealing with facts, and I hardly think it is competent for a member to get up and say that such a thing does not

exist. The MAYON here remarked that they were getting: a little out of order. Referring to the complaints made by Coun- cillor Platt, he said that he had never before heard of any- thing of the kind. nor did he think it within the power of the School Attendance Committee to dictate to the school masters or mistresses, and they had not the slightest control over the managers. Their duty was confined to see- ing that the children attended school, and when that was done their duty was at an end. But he thought the School Attendance Committee were very solicitous to see that everything should be done that could be done to overcome the difficulty. Councillor Platt might rest assured that they would not ha any way sanction any proceedings that could be considered of an al bitrary character. When the School Attendance Committee met again they would have the matter considered. Councillor WALLINGTON said that the Mayor had antici- pated what he was about to say. What the Mayor had just mentioned was the work of the School Attendance Com- mittee, and they tried to do it in the best manner possible. No order ever went from that cmnmittee to any school manager to turn away half-timers. Councillor Wallington continued: I have had the privilege of looking at the school in Crossley-street, and it is a very good one and is very full, but the way to it is a most wretched one—a flight of steps I should think as high as this roof. There waste a new school building. A school board is wanted. ("No, no," and laughter.) There wants a raved school, and there wants a school beard to build that—(more laughter)—and we shan't accomplish the things we are wanting to do without a school beard. (Laughter.) The minutes were then passed. NO COXILENT. The proceedings of the Library, Musette? and Arts Cam- raittee, tie Cemetery Committee, the Tows Hall, Park and Baths Committee, the Sanitary Committee, the Finance Committee, and the Markets Committee were confirmed
without comment. TIE MARKRTS.-PROPOSED EXTENSION.--TRE DRAPERY _

STALLS DENOUNCED. Alderman CHANDLEY. ih moving the confirmation of the proceedings of the Markets Committee, alluded to the pur- chase by the Corporation or: the property in Market-street, lately in the occupation of Mr. Geddes, at the price of £1,300. He said there had been a popular error that that property belonged to the Corporation, but nothing could be more erroneous. A meeting was held, six or seven years ago, by the Markets Committee then in existence—and of which he was not a member—and it was concluded mot to take any notice at all of the property. Mr. Chorley (the borough treasurer) then purchased it entirely on his own responsibility. He dared say Mr. Chorley felt that some time or other the property would be required for market purposes. It had cost him some £1,200, and he went be- fore the committee and told them they should have it at the price he paid for it, as he did not wish to make anything out of the Corporation. Well, the committee felt that that was a generous otter, but they did not feel justified in taking advantage of it quite as it stood, and they concluded to give Mr. Chorley £l,3oo—which repre- sented a little more than six per cent, on his outlay. The committee, he repeated, felt that Mr. Chorley had been most generous in the matter, for he (Mr. Chandley) knew per- sonally people who would be glad to give £.300 or fe4oo more for the property forithe purpose of selling it again. Thanks were due to Mr. Chorley for his disinterested conduct in the matter. Councillor J. PZERPOINT seconded the confirmatien of the proceedings of the committee. Coancillor Sceereer thought it was very reasonable and very generous of Mr. Chorley to let them have the,property for the figure mentioned. Turning to that portion of the committee's proceedings which empowered the borough surveyor to prepare advertisements for the sale of the build- ing materials forming the property, Mr. Sutton asked whether the committee had, before passing that resolution, fully considered the quention of the present necessity for the extension of the market accommodation. He also wanted to know whether the ac- commodation for the eale of vegetables and other :farm pro- duce was sufficient to meet the present requirements. If it was contemplated to extend the market spade for the benefit of those who at the present time bring drapery goods and other wares into the market, their object beicg to get all the money they possibly can and take it away +with them to the detriment of the tradesmen of the town, -cn whose shoulders the mincipal burden of the rates is fixed, then he said it was a great mistake. If, however, it was desired by the extension to make better provision for the winblesale po- tato market, then be thought the alteration would be a good one. The extension ought to be considered in the interest of the ratepayers, to whom no harm ought to he done by the extension of the drapery stalls. Councillor Dr. MACKIE protested with hie whole heart against more provision being made for the drapery and other stalls. Trade in Warrington was in a most wretched state so far as the shopkeepers were concerned.; agd he had been told again and again that every Wednesday not less than £1,20C of ready money was taken out of the town by these stall-holders, who paid only 2s Gd and 2s.Gr: per stall. He hoped, therefore, that the committee would seriously lay to heart these matters in the interests of the ratepayers, and to say decisively what they iatended to do for the future. CouncillGr J. PIERL'OINT intimated that he should attend every meeting of the Markets Committee with the view of opposing the extension of the drapery stalls, an he had always done, in the interests of the ratepayers. Councillor BURGESS was convinced that those gentlemen upon the Markets Committee who entertained similar views to Dr. Mackie, as to the non-advisability of extending stall accommodation for drapers and others in the market, would , feel their hands strengeleened by what hal been said. Councillor 1-3ARKER said if the committee had given some indication of their intentions it would have saved all this discussion. Alderman HOLMES intimated that he was opposed to any 1 extension of the drapery stalls. Councillor WALLINGIK3N said the committee were formed to make the most of the property for the Corporation and the public. These stalls were patronised by the ratepayers who paid the rates, by walking people whose wages were not high, and whom it behoved to make the most of What they received. Councillor .HeeeeCneNsote called attention to the construc- tion of something of the nature of a shop in the old market shed, and said if it were allowed others might be pct up. He asked if it had been erected with the consent of the com- mittee. He hoped to live, he said, to see the day o hen there would be no tabling—which was a nuisance in the evening considering the way it was knocked about—nnder the old marked shed. The, MAvon-syrapathised with the committee in the dif- ficulty in which they were placed, as they had two closes of ratepayers to cousider—the shopkeepers and the public. He believed that if the committee were to put an emd to vendors of small articles coming to the market they would give very great dissatisfaction to those people who visited it, an who did not hesitate to say that they could there ob- tain bargains, bargains cheaper than at the shops. The question was altogether a more difficUlt one than appeared on the surface. Alderman CRANDLEY, in replring, said he thought it was very unfair indeed to charge the committee with doing anything injurious to the idaterests of the shop- keepers. but he would remind the members of the Council that they were as deeply implicated as the Markets Committee for sanctioning the proceedings. If the drapery stalls were bad they ought to be eiscontinued, if good they ought to be extended, for there could be no mid- dle course in a principle. The object of the Markets Com- mittee was at all times to do what they believed to be for the best interests of the ratepayers ; and personally he did not believe these stalls were injurious to the shopkeepers and the ratepayers. As long as the motto of the committee was the greatest good for the greatest number, they really must maintain the stalls with an inferior class of goods for those ratepayers who wanted an inferior class of goods at an in- ferior price. It was the duty of those members of the Council who opposed the proceedings of the committee to move an amendment to them, otherwise they were not con- scientious in the discharge of their duty. IWieh regard to the extensions, he remarked that he believed the committee were to be memorialised with the view of providing a rem- mittee-reom, hut he could not promise that would he erected. The market gardeners were, he said, the first to be accommodated. The proceedings of the committee were confirmed. THE QUALITY OF THE GAS. Alde-Mall HOLMES, in moving the confirmation of the proceedings of the Gas Committee, remarked that additional steam power had been provided at the Gas Works for the injector or ejector at Latchford referred to at the last meet- ing by Mr. Councillor Dixon. The worthy alderman added that if the committee could by spending some £5O or £l.OO psaleavesusortenteo dL2OOO sso.e £250 it was not only their duty but their Aldelman CHANDLEY seconded the confirmation of the !ninnies. Councillor DIXON complained of the quality of the gas, and said he believed some of the meters in use did not register correctly. Aide. man 110T3IES said he wished Mr. Dixon would speak

to him in the street about these matters whs they met. The 1 I committee would, he added, test any meter brought to than. ; If it registered correctly the consumer would have to pay the expense of the test; if incorrectly the committee would defray the cost of examination. Minutes confirmed. THE SHIP CANAL The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the proceedings of the General Purposes Committee, which comprised the fol- lowing item: "Resolution that the Town Clerk and Mr. Longdin be instructed to draw up a report, showing in what manner the Ship Canal Scheme affects the borough and the river Mersey in its &Anse through the borough, and they invite representatives of the manufacturers interested in the question to confer with this committee when considering the report." Alderman HOLUES seconded the motion. Councillor Dr. MACKIE said he did not sea why the manu- facturers should be selected for exclusive favour, and after a short conversation the words "and others" were inserted in the resolution, after the word manufacturers. This was,all the business.
ST. PETEUS
WARRINGTON.
ANNUAL 'TEA. PARTY.

The annual congregational tea party in conn,cticm with St. Peter's Church, Warrington, was held at the Pulic Hall on Monday evening, and was attended by about 230 persons. The hall was neatly adorned with a number of ban- ners. After tea an entertainment, interspersed with speeches, was gone through. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) pre- sided, supported by the Revs. M. Schonberg, T. Schonberg, E. C. E. Carleton, F. Slater, J. G. Richards, J. Hatton, and Mr. G. Powlson.—The MAYOR (who was warmly received) remarked that he attended there with feelings of unalloyed pleasure, because he thought it was the duty of the person placed in the position which he had the honour to hold at present, never to hesitate for a moment to undertake duties of that kind, and which might perhaps be called collateral duties, being outside the strict and proper duties appertain- ing to the office. It was with great pleasure he came there to help forward the good cause which their friend the Vicar had so much at heart. (Hear, hear.) Let him first of all wish them a happy new year, and that the end of the year would find them better Christians than they were twelve months ago. He also sincerely hoped that the efforts the Rev. M. Schonberg and other zealous friends were making with him to erect a new church would result at the close of the year, at all events in seeing that structure commenced, and that when it was completed it would be one worthy of the clergyman, the congregation, and of the services which would be celebrated within its walls. (€ear, hear.) His attention was drawn to a letter in the Warrington Advertiser of Saturdry last in which the writer alleged that nothing had been done towards buildings new church except talking. He (the Mayor) knew that great exertions were being made at the present time to. erect a new church, and he firmly believed that ultimately they would possess one worthy of the congrega- tion attending St. Peter's. (Applause.)—The Rev. M. SCIION. BERG followed with a few remarks, and p Anted out the many difficolties which beset them in endeavouring to erect a new place of worship. They were not situated like the Parish Church, St. Paul's, or St. Anne's, as those churches had fields in their parishes. His was in the centre of the town, where nearly every inch of the ground was occupied, and the few patches of land which were to be had would be sold at a very heavy price. There was a time when one could secure land in Warrington at lid per yard, but that was in days gone by. Now it was nothing but 9d, is, and Is 6d per square yard. They saw, therefore, that their dif- ficulties were very great, but they hoped to surmount them, and that during the year 1884. (Hear, hear.) They hoped at any rate to have begun, if not completed the work at the end of the year. Hitherto they had collected £1,500. (Ap- plause.) They had £2OO or £3OO at the bank, and the rest was promised. Lord Winmarleigh had promised £2OO on condition that the total amount required was collected by the close of the year 1883. Mr. Powlson took upon himself to write to Lord Winmarleigh stating that they h'ad not done this, and asking him to extend the time. His Lordship npon this consented to give them another year. r Applause.)—The Rev, E. C. E. CARLETOti subsequently briefly addressed those present, remarking there was no one who deserved to have his work successfully accomplished more than their vicar, the Rev. M. Schonberg, and he hoped they would not have another tea party without teeing the erection of the new church commenced. (Hear, hear.)—The masical pro- gramme was as follows: Song, "Love was once a little boy," Miss Richardson; song, "Friar of Orders Grey," Mr. Booth; song, "When the tide comes in," Miss Bed- dard ; song, " Norah, the Pride of Kildare, Mr. Reddish; song, " Ehren on the Rhine," Miss Woods (Salford); song, " The lover and the bird," Mrs. Rigby; comic song, "Smiling Tom," Mr. George Parr; piano solo, Mr. Galla- gher. Part II: Song, Miss Bei:Liam ; song, "The wolf," Mr. Booth; song, "In sheltered vale," Miss Richardson; song, "Alice, where art thou ?" Mr. Reddish; song, Mrs. Rigby; comic song, The grocer's boy," Mr. George Parr; God save the Queen. Mr. Booth, jun., accompanied—ln proposing a vote of thanks to the performers and orders who had assisted that evening, the Rev. T. Se—HONBER3, son of the Vicar, took ocression to refer to several matters con- nected with the Church of England. It was said by some that Church people depended almost entirely on endow- ments, and knew nothing of the voluntary prireiple. He re- minded theta, however, that since IE4O the Church of Eng- land had been prcvided by the voluntary subscriptions of her children with no less a sum than £18,003 per year for the building and restoring of churches. Regarding the church's educational work, he said that since 1870 (when compulsory education became law) and IEB2 the Church of England raised by the voluntary subscriptions of her mem- bers no less a St.lll than five million and a half for increass. ing the school accommodation. When those schools had been built it •became necessary to maintain them, and the Government grant not being sufficient for the purpose, each year the Church of England raised £600,000 for maintain- ing the schools after they were built. (Applause.) When the Church of England had made such sacrifices for the people she must know something ef the voluntary principle. (Hear, hear,) A very pleasant evening was spent. Trays were given by the following :—The Mayoress (Mrs. Harr:son), Mrs Litton, Miss C Harvey, Miss E Her- vey, MPS Dun. Miss Smith, Mrs S Reynolds (ss), Mies; Schonberg, Mr J C Parr, Mr P Stubs (2), Mr J Marson (2), Mrs Haines, a friend, Mrs Wilkinson. Mrs Decrial', Mrs' Nicholson. Mr Kilshaw, a friend, Mrs Carleton, Mrs Wheel-, don, Mrs. J Geddes, Mrs J Hatton, Mrs J Rawson, Mrs W Owen, Mrs Fletcher, Mrs P Leigh, Mrs Warburton Mrs Shaw, Mrs W J Burgess, Miss Reid, Miss Sutton, Mr Jeans, Mrs Mackie, Mr Jolley, Mr Coates, Mrs Shill- cock, Mr Hales, Mrs Blease, Mrs Edgar, Miss J Edgar, Mrs Budd, Mrs Balshaw, Mrs E Hate, Mr J. div.head: LYMM WESLEYAN SUNDAY
div.p: THE LYMM WESLEYAN SUNDAY
SCHOOL.

On Tuesday evening, the annual social tea meeting in connection with this school was held, and was well attended. A public meeting was afterwards held in the chapel. The Rev. .1. McTurk, on Warrington, presided, and there were also on the platform the Rev. T. Rippon (Warrington), Messrs. Edwin Brown, son. (superintendent of the Sunday school), Ashton, T. Morley, and John Bridge. —Mr. BROWN addressed the meeting, and said they had cause to be thankful that they still had a Sucday school. The first thing they were short of—let him speak very plainly—was a few volunteers for their Sunday morning ' work. They required two or three female teachers who would be prepared to take up the work and come and help them. The average attendance at their school on Sunday morning was as good as he found the average of most schools. It was a deplorable fact that so many Sunday schools had to mourn ever the slender attendance on Sunday mornings. Those of them who had anything to do with business knew that art hour in the morning WAS worth two in the night. They bad no right to be satisfied with an average attendance of O. He had marked this: that When they had a scholar in the school, if that scholar began to absent himself on Sunday mornings, they looked very fear- fully towards that scholar, and in a short time he would absent himself altogether.—The CHAIRMAN followed with a few remarks, and said if they worked with all their hearts there would be abundance of Divine blessing. He was glad to know that the school had been carrying on its work for 86 years, and he was glad to be at its 80th birthday. (Applause.) -Mr. Mona.v..v, in a practical address on Stinday school work, said : The question was, were they, as teachers, keeping pace with the requirements of the day? They ought to have some definite aim before them, and they ought to come to the school with some object in view. Mr. Morley referred to the disadvantages they had to contend with, and then passed on to speak of the advantages, and said that Sunday school work must not be looked upon as a pastime. They must work while it was day. Ile was pleased to hear they had a Band of Hope in connection with the school. They had one at Sale some years ago, but it WAS badly officered, and it collapsed for some reason or other. They had recently started it again, and he was glad to say it was a great eac- ceas. He wished every success to their Sunday school, and hoped they would have a blessed, happy, and prosperous year. (Applause.)—The Rev. T. RIPPON said he believed the two hardest worked people in this country were Metho- dist preachers and newspaper reporters. He was at work until half-past one that morning, and had beau conducting services during the day. The first thing he wanted to say to them was, Be of good cheer. That was a capital meeting and the attendance was better than last year. He was sure there was a large constituency of young people in Lymm and neighbourhood whe were not identified with any school, who were, perhaps, the children of parents who came to that chapel. They wanted the beat men and women in their Sunday schools and in their choirs. (Applause.)—Other speakers followed, and the meeting terminated with the ucual votes of thanks. Several pieces were sung by the choir, Mr. E. Brown, jun., presiding at the organ.

EXTENSIVE ROBBERY BY WARRING- TON WORKMEN. On Wednesday, at Warrington Police Court, Edward Solomon Ashton and his wife, Mary Ashton, of 61, Aiken-st., George Roberts, ef 36, Cairo-street, and William Alexander, of Hamilton-street, all of whom with the exception of the female. prisoner were employed by Messrs. S. E. and R. , Johnson, cabinet makers, of Rylands-street and Ship-yard, were charged with stealing within the last months a quan- tity of articles used in the cakinet making and uphoNtering trade, the property of Messrs. Johnson. The charge was a long one, and among the articles mentioned therein being walnut, oat, brass castors, arm chairs, chair backs, brass nails, brass springs, pole rings, mccette cloth, wadding, boxes, expensive tiles, curled hair, and a large quantity of timber. The goods enumerated in the charge were produced in court, giving to it the appearance of a cabinetmaker's work- shop. The articles stolen by the Ashtons were valued at £3, those stolen by Roberts £4 17s, and those stolen by Alexander a.—The Chief Constable said that the prisoner Ashton had been employed by Messrs. Johnson at their work- shop in Ship-yard as chairmaker, Roberts had been their foreman for the last 15 months. and Alexander had been 'employed as carver for about six' months. For the last week or ten days Sergeant Spinks had been specially employed to watch the premises of Messrs. Johnson, Ship- yard, but more particularly the prisoners Ashton and their son Charles, the latter being a lad apprenticed to Messrs. Johnson. AbGut noon on Tuesday Sergeant Spinks saw Mrs. Ashton enter Ship.yard and sand a basket to her son Cbanes. The basket apparently contained the dinners. of her husband and son. Mrs. Ashton remained some tune near tile door, and the boy then returned with the basket. ' Sergeant Spiuks noticed that it seemed to Se niguch heavier • than before, and be watched her cross Bridge-street, go along Rvlands street, and up Bold-street, where he accosted her.

He looked into the basket and found the timber produced —oak, cedar, Sm. Mrs. Ashton said in answer to a question that her husband had bought the wood from the foreman. When near the Pelican public-house, on the ray to the police staticn, she threw the basket down and Cried to es- cape. Ashton was also brought to the police I station, and when told that his house would ' be searched, he said that nothing in the house belonged ^to his masters, and they could search for it. The house was searched, and there was found a gentleman's easy chair, partly made, four brass castors, 31bs. of glee, a quantity of mocette, which had been missed by Messrs. Johnson, and a good many other articles. When these were found Ashtcm said, "I will tell the truth. I will tell all I know, and give von as little trouble as possible." He then said that Roberts, the foreman, gave him the brass castors, and that Roberts had two chairs at his lodgings which he had made up for him, and which were moulded at the shop. Continu- ing, he said, "The timber in the chairs is Mr. Johnson's, and the chair springs Alex gave them to my lad. He has a chair at his house I made up for him at Johnson's. It is Mr. Johnson's material, and there are six springs in it." Ashton made this statement of his own accord. Roberts was then fetched to the police station to identiff the articles, and on the way he said, also of his own accord, that he could not identify the things, and that he had never had anything.' of that kind to do before. When at the police statien he failed to identify the articles as having belonged to Messrs. Johnson, but afterwards admitted to the Chief Constable, when the latter 'told him that his house would be searched, " that there were two chairs at his lodgings which Ashton had made for him, but that was all he had that he knew of." His lodg, ings were searched and the chairs were found. Alexander was also arrested, and when charged he said, "I have only one chair aad a few tacks. Ashton made the chair for me, but T didn't know it was Johnson's wood. He made it at his own house and I fetched it to my house." A search was made at Alexander's house and the chair was found. While the search was being made Mrs. Alexander adroitly slipped out of the back door with a quantity of wadding, but was seen and brought back. A number of chair springs were found in the cupboard. Respecting the chair Alexane der said, "I won't tell you who did the upholstering; I will saffer death first. The three male prisoners were then locked up. He (the Chief Constable) was in possession of information which showed that Ashton had sold a cer- tain table for a sovereign, which was worth cons'clerably more, and that he had also disposed of another table. There were also found at Roberts' lodgings six or eight lame boxes. The three large boxes produced had been made by Ashton, to whom Roberts pointed out the wood from which they were to be male. The very valuable tiles produced, to which Mr. Johnson could swear as being his property, were found in the boxes. The boxes appeared to have been made for going abroad, and he believed Roberts some short time since intended emigrating.—At the request of the Crnef Constable the male prisoners were re.nanded until Friday, Mrs. Ashton being allowed out on bail.—On Friday the prisoners were again charged, when M. Ridgway appeared for the prosecution, Mr. Smith, of Manchester, for Roberts, and Mr. Percy Davies for Alexander. Each 'of the three male prisoners pleaded guilty, and Mrs. Ashton was dis- charged at the request of Mr. Ridgway, who assumed that she had acted under the direction of her husfaand. In addi- tion, she had a large family who, if she were taken away, would suffer. Mr. R. Garnett gave the prisoner Ashton an excellent character for a period of 18 years, during which time he had been in his eraplov.—Ashton was sentenced to 13 months' imprisnement, Roberts to a similar period, and Alexander to three months' imprisonment, with hard labour in each CZ•3O3.—Mr. Ridgway then said that a good Bcal of valuableproperty had been re- covered from private ewners, and he applied for an order for that property to be handed:over te 'Messrs. Johnson. As being persons from .whom such property had been recovered he mentioned the names of Messrs. Siddall, Evans. Sandell, Gleave (a fire screen), Roscoller (a fotding chair), dm , each of whom had obtalned the articles at ridiculously small prices.—Mr. Davies contended that Mr. Gleave had given for the Ere screen as much as it was worth, and he opposed Mr. Ridgway's application.—Thenench decided to make no order.

The choir sang aII anthem with great taste, asd in the intervals the Vicar of al Cuthbert's, Liverpool, the Rev. E. Gallagher, the locum. bent, the Rev. E. div.head: WARRINGTON ART GALLERY. EXPECTED LOAN FROM THE NATIONAL
div.p: WARRINGTON ART GALLERY. EXPECTED LOAN FROM THE NATIONAL
COLLECTION

The following correspondenoe, which sufficiently explains itself, will be read with interest : Lyn Clerk's Office, Warringt6d, 80th liey, 18S3.—lisar Sir,-1 am directed by the Council of this Borough to apply to ' the Trustees of the National Gallery for a loan ef pictures or works ~f art for public exhibition in the Art Gallery of this town, under and subject to to the National Gallery (Loan) Act, 1883. Will you be kind enough to inform rue in what form the application must be made ?—Yours truly, W. H. Bnoox.—C. L. Eastlake, Esq., F.R.1.8.A.. Keeper and Secre- tary, National Gallery, Trafalgar Square, London. London National Gallery. 28th June, 1883.—Sir,—In refe.- enee to your letter of the 30th ultimo, making an application tsr the loan of pictures under the blational Gallery (Loan) Act of 1883, I ans requested by the Trustees and Director to make the following enquiries .1-1 What amount of lineal wall spew is available for permanently exhibiting the pictures in ques- tion? 2 What security does the building afford against fire and ether accidents? S To whose management is the gallery entrusted? 4 Under what conditions are the publid admitted? 5 What is the present population of Warrington? 6 Are the authorities prepared to meet the est of insurance, carriage, and packing of any pictures which may be lent by the National Galisry ? On receiving answers to these ques- tions, together with soy farther particulars to which you may think it desirable to add, the Trustees and Director will give the application favourable consideration.—l am. Sir. your ' obedient servant, CHARLES L. EASTLAKE, Beeper sod Secre- tary —W. H. Brook, Req.. Warrington. Town Clerk's Office. Warrington, 29th June, 1883.—Sir.--I am directed by the Museum. Library, and Arts Committee to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of yesterday's date, and to inform you in reply thereto :-1. That there are 90 lineal feet in our Art Gallery for permanently exhibiting the pic- tures in question. 2. That the Art Gallery joins the Museum, but is not attached to any other building. It is of modern construction, and was erected for the purpose of exhibiting pictures. There are two hydrants of the ,argest size and a sufficient supply of water within the building, and there are other hydrants in the street opposite the building. There is , always an attendant in the Art Gallery when it is open to the , I public. There are two means of exit from the Gallery. 3. The Gallery is entrusted to the management of the Museum, Library. and Arts Committee appointed by the Town Cornice, to whom the property belongs. 4. The public are geneially admitted free, but cn .pecial occasions a small chaege is made. If any charge is made to the exhibition of pictures lent by the National Gallery, ills proposed to devote the proceeds to the completion of anew School of Art whioh is now in course of erection. 5. The population of the borough is about 42 OM. 6. The committee are prepared to meet the oast of insurance, carriage arid packing Of any pictures which may be lent by the National Gallery.—l am, Sir, your obedient servant. W. H. BROOK, Town Clerk.—Charles L Eastlake, Eeq., Keeper and Secretary National Gallery, London. Town Clerk's °floe, Warrington, 11th December, 1883.- 81r„—I am directed ty the Museum, Library, and Arts Com- mittee of this town to enquire whether the particulars fur- nished In my letter to you of the 29th June last were satisfac- tory to the trustees and director of the National Gallery; if so. the committee direct me again to urge your attention to their application fur a loan of pictures under the Act of 188:I.—. I am. sir, your obedient servant, WILLIAM H. Bstoox.— Charles b. Pastlake, Esq., keeper and secretary. National Gallery, London. National Gallery, London, 12th December. 1883.—Sir,—In reply to your letter of yesterday. I beg to inform you that your previous conatnuhication, dated the 29th stIIIB last. was duly laid before the Trustees mod Director of this Gallery and approved. As soon as the various applications from provincial galleries under the National Gallery (L(oan) Act had been re- ceived the Director proceeded to the allotment of certain pictures among them,but circumstances intervened which pre- vented him 'from completing this work before he left London for his offidal journey on the Continent. The Director is ex- pected to return about the end of this month. when'he will resume the allotment, and as soon as It is completed the pic- tures proposed to be lent will be despatched to their destina- tion sutriect to the conditions already speoffied.—l am Sir, your obedient servant, CHARLES L. Easytaxx.--Win.ll. Brook. Esq., Town Clerk, Warriogton.

div.head: VIOLATION OF THE FACTORY ACT
div.p: VIOLATION OF THE FACTORY ACT
- - - - - AT WARRINGTON. HEAVY PENALTIES.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Frederick Wright, of Horsemarket-street, was summoned for having, on the let December, be then being the occupier of a workshop under the meaning of the Factory and Work- shops Act, employed Rhoda Hamper= after four o'clock in the afternoon, the earns being Saturday, contrary to the Act. He was similarly summoned with respect to each of the following :—Mary Lyons, Annie Fryer, Helen Davies, Ellen Burrows, Louisa Worrell, Sarah Jane Worrell, Annie Eyre,,Annie Armsby, Jane Taylor, Hannah Wellfare, Ellen Mary Stewart, and Emily Armsby.--The defendant pleaded guilty.—Captain Mead-King and Mr. Arnold, inspectors under the Factory and Workshops Act, appeared to prose- cute. The former gentleman said that the defendant was the occupier of a millinery and dressmaking establishment In florsemarket-street. The Factory and Work- shops Act provided that all women and young persons employed in the workshops shall have a half-day holiday once a week, the day fixed being Saturday. Under certain conditions another day might be substituted, but in this case no other day had been substituted. In wostshops at which the hours of work did not commence before eight in the morning, women and young persons might be employed until four o'clock, but under no condi- tions later than four. There was, however, reason to suppose that the practice of encroaching on the half-holiday had been rather common. In this case the women and young persons were found working at 4-25 p.m. The defendant said, that his clerk paid the young women their wages at half-past three, and he (the defendant) was not cognizant of their working after the specifiad thne.—Alderman Davies : Do you mean to say they could work on your premises without your knowing ?—The defendant replied that he did not kuow they were working.—l he Inspector: The duty of the occupier of the premises is to tee that they are not work- ing. The defendant in reply to a question said that the persona enumerated in the summonses were not paid by the piece but by the week.—Alderman Davies: And you did not know they were working over ? The defendant: No, sir.— ' Aldeman Davies: You must let there be some logic ;in what you say. On what principle would they -ctop longer than required ? What inducement was there P—The defendant was understood to say that he did not kuow.—Major Cartwright said that under the cir- euinstacces it did not seen, to him to be a bad case. To the Inspector) : You don't presg for a heavy penalty ? The Inspector said he would leave that in the hands of the Bench. The defendant, howevengsad pleaded guilty, and there must therefore be a conviction in each case.—The Mayor: Were they very youne people who were working? —ln reply it was stated that they were about 14 years of age.—Before giving their decision the Bench decided to hear the next case.—Wm. Hodgkinson, Bridge-street, was then called upon, being similarly samononed to the last de- fendant in respect to Lizzie Brennan, Harriet Corney, Annie Broady, M. McKenzie, and Henrietta Jones.—The Inspector said thatUiis was precisely a similar Case to the last, with the exception tliat there were not so many women working, but they were found working later—'6-20 p.m.—The defen- dant said he believed they were not all working, but that some were waiting for the others. He thought most of them wete in the act of leaving the premises when the Inspector entered:— The lklayor. Are you in the habit of keeping these girls after the time P—The defendant: No, lam not. I endeav- our to keep them within the Act —The Mayor: Then this is an accidental circumstance 2—The defendant: I think it was.—Alderman Davies: Da you blame your forewoman for this 7—The defendant: Well, I don't blame her exactly; but ehe is responsible to see that they go.—Mr. Arnold, in- spector, said that when he entered the defendant's premises the forewoman and her sister were at work, and although the others were not, so long as there was work going on the defendant was icually Halide for them.—The Mayor said he could not help remarking that these were very arbitrary cases. He did not say that the inspectors bad acted in an arbitrary Writ, but it did seem to him an arbitrary law that they should have to inflict fines in all these cases.—Captain Mead-King said that they were allowed to work longer than factories, that they were confined in les-ittcl and sometimes very crowded rooms, and he thought they required all the relaxation the Act provided.—The Mayor Well, all that we have to do is to administer the law. We shall inflict a penalty of is and costs in each case.—The total amount to be paid in the first case was £7 03 dd, and in the second case £3 7s.

A man named Thomas Coune, residing at Oswaldtwistle, died on Thursday morning from injuries recebred last week by falling from a table. Deceased while drunk attempted to tarn a somersault on the ta.uie when he fell and broke his neck.

WHOLESALE CRIME: FOCH CiIRLS INIVEDERED.—A man 1 named Huge Schenk, describing himself as an engraver, was arrested on Wednesday, at Vienna, on the charge of having since MD murdered four eirls after obtaining pos- session of their savings by promises of marriage. His last victim was a cook named Ketteler, who was found mur- dered in August, 1.853, unds.r mysterious circumstances, which created great sensation at the time. THE NEWINGTON INIVIRDER: IMPORTINT ARREST.—The Watford police have arrested a man in connection with the Stoke Newington murder. It appoars that the prisoner, who is a man of gentlemanly appearance, arrived at Wat- ford on Wednesday evening, and put up at an inn in the Market-place. He had black eyes, a wound on his nose, and was wearing a chain similar to that owned by the murdered man. The police are very reticent about the affair.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
CADIt3E:EAD.

A very successful bazaar and Christmas tree were held in the day school on behalf of the Trust Fund of Cadishead Wesleyan Chapel on New rear's Day. The room was decorated with skill and taste. There was an ample supply of gc)ds. useful and ornamental. The Christmas tree occu- pied the centre of the room, fruitful .of toys of every des- cription, to the great delight of the children. The tea in the infant schoolroom was well patronised. Altogether it was one of the most successful bazaars held at Cadishead. The sum realised was £61.111s 4d. .

- A watch-night service was held in the large reEtry of the G.7.dishead Wesleyan Chapel on the last night of the old year. There was a good ttendance. The service was con- ducted by the Rev: R. Dillon, and Mr. Hopewell, local preacher. The meeting was devout aid attentive, and the addresses thoughtful and impressive. After a few minutes of silent prayer, the hymns "Come let us anew Our journey pursue" Sm. was sung with spirit. In a few chosen words, the Rev. R. Dillon concluded the service by wishing all present a very ilapprNew Year.

div.head: DUNHAM MASSEY.
div.p: DUNHAM MASSEY.

TEE BATING 07-BAILWAYS.—At the Altrincham Petty Sessions on Monday, Mr. Preston appeared on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company in answer to a summons issued against them by the Overseers of Dunham Massey, for payment of the sum of £lOB. Mr. Fletcher, assistantoverseer, appeared on behalf of the township. Mr. Preston, after consulting with Mr. Fletcher, said that they had received a summons for payment of a rate in respect to which an appeal was now pending. The appeal was against a rateable value of £4,353, whereas the old rate was £B6O. He had no desire to put the parish or the collector to incon- venience. He was quite prepared to recommend the direc- tors to pay £2O 103 and to allow the summons to be with- drawn.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Harris) said this was all the magistrates could do provided they issued a distress. —Mr. Fletcher said they could not do without it.—The Chairman (Mr. Jovnson): You will have to do without it. —All we can do is to issue a distress for the amount of the last rate, £2O 10s.—Mr. Preston: I am quite willing to think it is a mistake, and perhaps a little injudicious to rush into law. I shall not ask for costs or anything, but look upon it as an error of judgment. At the suggestion of the Chair- man, the summons was withdrawn. FARNWORTH. .

MAIIRIAGE AT FAINWOHT'II—CTEM—R-01.—The marriage of Miss Wareing, eldest daughter of Captain J. W. Wareing, of Pea Hill, Widnes. to Mr. Edgar R. Makin, of Liverpool, took place at St. Luke's Church, Farnworth, on Saturday raorning. The ceremony wanwitnessed by a large company of ladies. The wedding party drove from Pea Hill in car- riages supplied by Mr. Fowler, of the Central Hotel, who introduced three antique coaches of very handsome con- struction. The bride, who was given away by her father, was attired in a handsome dress of white brocaded satin with a wreath of orange blossoms. The bridesmaids were Miss Harbridge, of Birkenhead, and Miss Edith and Lily Ware- ing, sisters of the bride. The first-named wore a rich dress of ruby satin, and the Misses Wareing each had dresses of ruby velvet, with hats to match. They also wore gold bracelets, the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. A. Waring acted as best man. There were also present Mrs. Wareing, Mr. F. Wareing, and Mr. and Mrs. John Taylor. The Rev. U. Bond, M.A.., performed the ceremony, and at the close the choir—Mr. Watts, M.A., being at the har- monium—sang an appropriate hymn. ()lithe party leaving the church Mr. Watts played Mendelssolin's ." Wedding March."

div.head: HOUGH GREEN.
div.p: HOUGH GREEN.

SrPPOSED SITICIDE.—Late on Wednesday evening the body of Mary Maddox, 30 years of age, wife of John Mad- dox, a platelayer on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Railway at Hough Green, was found dead in a pool of water near her own home. lier husband, who was ill in bed, saw her leave the house about six o'clock on Wednes- day morning. She did not return, and the Ending of a shawl in the pool led to the recovery of the body. It is supposed the woman committed suicide.

LYMM. SAD DEATH OF A SCHOOL GIRL: A Carnos TO SCHOOL MANAGERS.—On Thursday afternoon an inquest was held at the White Hart Inn, Warrington, on the body of Eliza- beth Wilkinson, J. 4 years of age, daughter of Joseph Wilkin- son, fustian cutter, Newfield, Lvyam, who died at the Warrington Infirmary on Monday, from injuries she received on December oth. From the evidence adduced it appeared that the deceased attended the Lvmm National Schools, and daring the dinner hour on Thursday, December 6th, she was near the fire with other children, when her dress—a , print one—caught fire. She ran into the school ytrd, where she was noticed by a teacher, Miss Agnes Forrest, in flames, and John Daffy, a fishmonger, by means of a hearthrug succeeded in extinguishing them, but not before the unfor- tunate girl was severely burned on the lower part of her body. Deceased was seen by Dr. Giallimore, who ordered her removal to the Infir- mary, where she was attended by Pr. Richmond. The wounds, however, did not heal, and she died on Mon- day night at twenty minutes past ten.—The mistress of the School, Miss Annie Deredon, stated that when the accident happened there was no guard around the fire•place, but one had been put there since.—A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned, the coroner and jury expressing their sur- prise that in a room where young children were allowed to remain during the dinner hour there was no protection for then' in the shape of a high guard around the fire-place. WHARTON. The annual parochial tea and entertainment at Christ Church, Wharton, Winsford, was held as usual in the Wharton National Schools, and passed offin a very success- ful way. Addresses by the clergy of the neighbourhood and other friends of this church were giver!, and a long and varied programme of music and recitations fully occupied the evening.

div.head: MaIIINER.
div.p: THE MaIIINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 12, 1884.

Mr. HENRY GEORGE, who has acquired a world-wide popularity as the anthor of " Pro- I gress an Poverty," an economical work of great value—and one which, perhaps has , ' done more than anything else to awaken a lively interest in the land question as it affects this and other countries—is now on a visit to England from America. He is to re- main in this country for three months. It is intimated that he will address somewhere about twenty-five public meetings in different towns in England, and also that he and Mr. MICIikEL DATITT will lecture in Scotland, going as far north as Wick. It maybe safely as- sumed, therefore, that before Mr. GEORGE leaves these shores he will have made us all familiar with his bold scheme for nationalising land. Other land reformers have not hesitated to advocate the right of the State to resume the property in land, but we believe they have all been in favour of granting some measure of compensation to the landlords for loss of rent. Professor WALLACE, for instance, in his work on "Land Nationalisation," says he would give compensation not only to the landowner but to any heir or heirs who might be living at the passing of any Act for nation- alising the land, or who might be born at any time before the decease of the owner. This, Professor WALLACE points out, would ensure to the owner himself, and to all persons in whom he could possibly have any personal interest, the income from the land which they enjoyed before the passing of such an Act. Mr. GEORGE, however, would do no such thing; his scheme is of a much more drastic character, for he would nationalise the land at the expense of the landowners, and at

their expense alone. To use his own words, "I do not," he observes, "propose either to purchase or to confiscate private property in land. The first would be unjust; the second needless. Let the individuals who now hold it still retain, if they want to, possession or what they are pleased to call their land. Let them continue to call it their land. Let them buy and sell, and bequeath and devise it. We may safely leave them the shell, if we take the kernel. It is not necessary to confiscate land. it is only necessary to confiscate rent." Mr. GEORGE continues, "What I therefore propose, as the simple yet sovereign remedy, which will raise wages, increase the earnings V capital. extirpate pauperism, abolish poverty, give remunerative employment to whoever wishes it, afford free scope to human powers, lessen crime, elevate morals and taste and intelligence, purify government and carry civilisation to yet nobler heights, is— 'to appropriate rent by taxation." There is no mincing matters here Mr. GEORGE arrives at his mode of taxation in a very simple manner. He proposes that the real value of the land of the country, as distin- guished from tenants' improvements, should be from time to time determined as it best can, and that then a land tax equal to the entire amount of the value should be imposed upon the proprietors. Such, in brief, is Mr. GEORGE'S scheme. There is no doubt that ' with it many people agree, and indeed Mr. GEORGE'S writing is so fascinating that even ' those who dissent from his conclusions must sympathise with him in his effo-ts to solve a difficult problem. I; is stated that in this country alone over roo,ooo copies of Pro- gress and Poverty" have been sold, and it has been translated into the German. Spanish, and other languages. Mr GEOR 1;E made his , first appearance on a public platform in Eng- land on Wednesday, when he delivered a lec- ture on his favourite subject in St. James's Hall, London. He then intimated that with the proceeds of such a land tax as he sug- gests--and which proceeds he estimates at something like three hundred millions a year —there could be given to every widow in the land, "from the lady who sits upon the throne to the widow of the poorest labourer." a pension of £roo a year; that it could pro- vide for the orphans; give every girl a mall dower; and every man, after a certain age, enough to live on for the rest of his life. All this could be done, Mr. GEORGE says, after paying the national expebditure, and still there would be more to spare. By this means poverty is to be abolished. This is a suffi- ciently roseate picture, but it is made still more roseate by the promise that in the nountry of the future "nobody will have to work hard and nobody will have to starve" Such, Mr. GEORGE tells us, is to be the ulti- mate outcome of the adoption of his pro- posal. He asserts, indeed, that the principle he advocates has already been endorsed by the English Parliament in the recent Irish Land Act, though we are afraid that there are few who will agree with him in this. ,We fail to see the principle there laid down that the land belongs to the people, and that it is theirs by right, though we confess the Act appears to tend in that direction. Without, however, in any way coinciding with Mr. GEORGE'S bold assertions, wethink it will be generally admitted that la-id does not bear its fair share of taxation, nor indeed theamount fixed by Act of Parliament; and also that it ought to be taxed much heavier. It will like- wise be admitted to be a great disadvantage to the country that the soil should be held by only a few; and further, that it is a mistake all the land of the country is not under culti- vation. There would, we believe, be some reason in compelling an owner who does Rot cultivate to relinquish possession; and some scheme of peasant proprietory ought to be matured. Before anything, however, can be done in this direction we must have a reformed House of Commons, and either a reformed House of Peers, or the present Chamber entirely abolished. In tbe -former Chamber there are no less than 198 landholders, and 79 sons and heirs of Peers who are great landowners; in the latter Chamber, of the 509 Peers, 438 are landholders possessing amongst them 14,251,132 acres, with a rental of £11,872,333. Until .there is a change in both these Chambers we can have no hope of any radical reform of the land laws. The landlords, and those interested in the land, will continue in the future as in the past to legislate for their own interests unless the people, the source of. all power, resolutely make up their minds that their voices shall be more distinctly heard in legislation. Let con- stituencies turn a deaf ear to candidates who are connected with the landed interest, and elect as their representatives gentlemen who have a public and not a personal interest to ser ye, and we venture to predict progress will then be made in the solution of the land problem.

TTLE COUNTY CORONERSHIP : THE SALARY ATTACHED TO THE OFFlcx.—As there seems to be a diversity of opinion as to the amount of the salary attaching to the office of county coroner for the West Derby district, now vacant through the fatal accident to Mr. Barker, we quote the following report of the General Finance Committee to the Court of Annual General Session, and which report is dated December 28, 1882:—" A vacancy having occurred in the office of coroner for the West Derby district, through the resignation of Mr. C. E. Driffield,on the 11th inst., the General Finance Committee have, in conformity with the standing orders, examined whether any and what alteration should be made in tbe salary attached to the said office, and beg to report that in their opinion the salary of the successor of Mr. Driffleld should be fixed at the rate of 11800 per annum, such amount to cover travelling, office, and ether expenses." This report was adopted by the court, and in accordance with its terms Mr. Barker was appointed to the office. APPOINTsaN'T NDER THE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS Any.—Mr. T. Perronet Edward Thompson, judge of the County Court of Lancashire, holden at St. Helens, has ap- pointed Mr. Joseph Bithell Leach, of the firm of J. B. and B. Leach, auctioneers, of St. Helens, Huyton, and Liver- pool, to act as bailiff to level distresses on holdings to which the above act applies in the jurisdiction of the St. Helens County Court, which includes the townships of Winelle, •Wiudl!3-with-Hardshaw. Ecelesten, Parr, Sutton, Bold, Preacot, Widnee, Widnes-with-Appleton, Crouton, Dttton, Hale, Halewood, Speke, Little Woolton Much Wool- ton, Huyton, Roby. Knowsley, Whiston, Rainf; rd, and Tar- bock. Mr. Leach is also authorised to act in any other'part of England and Wales. Similar applications were on Wed- nesday made to Mr. Thonmems, sitting at the St. Helens County Court, and granted as follows :—Mr. Riley applied on behalf of Mr. William Mills, auctioneer, Earlestown ; Mr. R. W. H. Thomas on behalf of Mr. Joseph Birchen, sem, and Mr. Joseph Birchall, jun., auctioneers, St. Helen!; and Mr. Malkin for Mr. Edwin Wood, estate and general agent, Widnes, and agent to Mr. Young, J.P. LANCASHIRE AND YORISHIGH HANIC.—The following report of tbe directors will be submitted to the shareholders at the eleventh annual general meet:og, to be held on Friday next :—From the annexed statement of the bank's accounts for the year ending 31st December, 1883, it will be seen that the net profits, together with the balance of £4,078 Bs. 3d. brought forward from the previous year, and after deduc- tion of all ordinary interest, expenses, and income tax, and providing for bad debts and for allowance of rebate on bills at 5 per cent. per annum, amount to £35,283 19s. ficl. The interim dividend of Be. per share, which was paid in July last for the half-year ending 30th June, amounted to £11,217 125.; and it is now proposed to pay a further divi- dend of 101. per share for the half-year ending 31st Decem- ber,. which will absorb an additional sum of £14,827, making a total dlvlsloe of nine per cent. for the year, clear of income tax. It is also proposed to add the sum of £5,000 to the reserve fund, and to carry to next year £4,182 7s. Bd. The reserve fund, after the addition of £3,000 as above, will amount to £105,000. During the year the new bank pre- mise! at Elland and at Bowdon have been completed and occupied. The two directors retiring by rotation are Mr. Joseph Davies and Mr. Samuel Rigby, both of whom are re- eßgible. The dividend warrants will be forwarded to the shareholders on the 11th instant.
