It will be no:iced from out advertising columns that the Farnworth New Grammar School building is to be opened on 'Thurschy next by Teed Winnerleigh. ACCIDENT AT FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCIL.OL. -- On Wednesdey Jahn Woedward, a gas fitter, w ho lives in Liver- pool, met with an accident at Fernworth Grammar School. He was at work on the roof of the new building, when he fell to the basement, a diet ince of 23 feet, breaking be his wrist. and seriously bruising his head. He was at once attended by Dr. Booth. itteeconN ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY —Oar readers will be eaatilled to learn that an effert, which will probably be saccessful, is being made to reeuscitate the Runcorn Or- chestral Society. Tile baud will he cnistituted entirely of lend arneteurs, and the first concert is expected to be given sh ;ray. Considering the local talent we possess in Run- corn, the band will no doubt be an excellent one. RUNCORN FREI CoNcERTs —The free concrts inaugura- ted by the Rev. W. Vauee still maintain their popularity, and the Ellesmere-street school was well filled op Tuesday , night, when another of the series was given under the pre- ' sidency of Mr. Isaac Stubbs. The concert was given entirely by the choir of the Widnes Methodist Free Church, and consisted of songs, glees, choruses, &c. Mr. John Betney conducted, and Mr. Alfred Ogden accompaniid. I 1E A. M. BRUNDRIT, or RUNCORN.—The last of the ! fast passages made by the schooner A. M. Brundrit, recently I launched from the yard of Messrs. Brundrit and Co., was I that completed on Saturday night. The vessel left Tar- mouth on Monday morning, and arrived in Liverpool on the following Siturday. This is considered almost an ex- traordinary passage, and is a proof of the excellence of Run- corn vessels and seamen. HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.-011 Monday ,evening the above society had a soiree in the Trinity Wesleyan Sunday school, at which the following gentle- men made speechee :—Rev 8 llees, Messrs R Hughes, S Barrow, A Rowe, sea and J Hancock. Songs were given by Miss Edwards, Mr J H GSMOD, and the Secretary. Messrs W Rowe and John Basnett contributed very much te the enjoyment of those present by giving humourous readings. SINGULAR INCIDENT AT RUNCORN —Ab3tH half-past one on Wednesday morning P.S. Loundes found Mr. H. Sefton, nightsoil contractor, of Ivy Cottage, Halton, lying in an un- conscious condition in Halton-road. The tricycle upon which he had been riding home was lying u eon him, and it was thoueht that Mr Sefton had met with an accident. He was removed into Mr. Haddock's house, where Mr. Car- ruthers quickly attended upon him, and said he had been seized with an epileptic fit. We are glad to say he is in a fair way to recovery. RUNCORN TM CA. HISTORICAL SOCIETY.—At the fort- nightly meeting of this society, held on Thursday evening, Mr. W. J. Duncombe Pink, F.R.H.S., held a lecture on "Six Centuries of Prussian rule" to a large audience. Mr. James Craig presided. The lecture was an exhaustive des- cription of the yeti ius Prussian dynasties, from the earliest times to the last scene in the eventful history of the Empire when Paris was in flames and the people of France ran- quished. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer on the motion of Mr. S. C. Beckett, seconded by 15Ir. Cover try A SATURDAY NIGIIT DISTURI.ANCE IN VICTORIA-ROAD.— At Widnes Police Court, on Moeday, before Mr. G. Pillting- ton, Thomas Costello was charged with being drunk and damaging police uniform.—P.C. Cotier said that on Satur- day night about ten o'clock he was in Victoria-road. He I saw the defendant with another young man and his wife, all being drunk, go into the Guards publichguse. He fol- lowed them in and told them they had better go home. The prisoner became very violent, seized him by the coat, which he damaged to the extent of is 6d. Several witnesses for the defence stated that the constable coLared the prisoner first, threw him to the ground and put his knee upon him.—The prisoner was ordered to. pay 17s. or go to goal for a fort- ' night. AGED PEOPLE'S TREAT AT RUNCORN. The Lannual Christmas treat to aged people will take place in Runcorn Public Hall on Thursday evening next. It will be remem- bered that this treat was inaugurated last year by. the Com- mittee of the Young Men's Christian Association, who enter- ' tained about 700 old people to tea, and then provided for them j an excellent entertainment, which the audience seemed to I greatly enjoy. ' On this occasion, however, the public have I not responded quite 90 freely as last year, and only 4001 tickets have been distributed. Amongst this number, how- ever, are included all the aged persons of somewhat indigent circumstances, and no doubt they will pass an agreeable evening, as a first class entertainment has been arranged for. The public will be admitted tie witness the proceedings on payment of 6d. each. LACROSSE : WIDNES V. ST. HELENS.—On Saturday. these clubs played their return match on The Widnes ground. The hone team again proved too strong for the visitors, winning by 7 goals to 1. During the first half Widnes kept the ball among their attacks, giving the St. Helens goalkeeper I plenty of work, and scored four goals while their opponents I I scored 1. After half time, 'St. Helens played with more I determination, the ball trundling to all parts of the field. I Three more goals, however, were scored by Widnes. E. F. I Gossage, at third home, did most work for Widnes, and all I the men showed better combined play than on previous occasions. The pick of the St. Helens team were Hartley and Varley, whose determined goalkeeping frustrated many hard shots from the Widnes homes. Helens: H Varley, M liammill, A C Carr, A Robinson, J J Hartley, E Foreman, I S Robinson. Booth, R Hosker, S Taylor, Tyrer, J Hough. 1 fame to his beautiful =do! Emma forte, better known as Nelson's Lady Hamilton, but a picture on these walls, the ] portrait of Mr. Jordan in the Country Girl, shows bow 1 fascinatingly he could put a lovely W-,man on his canvas. ] Near this hangs Sir Joshua's masterpiece. Sheridan's ] lovely bride as St. Cecilia 8-.3/!ti at the or .ain, two little ' angels liateuing in delight to her music. Mrs. Sheridon was the lovely Miss Liniey—heaury must have favoured that family, as tier loyalties portrait, by Crainstiorough, at Dulwich, silv9red very cfrarl v. One naturally lingers ] longest over the English pictures, bat tte idi foreign ' schools are well represented. There is a magnificent Murillo, duly assigned the place of honciir in the largest gallery. We know him in this country fur his sacred pieces. In Spain he is a portrait painter, second only to Velusquta. The splendid canvas from Lord Lansdowne's collection is a portrait of Murillo's great friend, Don Jastino, Canon of Seville, for whom the artist painted the famous altar piece in the church of St. Maria, and also the pictures in the hospital of the city. The canvas seems as fresh as when it left Murillo's easel, just 2C4 years ago. The explanation is that • for IfflO years it remained in the refectory of the hospital. Vandvell's Charles I. and his Henrietta Maria—the most splendid of all his many portraits of his patrons—flank this picture, and make it very hard to say which is the finest portrait in the gallery. .

The criminal classes are getting almost too 'cute for the officers of Justice. I have several times mentioned how bad shillings and half-crowns, and indeed sovereigns and half-sovereigns have multiplied within the last couple of Tears. The Grand Jury drew the attention of the Recorder to it this week, and suggested that " something should be done." They did not, however, suggest what the something should be. Ever since the sale of Hanoverian tokens was stopped the fabrication of false sovereigns has incresied. I do not say it is propter hoc ; but I am sore it is post hot. Another thing is that the Deputy Recorder is inclined to give short sentences. Now I have never heard of a reformed caiaer, and am told that the convict always returns to his old game, the shorter the sentence the sooner he is again at liberty to swell the catalogue of offence against the Mint. The •Treasery officials seem to know the personal appearance of nearly all their clients.

This being the first week in the new year, there was a most interesting transformation scene got up—of all places ia London—at the Old Bailey: Some prisoners were spending the night Mare their trial in the seclusion of a prison cell. It was dull, but they were bright; for it occurred to them that a change of clothes might improve their prosdects, if not their appearance, on the next morning, The plan was made and was carried out. The prisoners had been before the magistrates, and one had been tined, and the other, the more serious offender, had been committed for trial. They changed garments. The woman, who was to be tried, escaped in the morning in the clothed of the woman who bad only to pay a pecuniary penalty, and both offenders read with the greatest interest the account of their escape in the evening papers. TIIO Judge—Mr. Kerr— being naturally very angry at once threw all the blame on the unfortunate Public Prosecutor.

We are this week having a kind of competitive examina- tion amongst the railway companies as to which shall devise the best electric light for their carriages. On Monday the Metropolitan train that runs the short distance from Ken- sington to Putney was quite brilliant with swan lights. The success was undoubted, and I am told the cost was con- siderably less than that of gas. But no sooner was the ex- periment tried than it was abandoned. All through the week the carriages have been plying from one terminus to the other with the electric appliances ready and unused, end the gas bcrning dimly beside them. This company is always testing, trying, and abandoning. 'The Brighton Company, who also this week put on electricity as the illuminant of one of their trains, is continuing it, and we shall probably see the whole of the rolling stock fitted up with the new lamps—if the very simple machinery devised by one of the officials for developing the current is found to work. Of course, the rival company are always eager to trump their antagonist's lead. The South-Eastern don't care very much for home traffic, but having faith in Folke- stone as the future key to the Continert, they spare nothing to make their foreign system perfect. They are so very well abused that it i 3 only fair to give them praise when they merit it. I bear that at the present moment that they are altering their saloon carriages to suit illumination by electricity. With these different lines each trying its one method we must Neon arrive at whist is best and cheapest. Other companies are quite content to have the experiment tried for them without incurring any expense. They believe in the survival of the fittest.
ATTEMPTED BURGLARY AT RUN- CORN PARISH CHURCH.

Between Tuesday night and Wednesday morning a daring, but happily unsuccessful, attempt to rob Runcorn Parisi, Church was made. An entrance to the vestry was effected by prising open a window and then pulling bock the fastener. The object of the burglars was evidently to cirry off the plate, but although there were several oaken cupboards in the vestry, they had made straight for the one which contained the valuable plate, thus showing that they must have possessed some knowledge of the interior arrangements. The lock, however, resisted alt their efforts, as the marks on the door show, and even had they succeeded in opening the cupboard it would have been a task of some difficulty to break open the safe. There were several articles lying about the room, but none of these were touchtd. The police have no clue to the would-be robbers.

About sixty property owners were invited to meet the Highway Committee of the Widnes Local Board, on Thurs- day afternoon, with respect to the making or repairing of the streets in which their property is situated, a list of which is included in our report of the Board's proceedings on Tuesday. The followinc; members of the Local Board were present :—Messts. J. Midwood (chairman of the com- mittee), F. Martley, B. Dutton. J. Houghton, F. H. Pank- burst, S. Sadler, R. Webster, E. Johnson, D. Wright ; and the following pronerty owners and agents—Messrs. James Kent, E. Wood, A. Farrant, T. Davies, T. Watson, H. White- side, J. W. Carlile, John Green, J. Ward, Thomas Fisher, James Urnaston, Proud, Win. Sniith, J. Pace, J. Hewitt, Thos. Grundy, Joe. White, Thos. Fogg, J. Dickson, J. W. Lightburn, W. Fisher, Wm. Hailwood, Joseph Ireland, Taylor, Critchley, F. Nield, T. Rimmer, and Singleton. The Chairman explained that the Local Board bad re- ceived numerous complaints about the streets named, and they had thought it the best plan to call the property owners together in order to ascertain whether they were willing to have the streets made or keep them in repair. A few owners present were in favour of having the streets made, but the majority seemed to be in favour of deferring the work for 12 months, when trade might have improved. Eventually the Chairman said the .whole matter woald be carefully considered by the Board so that an amicable arrangement might be arrived at.—On the motion of Mr. Carlile, seconded by Mr. Ward, a vote of thanks was ac- corded to the chairman and the members of the Highway Committee for their kindness.

A letter, tinder date the sth January, was read from the Board of Trade, stating with reference to the application for permission to construct a sewer outfall in the River Weaver near Frodsham Bridge, that upon the receipt of the sum of 2s ed., as a nominal acknowledgment of the rights and interests of the Crown in the tidal lands which would be interfered with, together with a duplicate of the plan en- closed in the letter from the Board, the formal approval of the Board of Trade would be inscribed on both sets of plans, one of which would be retained in the records of that office, and the other returned to them as the Authority of the Runcorn Union Rural Sanitary Authority, so far as the interests of navigation were concerned, for proceeding with the work.

div.p: FEVER OTJTEREAK.

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported as follows :—" I have to report an outbreak of typhoid fever at Bradley, at a cottage occupied by Thomas Grine. Four persons in all have been attacked by the disease, viz., Mary Once, aged 31 years, , wife of Thomas Grice ; Sarah Grice, aged 10 years; Mar- garet Grine, aged eight years; and George Grine, aged six years, children of Thomas Grice. The son George is now convalescent, and has been removed; the three others are still very ill. The usual methods of isolation and disinfec- tion have been recommended to be carried out, as well as the disinfection and burial at all excreta. I trust' these measures will prevent an extension of the disease. I have to remark that the pigstyes are much too near the houses, and measures should be taken to prevent them from beißg used. The astipit to one of the privies also requires cover- ing. I can, find no fault with any other of the sanitary ar- rangements, nor with the milk and water supply." THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S QUARTE ELY REPORT. The quarterly report of the Medical Officer was read. It stated that durinr, the quarter ending December 31st, 1853, the registrar's returns recorded 149 births and SS deaths in the throe districts comprised in the Rural Sanitary district of the Runcorn Union. Of the births 73 were males and 78 females,—birth-rate of 77 per 1,000 as against 160— birth-rate 8.3 per 1,000—during the corresponding quarter of 1882. Of the deaths 57 were males and 31 were females —death-rate 45 per 1,000—as against 83—death-rate 43 per I,ooo—during the corresponding quarter of 1882. Thirty-three were under five years of age, 19 of those being under one year, and 55 were five years and up, wards.

div.head: HALF-HOLIDAY MOVEMENT AT WIDNES.
div.p: HALF-HOLIDAY MOVEMENT AT WIDNES.

An adjourned meeting of the tradesmen of Whines, with respect to the Shopkeepers Half-holiday Movement which was started some weeks ago, was held at the officers'-room of the Volunteer Hall on Thursday evening. Mr. Warhan was voted to the chair, and there were present :—Messrs. Briscoe, T. Smith, Peate (secretary), Lea, Booth, Read, Stead, F H. Pankhurst, Brorkes, %V. Tehbutr, G. H. Whar- ton, McCollam, Scales and Salter (reprysentative), H. N. Wharton, F. Tehbutt, and Sandland. 'The deputation ap- pointed the previous week had completed their canvass of the shopkeepers in the town, and Mr. Peete re- ported that all the tailors were agreeable to close on Thurs- day afternoon, and the drapers were also favourable with the exception of Mr. Briggs, of Mersey-road, while Mr. Birchall had not given a decisive answer, but there was no doubt that it would be in favour of the half holiday. Amongst the grocers there was not the same unanimity of opinion. Mr. Samuel Sadler was agreeable to close his establishment if Mr. Webster would follow the same course, while Mr. Johnson, of St. Helens, who has three shops in the town, had not been approached on the subject. It wee generally felt tbs.; if Mr. Johnson would agree to fall in with the movement, that the grocers would unanimously do the same. A deputatioa was therefore appointed to specially but- chers upon ad Mr. not Johnhseoenn generally as it was thought they would be unable to fall in with the arrangement on ' account of the peculiar nature of their business. With the exception of Mr. Matthews, rreapilovrt. canvassed, the bootmakers wished for the half holiday, but as Mr. i Matthews was very decided in his opinion not to close, the trade declined to do so. On the motion of Mr. Sandi, and seconded by Mr. Booth, it was decided to advertise that the 4rapers an clothiers would on and from the first Thursday in February, at oue o'clock, close their establishments for a half day each week. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

THE OPPOSITION AND THE SPEAKER - THE THEATRES-GILBERT AND SULLIVAN'S NEW OPERA-THE ENGLISH OPERA-THE PANTO- MIME-MESS KATE VIUGHAN-OLD MASTERS AT BURLINGTON HOUSE-COINERS-THEATRE ROYAL, OLD BAILEY-ELECTRICITY-AND THE RAILWAY COMPANIES.
LONDON, TuunsDAT.

I hear it is possible that after all there will be no contest for the Speaker's chair. The Opposition knew very well that the conclusion would be foregone. What would be the advantage of a barren defeat? They could not show their strength, and they might show their weakness. It is now suggested that Mr. Peel's nomination should be met by a speech from Sir Stafford, intimating that .acquiescence was not to he taken as a matter of course, and that this occasion should be no pr,cedent for the course to be adopted at the next Parliament. The Opposition, in fact, is in this difficulty, that It is not yet at all agreed who its speaker should be. To decide now would be premature, and yet to put forward an opponent to Mr. Peel would be almost equivalent to a decision. Sir Nlatthew Ridley has been spoken of; that is to say there was a rumour, and the rumour spread and gained in supposed authority, but the party have a strong allegiance to Mr. Raikes, who has been tried and not found wanting. If he is willing to serte, neither Sir Matthew, nor Mr. Sclater-Bootb, is likely to be preferred. The course the Opposition will take has not yet been absolutely settled, but I know that its leader has been consulting with many members of the party on the subjeet, and that at present be inclines to the course I have sketched.

In the musical world the past week was marked by two oonspieuous events—the production of a new play at the Surrey, and of a new opera at Covent Garden. ‘4 Piincese Ida" was most favourably received, but then the verdict of a first night is not always conclusive unless when it ends ia the damnation of the piece. Of the brutal sincerity of that kind of verdict there can be no possible doubt. "Princess Ida" seemi to have less spontaniety than the works which have preceded it on the same boards. Mr. Gilbert moved as if he was hampered, and so in truth he was He has merely suited his old comic opera, written a dozen years ago, to the style which he has taught his public to expect, and the result is that there is a sense of piecing and fitting and altering felt all through the work. More- over, there is no novelty in it, no surprises, and but little dramatic interest. The literary merit is certainly above average, though not above Mr. (filbert's average. But we know what we are going to see. It is a foregone conclusion, and the satire on women as lords of the creation is tame and eat. In Pinafore and Patience Mr. Gilbert shot folly as it flew past him; in the Pirates and lolanthe the plots were complicated, ingenious, and interesting, but the Princess disappoints, for the very illogical reason that we know what we may expect. The music is better than the libretto, and shows a change, or rather an advance, in the com- poser's style. Xhe songs are fewer and not BO good, the concerted music more ambitious, more elaborate, and more masterly. The piece has been mounted sump- tuously, and if only Mr. Gilbert had given Mr. Gressmith more lines, and if Nature had given Miss Braham more inches, the distribution of the parts would have been perfect. An insignificant Amazon is rather an anti-climax. Miss Bralam acts the part perfectly., but does not look it. It was strange that the production of this opera should, as in the case of "The Magic Ring" only a few weeks ago, be attended with the sudden illness of the composer. The truth ie that after attending many rehear- sals, and drilling orchestra and chorus indefatigably, the task of conducting on a first night is felt to be very severe. Sir Arthur, happily, is in no danger, needing only some rest, which he is well alge to take, and Mr. Clay seems to have turned the corner of a danger about which his friends have been undisguieedly anxious.

The other event of the week has been the opening of Covent Garden for a winter season of English opera. It is too soon yet to predict how a venture that is certainly to be recommended for its courage may turn out. On Monday a new opera was produced with success, though not of a very rapturoos kind. Such deficiency as there was was felt to be more the composer's fault than that of the performers. The Pied Piper of Hamelin is by Victor Nessler, a young Ger- man composer, and has had considerable success abroad. It will be followed by Faust and Trovatore, and the standard favorites.. The company seems to consist chiefly of seces- sionists from Carl Rosa's troupe. There is Miss Gaylord and Miss Franklein, Mr. Packard and Mr. Fox. One would wish a smaller theatre could have been secured. The sea- son is very short, and plenty of variety may bring full houses.

On Monday night the performance at Drury-lane went off very briskly. It was "Twelfth Night," and when the cur- tain fell a gigantic cake was cut up amongst the large population of small children who figure in the pantomime. I think in some respects it is the best that has ever been ; seen in Drury-lane. The libretto is poor, but fortunately education has not yet converted young children into dramatic critics, and adults don't expect much novelty from Cinderella. But the dresses are really very beautiful in colour, and the grouping most artistically arranged. Mies Vaughan has been got up after Millais' Cinderella, and looks very lovely. I suppose her diamonds are the most beautiful things about her, and are certainly the most costly, but personally I should most admire her dancing and her wigs. Is these two attractions she stands unrivalled amongst our present stage beauties. That part of her head which is generally called the outside has been furnished with a lavishness of expenditure which is only justified, I suppose, by what the wig covers. I think it is hundreds of pounds that one chetselicre cost—the one with the huge curls of flossy silk, not the popular gold of the modern dye that looks so exactly like the feathers of a moulting green canary, but a rich auburn colour, that sets off her pretty face. The wigs are now in their cases, and so are the dia- monds. The pretty actress sprained her leg on Tuesday, and for a week, at least, her dancing nights are over. The Amademy opened on Monday with a superb exhibi- tion. It was expected it would be a failure, and it has turned out a triumph. The usual classification has been adopted, and the first room is filled with representative can- vases of the British school of the last century. There is a magnificent collection. A view of the Thames with ship- ping and boats painted, with all the breadth and warmth and brownness of the Dutch school. It was only in the last period of his art that Sir Augustus adopted the cold grey tones which we find in his smaller pictures by which, unfortunately he is most generally known. Here, too, are some Reynolds that show the Grosvenor Exhibition, exhaustive as it seems, has still left some of the grandest works outside its walls. This room abounds with curiosi- ties. There are some "family pieces " by Hogarth-0116 with the painter himself playing a fiddle, and another a Breakfast piece," where some titled persons are collected round the refreshment of a tea-pot, all the portraits very characteristic and rather stiff. Then there is a picture of the Merchant of .Venice as it was given just a centary ago. Lofluiry, R.A., is the painter. What would Mr. Irving or Mr. Wilson Barrett say if they saw it. In those days stage Doges were dressed like English judges, and in fact one of the dignitaries is a portrait of Lord Mansfield. The picture was painted for a memorable occasion. It represents the last appearance of Macklin as Shylock, the actor having then completed his 90th year. In the large gallery are some splendid Romneys. This was the one rival whom the amiable Sir Joshua never could tolerate. He always alluded to him as "that man in Cavendish-street." Rom- ney's life, as told by Hayley, is a romance, and the first picture in the large gallery is a portrait of the biographer L and his subject. The fussy Hayley is in the foreground look- log as inspired as he can—a sort of glorified Duke of Wel- lington, while Flaznian with deft fingers models the least which is to transmit to posterity the features of this third- rate poet. Romney himself peers out from the corners, an amused spectator of the whole scene. This artist has scarcely Eot his due. He owed, perhaps, a large share of his

Before the ordinary: busiTess---oi the meeting was com- menced, a short conversation took pince with regard to the election, several members expressing disutisfaction with the time fixed by the returning officer. it wss thought that if possible, the time of holding the triennial election saould be changed, and it was understood that before the next election the 'Board would memorialise the returning officer on the subject. —The CLBRJE produced a mrtilicate of the returning officer, stating that the following had been duly elected members of the Board in conformity with the requirements of the Education Act: Revs. Canon Barcian and W. div.head: _SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION WANTED.
div.p: _SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION WANTED.

The question of school accommodation arose, the CLERK remarking that if they took the population and divided it by one-sixth and one-seventh, and took the tiiimbers allowed \for floe-attenders, it was perfectly obvious there was no defi- ciency of school accommodation, but it was just as true there was a deficiency of accommodation for girls while there was an excess of accommodation for infants.—Mr. SIMPSON remarked that the reason why the accommodation for girls was so large at the Wesleyan School was because they had a very large ciass-room, which was included in the accommodation provided.—The CLERK: Practically your school is full, but if measured according to the arrange- ments of the Education Department it would show a %atter of over some 60 children. He pointed out that if they took the number of girls on the rolls of all the girls' schools in the town for the last quarter, they /would find 118 more girls whose names were down for whom there were no places, bnt that might be elucidated as it was possible that some of the girls' names might appear in itwo or more schools. At the last meeting of the committee they had a man there who protested that his girl could not get into school. That morning she had been to every school in the town, and had not been able to get admitted. It was quite plain that if they had girls going to school with the pence in'their hands and unaole to get in it was impossible to proceed against the parents of girls who did not attend. If they took the number of girls on the rolls in round 'figures they had. 200 more girls than there was accommoda- tion provided for, but if they took the average attendance it would give them very Basall room for any girls seeking ad- mission.—Reference was made to provision for the residuum ' of the population.—The Catanues observed that somebody must have the residuum—even if they had to provide a school for thern.—Tne CLERK said they must educate the residuum, or the Education Acts were nugatory.—Mr. Parr- CHARD thought that looking at the fact that the boundaries of the township had been recently altered, and that there was a probability if the Canal Boats Amendment Act was 'passed that they would have to provide for a large number of boat children, it would not be wise to press the matter at the present time. He suggesed that a temporary arrange- ment should be made by the Board hiring a building which the girls might attend.—The CLnatt said if the Board took a temporary school it meant spending a great deal of money.— Mr. PRITCHARD said that was what be MIS afraid of, but it would only be a temporary arrangement, and the Depart- ment might sanction it when they knew that they were in- tending to provide a new school.—Mr. Noumax thought the Ellesmere-street school, if it could be obtained, would be a very suitable building, or probably the school in Regent- street.—The CHAIRMAN thought Ellesmere-street school the most suitable.—The CLERK stated that in the various schools there was now accommodation for 994 boys and 706 girls. He laid before the Board the plans which were pre- pared some time ago by Messrs. F. and G. Holmes, archi- tects, for alterations and additions to the Mill Brow School, which would give them accommodation for 260 boys and girls.—The Board directed the Clerk to consult with the architects with regard to the suggested alters- tions.—A Government return containing a number of questions which had to be answered was submitted.— The CLERK suggested that the return should be filled up tj the effect that there was a deficiency of school accommoda- tion In the district for'girle, and accommodation was re- quired for 260 more. The accommodation for boys and infants was ample. He pointed out that the average at- tendance of girls was 80 per cent., while the average for boys, girls, and infants combined was 75 per cent. If the I Board provided accommodation for girls and allowed pri- vate enterprise to find accommodation for infants, the rate- payers would have the best of the bargain. A short discussion took place on the inconvenience of the present mode of remitting fees through the Guardians of persons who were unable to pay them. It was pointed out that a much better system would be for the Board to remit the fees, the Board of Guardians accepting the School Boaid's decisions without question. This system, it was observed, was in use at Widnes. The Clerk remarked that the Board of Gnardianawas a body distinct from the School Board, with certain duties assigned to it by Act of Parlia- ment, and declined to become merely a recording authority.
IMPORTANT DISCUSSION: MR. SIMPSON AND THE CLERK.

A man named Henry Skelding brought his girl, Mary Alice, before the Board to complain that he could not get her admitted into a school.—ln reply to the, Clerk, the girl said she went to tirafiville-street School that morning, that the teacher declined to receive her because there was Is 4d owing by her father for school fees.—Mr. SIMPSON informed the man, who said he was a ship painter, that he could not expect the teacher to take the child into school when he owed Is 4d and the girl only took 41.—SKELDING : I have not got the money.—Mr. SIMPSON : How can you expect your child to be educated unless you Day the fees 2—SHELD- ING replied that he would pay the fees when he got the money.—After some further observations from Mr. SIMPSON to the man, the CLERK pointed out that the teachers were not bound to take children into school unless they took the fees. If they did take them and allowed them to get into debt they could only re- cover the debt as they recovered for groceries. They could not in respect to the next week say "We shall not take the child into the school unless you pay is 4d," be- cause if they did the action of the School Board authority would fall to the ground altogether' and the school jeopar- dised its grant.—Mr. SIMPSON: Of course, the managers understand that, but is it right 2-The CLERK :It is one of the Board's chief difficulties—it is almost our greatest difficulty we have to contend with—and if a child is not admitted into a school when there is room for it, the whole machinery of the School Board is absolutely worthless.—Mr. StarrsoN said in this case the daughter was allowedeo go to school for two or three weeks without paying the fees, and now the parent insisted upon the child being taken into the school, without a single word being said as to arrears. He asked was it fair. The manager of any school in the town would he prepared to run the same risk sooner than educate chil- dren under such conditions. It was not the thing when a man came in this way for the Clerk of the Board to tell him so plainly that he can insist upon the child being ad- mitted into the school. The man would go and make it known generally,and all the parents who owed fees for their children would make the best of this, and insist upon their children being admitted into the school.— The CLERK: es regards the clerk, it is in his duty.—Mr. SterrsoN: The clerk has nuthing to do with the managers of other schools.—The CLERK observed that the man's peel- ' tion was this, that if be did not get his child into school he would be prosecuted.—Mr. SIMPSON: Why cannot the father go and say " If you take the child in I shall be able to pay the arrears shortly and I will do so."—The CLERK : He says be did so. It is not a new case.—ln answer to Mr. NORMAR Skelding said he had not been to school that morn- ing.—Mr. SIMPSON: It ices I expected.—The CLERK: But the child went.—The CruanstaN (to Skelding) They would not refuse to admit the child if you had said you would pay the arrears as soon as you could.—Mr. NORMAN: I quite agree with Mr. Simpson.—Mr. SIMPSON: It is taking an un- fair advantage of the teachers to put them in such a position as that—even for the matter to be talked about in the Board. —The CLERK: The teachers have it all in their own bands. Why do they let them get into debt 7—Mr. SIMPSON : When they come and say I cannot possibly pay now but I will pay shortly, the teacher's compassion is excited. Then th.y don't do it, and they come and insist upon the child going in the school.—The CLERK: Bowyer, is not that one of the ereat difficulties you have to deal with 7—The Visrroß: Yes.—The CLERK: Bowyer has complained to me many times.—SKELDING said the teachers at Granville-street told him to take his child to some other school. The Board said if he did not send his child to school they would sum- mon him. What was he to do ? He had lout half a day now, when be might have earned enough to pay the school fees for two or three months.—Mr. SIMPSON: He said he had no work, and he might have gone to school this morning.— SHELDING Said he was a jobbing painter, and had to look for work.—Mr. NORMAN advised him to go to Miss Peacock after dinner and promise to pay the arrears, and she would admit the girl.— Skelding then left the room; and the CLERK observed that they could not work the Education Act to make it pleasant all round. Somebody Must find it unpleasant—either the teacher or the father. It was nios more the father's duty to go with the child than it was ele- mentary s his duty to go. If the child presented itself atapb school within the proper hours, with hthe fees in its hands, there was nothing more to be done, parents to get into providing there is room, and if the teacher chose to allow arrears they must make the best of it,thpat was all.—Mr. SrmesoN: I don't think it is wise and considerate to the managers of schools for the man to be told so plainly that Ihe is justified in his position—that he can insist upon his daughter being admitted into school or else he can take such steps as will lead to the reduction of the grant at Granville. street school.— The CHAIRMAN: It rather justifies what his been said outside that there are too many managers on the Board. The CLERK: I am not a representative of the managers. I am a public official. I am here as clerk to an Authority elected by the ratepayers, and I am here-as far as I can, and I intend to do it—to protect the interest of the ratepayers. Whether it is the interests of the managers or not it is not for me to inquire. That is my answer.—Mr. SIMPSON ad- mitted that there was a feeling against the managers sitting on the Board, and he had felt rather glad at the idea of retiring and for other reasons; that there would then be one manager less on the Board. Ile thought it would be a good thing if the whole of the managers ot schools were to retire and let there be a Board elected independently of managers and denominational interests, and let tkete see what they could do.—The CLERK: I am a Manager my- elf, I believe.—Mr. Sammie (smiling) : of course there are managers and managers.—lt was observed that Skelding had been before the Board again and again.—Mr. 3oßatax : Ile II a bad man.—The CLERK: But

that is no 'reason why he should be done an injustice.— Mr. SruPsoN objected to tile man being told plainlythat if be only took proceedings against the school he could get the grant stopped.—Mr. Liu: We are no doubt in the same fix as you are —Mr. PRITCHAICrt The only ,remedy is "No credit." That is the only cure for it.—Tae discussion then ceased.

MR. SLMPSON'S FAREWELL. Mr. SrraPsow said as this would be the last meeting he would have the pleasure of attending, be hoped they would allow him to propose a vote of thanks to the Chairman for his services during the past two years. He did not need to tell them of the way. in which Canon Barclay bad dis- charged the duties of the office. The kindness, courtesy, and consideration which he had shown both to the mem- bers of the Board, and also to the parents and others who had to come before them from time to time, he WAS sure must have given great satisfaction to all the members of the Board. It was very pleasant to look back upon the laic three years and think of the very great Unanimity and kindly feeling which be believed had existed during .the whole of the time. (Hear, hear.) He believed they had all wished as far as they possibly could to carry out the intentions of the Education Act, and to promote the education of the children of Runcorn in the best ay they possibly could, and there had been no difference ok opinion. They had talked things over and they had all agreed as to what was the best course to take, and so the matter had been settled without having come to a vote upon it. Mr: Pancake") seconded the motion, and said he was care the members would agree with the observations made by Mn. Simpson with regard to Canon Barclay's good offices in the chair. This period had been somewhat uneventful in the history of the Board. Their duty bad been consider- ably confined to forcing the attendance of children at school, and he thought they might say that good results had followed even from that particular duty. They had now in average attendance about 300 children more than were in attendance three Years ago. The CLERK put the motion to the meting, and it was iiarried unanimously. _

The CHAIRMAN said he was very much obliged, especially to Mr. Simpson, for the kind observations he had made, and to the members for so cordially carrying the motion. They were all very sorry to lose the benefit of Mr. Simpson s services. For regularity and punctuality of attendance he had set some of them, not excepting himself, A very good example. For courtesy and harmony and (he business habits which he had brought to bear upon the business of the Board they would miss him very touch indeed, and he was indeed sorry to lose the benefit of his services. He hoped he would have in his retirement that comfort wkich he deserved—(hear, hear)—after a lung *aurae of public life. He was very mach obliged to then for the kind man- ner in which they had recognised his services, and c eluded by moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Simpson.—Mr. BaISCOE had great pleasure in seconding the motion. In the absence of the chairman Mr. nirnpson had always dis- charged the duties of the office in a very becoming meaner. —Mr. PRITCHARD supported the motion, expressing regret at Mr. Sirnpson's retirement, and referring to his long con- nection with educational matters in the town.—Mr. NOR- MAN was sure no one felt the retirement of Mr. Simpson more than be did, and he endorsed all that had been said with regard to Mr. Simpson and the Criairman.—The motion was carried unanirnously.—Mr. SiMpSON, in replying, said he had felt a good deal in saying farewell to gentlemen he bad been in the habit of meeting with month after month for such a length of time. He bad been a manager of schools for nearly 33 years, and he bad taken very great interest in the education of children. He became a Sunday School teacher when he was about nine years of age, and having been brought in contact with chil- dren so young, and continuing his connection year after year, he supposed he was led to take greater interest in the welfare of children than perhaps he might have done. He had always taken great pleasure in doing wnat be could in promoting the education of children in Runcorn. When the School Board was formed, he must confess, he should have felt very much disappointed if he had not been returned as one of the members. He had' felt grateful during the last nine years that he had been a member of the Board, and it had been very pleasant to meet month after month with gen- tlemen who were interested in educatioe, and in discussing what they could to promote the great object they had in view. It was not because he felt les., interest in the matter of edu- cation at all, but he really thought that it would be better if some one who was not a school manager were to take the place—but at all events some one who had all his faculties, and could really express the views which he might have in a manner which he (Mr. Simpson) had not been sometimes able to do. With regard to the clerk, he should like to say that whatever might have been said that morning they had had an efficient clerk during the last nine years. (Hear, hear.) He did not think they could have found a gentle- man who would have discharged the duties of the office more efficiently, and with less trouble and less anxiety to the Board, than Mr. Rigby bad done. He was very glad that they appointed him in the firit instance, and that each suc- cessive Beard had ratified the appointment which they made nine years ago. He trusted that whatever the future of the Board might be, that the cause of education would be more efficiently carried out than it had been in the past. It was with feelinge of great regret on many accounts that he said "farewell," and he must say with the kindliest feel- ings towards each member of the Board and Mr. Rigby, the clerk, and also towards Mr. Bowyer, a very efficient officer they had had working since very soon after the formation of the Board.—The CLERK .said perhaps he might be allowed I to add his tribute of regret at Mr. Simpson's retirement, and say with the members of the Board that at his hands they had received every manifestation of sympathy and of courtesy, and the ratepayers to a larger extent than they were aware of had benefited by his experience and by his regularity of attendance. With respect to the remarks that were made that evening. the Clerk explained that he took his action in juatice to the man, and the only warning he could give teachers and Managers was not to allow children in school who did not bring their* pence with them. • His last words to Mr. Simpson in wishing him farewell and ex- pressing his great regret that he was going were that he (the clerk) and everybody else present hoped he would have a happy future in store. (Hear, bear.) The meeting then terminated. VISITORS' REPORT.

The prisoner pleaded guilty to threatening Mr. Bowyer, but added that he did not mean to do him any harm, and he thought no more of the matter after he had used the threats*. div.head: LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL
div.p: THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL
TRADE.

A somewhat despondent tone characterised the market on Tuesday, and the year may be said to have opened dis- couragingly so far as business in the iron trade of the Man- chester district is concerned. There was a fairly good at- tendance on 'Change, but the actual weight of business doing was very small, and the tendency of the market was in a downward direction. The most unsatisfactory feature el the market is the fact that although iron is now being offered at prices which would have been an inducement prior to the holidays, buyers still hold back. Local and district makers of pig iron are nominally holding on to the basis of the rates ruling at the close of last year, Lancashire makers still quoting 455, and Lincolnshire 44s 10d to 45s 106, less 21 for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester. At these figures, however, business is im- practicable, as there are brands of pig iron being offered in this district not only at prices very much under these, but with sellers open to book for long forward delivery at low rates. In finished iron quoted prices nominally are un- changed ; there is, however, very little doing; many of the makers are getting short of work, and the market is weak. The average prices remain at £6 to £6 2s 66 for bars, £d 7s dd for hoops, and £7 15s for sheets, delivered into the Manchester district; but it can scarcely be said that values are really tested by the small weight of actual business doing.— Business in the coal trade of this district opens after the holidays with only a moderate demand for all descriptions of round coal. but there is an absence of any actual pres- sure of supplies upon the market, owing to the restriction of the output. The exceptional mildness of the season is tending to curtail requirements for house-fire purposes, and the general slackness in trade causes the demand for the commoner sorts for iron-making and steam purposes to be only limited. There is no general material alteration in quoted rates, but in some cases colliery proprietors who have been holding out for the top rates have given way 61 per ton, and the tendency of prices is in a downward direc- tion. At the pit mouth the average prices for best coal re- mains at 103 to 10$ 61; seconds 8s to 83 66: and common round coal 6s to 7s per ton. Engine classes of fuel are in moderate demand at about late rates, burgv fetching about 4s gol to ss, and good ordinary slack 3s to 4s per ton, with a little more being got for some of the best sorts. Shipping has been only quiet, with Lancashire steam coal not averag- ing more than Sc to fis 3d per ton, delivered at Garston Docks or the high level at Liverpool.

And in this shape, transformed, for the third time by the aid of the hundred pounds re- ward, the reader meets again Gentleman Jack. He is evidently in great spirits, and with good reason. For the first time in his life, his pockets are filled with money, the possession of which there are no creditors near to dispute; he is quit of the army; be is going, no he thinks, to meet Stephen; and above and before all he feels once more that he is in appearanc,, aspect, and prospeets again Gentleman Jack, in spite of the cockade, and of all he desires it to imply, for the present. "So this is the Earl's garden ?" he is saying to the ser- vant, as he takes an enjoyable look round; and adds to himself, "Good! lam here, and here I shall remain. Let all and sundry take note of that little fact! " Again he looks round, before he continues his colloquy with the servant, which does not seem to have been so pleasant to the latter as to Gentleman Jack, for he looks sullen and disinclined to speak, while watching the stranger narrowly. "Nice place! Very, very nice ! You say you can't hall when the Honourable Stephen Chandos Fronde is expected from his travels?" " No !" was the curt answer. "Then allow me to impart to you from my superior know- ledge, that lam sure he will soon be here; but whether to- day or to-morrow he has not informed me." Then, noticing the yacht and the flags, he continued, "Row gay you are with your bunting! Anything up to- day? I've only just come by the night train, and have the gossip of the place yet to learn." "I thought by your talk you knew everything," said the servant. "Rem! There are gaps in my knowledge. You, per- haps, are more fortunate," responded Gentleman Jack, see- ing and appreciating the prospect of a little mental sport to brink his faculty iAto play: and to rub off the rust of the "barbarian and brutal life" of the camp, as he was ac- customed since he had left it to say. "Anyhow, my business isn't to answer questions," bluntly responded the servant. "Really, James,—" "I'm not James!" "Well, John, Anthony, Mordecai, anything you like, I was going to say when you rather rudely interrupted me by a disquisition on names, that I find your native frankness so refreshing after the commonplaces of society, and the place you live in so full of charms, that I cannot but ac- knowledge I begin to feel quite at home." "Your manners seem very much abroad," retorted the servant. "Eh ?" exclaimed Gentleman Jack, with a little but by no means disagreeable surprise, as he said to himself, " Oh, , a larder wit! I mast pat him down!' Addressing himself accordingly to that business,he said,— Time letter, is from my master, the Honourable Stephen Chandos Froude ?" giving the words with the old sonorous majestic ring, which impressed himself as well as those he was brought in contact with. "No," was the response. "I'll take it !" said Gentleman Jack, holding out his hand in the most innocent Manner possible. "No, thank ye," the setvaht drily said, turning away. "Yes, I will, said Gentleman Jack, but only after he had slyly snatched the missive from the unsuspicious hand. Then he added, " There, I knew it i It is for Miss Vande- leur !"

"I desired, Frances," said the Earl to her, as they entered, she leaning on his arm, and looking very pale and sad, to draw you away for a few minutes from our gueas. I bring a bridal gift. One that has cost no little to 41btain, but has been obtained at last—Stephen's pardon, after many weeks' imprisonment, granted most grudgingly, arrough the Colonel's obstinate behaviour—and only given at last OR account of the previous good conduct of the pri- soner, and his share in the suppression of the riot, in which be is believed to have saved the life of his commanding officer, Major Ethereclge, all of which the Latter pressed upon the authorities, almost to his own injury with his Colonel. "Your gift touches me deeply, for the Countess's sake ; and I receive it as you would wish," was all Miss Vapde- leur could find words to say. "He can scarcely get here till to-morrow, but my mother presses meal! the same to put off the marriage till he does come." Miss Vandeleur could hardly conceal the embarrassment she felt in being obliged to say to Lord Harlaxton— " She has begged me again to ask you the same thing." "But can ItOn tell me, Frances, what is at the bottom of all her mysterious sayings and doings; her first warning to me to beware, the recent expedition to Ireland, and now her ceaseless anxiety for Stephen's immediate presence ?" "The Countess has confided nothing whatever to me," responded Miss Vandeleur, in faltering ac- cents. "Bnt I must fear a recurrence of her dangerous ill- ness if she is refused." "Well, delay is possible, certainly, having a special licence, the clergyman living at hand, and our few guests being none of them, as ar as I know, pressed for time. But de you wish it? If so, I yield." "Not for my own sake," exclaimed Miss Vandeleur; and then relapsed into silence, as her only safe shield. "I wonder," continued Lord Harlaxton, "that the circnuastances attending Stephen's departure from his home, do not of themselves show my mother he cannot wish us to delay, and therefore she should not. Would you mind call- ing her attention to that point ?" "I will tell her what you say," said Miss Vandeleur, controlling as she best could the increasing agitation she felt.

" And as to other matters you find we dead to all," said the Countess, in tones of the deepest melancholy. "I have miserably failed—l abandon all idta of further attempts. I now wait only for my sou's presence to tell him the truth, to see Lord flarlaxton dispossessed of title and estates, and myself exposed to all the malignant gossip and scandal of the world."

But what then could be mether's mstive in sending for me SJ orgenfly ?" "Oh, the old, old story. To keep me pinned to her apron strings, as if her one business in life was to watch over me, and do nothing to help me in the business of taking care of myself.

"They are then to be married alter ill! And lam called home in time to see the whole job done before my very eyes; if only I am weak enough and foolish enough to abide the spectacle, and witness his triumph and her sacrifice. For I am sure she only cares for me. " 'There is no help for it! I must again take flight, if only for a few hours or days. But toy mother shall under- stand plainly this time why I go. I will find her at once, tell her my whole mind and then go, to return only when bride and bridegroom shall be far away. Ha! She ap- proaches, and Miss Vandeleur with her, buy not yet dressed for the Altar of Sacrifice. Oh fool ! fool ! Gaze on, while you own bow lovely, andbow true in mind and character, to all her loveliness suggests, is the girl you might have won, and have last!'

"May not Lord Harlaxton resist, and fight the legal I battle to the last extremity? He is in possession, and be : has ample means," said Mr. Lynx. "Ample means, indeed! But all belonging to my son ! " interposed the indignant Countess. " Yes, but not the less valuable for that reason to the Earl in a contest. He has them, and would certainly in the event presumed use them." "Yes, I suppose so," sighed the il.;ountess; "while I have so little, and Stephen has nothing wherewith to support a costly, perhaps interminable, litigation !" ' "But does your ladyship see no hops in any other direc- tion?" "Well, I sought for an ark of safety betimes, supposing things should come to the worst by the failure of my princi- pal scheme. "Since Stephen and Miss Vandeleur could not or would not shape things for a marriage, so that out of that might grow the compromise.[ sought for, Lord Harlaxton, retain- ing title and estates, but resigning Miss Vandeleur ; there re- mained only a reversal of the plan—Stephen regaining all 1 his rights, and Lord Harlaxton obtaining with Miss Vande- leur sufficient wealth to satisfy his utmost desire.

Keeping himself carefully out of eight, he withdrew to watch for an opportunity of finding the Countess alone. "Do yon say, Frances, Lord liarlaxton offered to delay, and vet you could not for your own sake accept ?'' "How could I rightly accept, knowing the marriage must take place, and knowing--" there the low, melancholy, sweet voice paused, unable to pursue so dangerous a theme. But the Countess understood, and took up her sentence where she had stopped. "And knowing what you have felt for Stephen ! My (Jelling girl, your blushes and your distress tell your whole position and story so plainly, that my business as your best and dearest friend is to see whether even at thie last hour you can be saved." "Oh, no, 00, Ile 11 eleelairned Miss Vandeleur in iretecs- ing agitation and alarm. "It is impossible !" "Do you mean—?" began the Countese, "I mean, since I must let you see all that is in my heart that I am—at least I was—prepared to accept my husband in a right spirit," and tread down all unlawful degree. But God only knowe what will become of me, if you reopen the past; if you bid me hope, when I knew that such Dope can only lead to a deeper, blacker despair l" "At this moment Gentleman Jack, who in fulfilment of his duty, had kept near to watch the arch of entrance through which the bailiff might try to find a way in, caught sight of the ladies, and managed to get into the alcove once more to listen. "At present," rejoined the Countess," I caa only say this. Some old hopes and fancies have come over me so strongly, that I cannot well resist on, more trial of their worth. And to begin with :—The marriage shall wait Step- hen's aerival—as myself will now make Lotd liarlazton plainly understand. You shall be in no way compromised by my attempt. Trust me for that." She paused, as though thinking she had said enough. But in a fele seconds she resumed, in a voice so plaintively sweet and winning, with no sort of intention in its tones, but which were the pro- duct of the new emotions rising in her breast that Miss Tan- delenr listened to them as if she were under a spell. "I saw just now from my watch tower that I have been so often visiting yesterday and to-clay, a form in the distance that set my heart beating in the belief it was Stephen. I may be wrong, but the mere fancy, if it was no more, in- fused such new power and hope, and such an undercurrent of joy, and sense of renewed possibilities, that instinctively rather than purposely I sought you. "Well we shall know presently if it was he. These papers [she took them from her pocket] I do not wish to have about me, if my first interview be with Lord Hellas- ton. Take them, my dear, to the jewel case in my bed- chamber. Lock the inner drawer, and the case itself care- fully. They are a precious deposit. "Do not look so frightened—so amazed. Give way to the flickering radiance I see dawning in your eyes. Life's sun- shine has yet to come for you!' Taking the papers, unable to say one single word, nn- certain whether she ought to have listened to such thoughts, but unable now to take any remedy, Frances was going away to do the Countess's bidding, when she stopped, looked at the Countess, who smiled, ran to her, aril clasped her in her arms ; kissing the pale, aged lips passionately, and at last murmuring to her— " You would not teach me to do a great wrong ; I dare think no further ;" and then hurried away, followed fur- tively by Gen:it:man Jack. "And is not that idea now 'going to success ?" asked the lawyer. "Will not that satisfy both parties ?" "Yes, by the sacrifice of me, and the sacrifice of the hitherto stainless fame of our ancestry. It may be success for them; it is despair and ruin to me !" "Bat when Lord Harlaston has married Miss Vandelcur, is it so sure that he will be ready for submission even then?"

"No, I fear not. It is well that you did come. So now to business, Avoiding publicity, prepare everything, just as if you knew Stephen's claims were to be opposed." "ek good policy," said the lawyer. "Men will often yield to marshalled forces, when they would merely laugh at the antics of an undisciplined mob. So is it often with facts— and actions at law."

"Employ, if you see occasion, the ablest counsel. I will spend," she said, in a voice full of stern purpose, and animation, "my last shilling if he dares—but no, he will not! I believe firmly in his honour and principle, if only he sees that honour and principle are the things really con- cerned, not law-washed wealth, and bitter unending family dissension. Pity not defiance, patience not hostility, is his due. And yet how bard it is lobe just! I know not what ails me. I spend my nights and days in vague fears and haunting surmises, which grow darker and darker. Would Stephen were come! Alarms steal over me as I reckon hour by hour how long he is past his time. Sometimes the old hope, the old plan seemingly so dead and buried lives again; and I ask myself what may not yet be possible, when the great revelation is made,—when all the truth becomes known.

"Idle dreams! Do not trouble yourself about them, or fear for me. I knew well how baseless they are. Come, I am sure you must need refreshment." As they paced slowly away, their voices dying by degrees in the distance, Gentleman Jack emerged from his hiding place in the Alcove, bursting with exultation. . .

CHAPTER LXIV.-GENTLEMAN JACK'S LOVE EPISTLE.

And as if to give Gentleman Jack time for the due con- sideration of so interesting a theme, and for the accumula- tion of all the facts germane thereto, before beiag tempted or driven into action, the one interesting actor in the drama passing before his eyes, whom he had not yet seen and heard to-day, now came en the stage; and Gentlemaa Jack, keeping a little in be background, prepared himself accordingly, a 5 Stephen and the footman came front under the arch,

"Here's the person that says he's your servant," observed the man respectfully. "My servant!" exclaimed Stephen in surprise, as he looked round, and saw Gentleman Jack standing there, looking mere gentlemanly than he had ever before seen him, with the cockade in his hat as the only visible sign of his vocation of service. "Oh. it's you," he said, and Gen- tleman Jack touched his hat, servant-like. So Stephen disraissed the footman, and then asked " Jack, what is the fneaning of this ?" "I wrote, begging you to let me be your servant, no mat- ter in what capacity, and saying ,T would present myself this very day if I could get no reply." "Ana I did reply, saying decidedly 'No!'" responded Stepbt"di " Thet'd unlucky! 1 neVer got the letter !" Vi hal's that you have just pulled a little out of your breast-pocket with your handkerchief ?" " This!" said Gentleman Jack, looking at the white edge projeeting from the pocket "oh, my list love epistle ! They are always following me." "Allow me said Stephen with great suavity of manner, RS he caught at and drew forth the love-epistle. "My letter, Jack! giving you the lie before all the world !" " This yours !" cried Jack, greatly surprised, or seem- ing so. " Dear me ! I put it by as a thing of no conse- quence, to read at my leisure. And I was just going to " "Invent fresh lies to cover the stale one !" Gentleman Jack shook his head gravely at this sad im- putation, before saying— " Men do lie, I know, but I am above all such prac- tices!"

He thought it was exec esbiegly 'bold. But recently he came across an extraordi /eery bold idea. This time, however, it came from ?the Yankees, who they knew were above all • eether men the most in- dependent people ce 1 the face of the earth. (Laughter.) An A Aviicin firm had actually had the audacity to driv 4 a tunnel to the crater of the great I volcanic mountain <of Popocatepetl, in the Island of Mexico, and inten, etd erecting vitriol works in the neigh- bourhood, depep Aran on the volcano for the supply of sulphur. (Lau gfeter.) They might laugh, but in these go- ahead days of science and economy goodness knows wnat we should do. +nem He thought the lecturer would be able ,to tell their A semething about the assertion—which he (the I chairmar .) sew just after the dreadful earthquake in Java. One of our great scientists had asserted that he should be , able t 4 foretell the time of the next shock. It was a most ext-eaordinary thing if that assertion was right. He knew they weld tell to the exact moment when a comet would be Iseen, or when an eclipse of the sun would take place, but it would be a very remarkable thing if they proved themselves able to foretell the time of a shock of eat thquake. Who, he asked, would have thought a few years ago that anyone would try to make a volcano useful and a paying concern ? Ile wished success to those who were trying to get money out of the volcano in the Island of Mexico. (Applause.) The LEC PURER, referring to a remark of the Chairman, said that if anyone were disposed to run the risk of erecting vitriol works near the crater of a volcano there would not be much difificelty in making it a plying concern, eo long as it was safe because most volcanoes sent up vast quantities of chemical products, such as sulphur, set-ammoniac, and boracic acid. It was, therefore, quite possible that the firm , who had bored a tunnel to the crater of the volcanic moun- tain of Popocateperl might make it a paying concern ; but it was equally possible that there might be an eruption in about half a century or so which would work dreadful des- , truction. The firm, however, seemed disposed to risk it. Turning to the question of scientific men being able to fore- tell the time of 4 shock of earthquake, the lecturer said that 50 years ago it would have been thought very absurd to attempt to predict the time of a shower of meteors. But such was not now the case, and scientific men ventured to hope that they would also be able to predict the time of an earthquake. It came about in this way: Near to several , volcanoes observatories had been erected which were fitted up with most delicite instruments for detecting slight vibrations on the crust of the earth, and scientists hoped that by collecting a vast number of facts respecting these vibrations they would be able to form a theory on the sub- ject, then they would watch the actual events to see if they squared with the theory they had formed. The lec- turer then remarked upon the vast power that comes into operation at the time of an earthquake, and referred to the earthquake which took place in Chili and Peru in 1822 It was proved, he said, that by that earthquake 1,200 miles of that long range of mountaiKs bad been lifted 1113 two or• three feet. Then three years earlier than that an extent of territory of 2,000 in the delta of the Indus sank several feet, and some 50 miles north of that there was are elevation of a similar amount of territory. He also referred to the remark- able earthquake of Lisbon, which took place in 1755, when 60.000 people lest their lives. It wee stated on scientific authority that that shock was felt over an extent of the surface of the globe four times the extent of Europe. These facts would give them some idea of the enormous power which wag exerted by an earthquake. Turning to the sub- ject of volcanoes, he remarked that there was close connec- tion between them and earthquakes. There were 250 or 300 active velcanoes,and it was said that they acted as a safety valve to the earth. That was to say, they allowed an es- cape for a quantity of the vast force confined within the crust of the earth, which, if kept confined, might do seri- ous mischief. Volcanoes were often spoken of as burning mountains, but that was sometime hardly -a correct term, because a vo a ano was not necessarily a monetain. Volcanoes occurred on plains, and in all probability the first time there was an erruption in a district it would be on a plain, but every errurjon that came tended to form a mountain. The LECTUiER then went on to explain various details of the action of some of the principal volcanoes, referring to those of Etna and Vesuvius, and to the destruction of Pompeii and Herculaneum. He next spoke of the opera- tions of hot-springs, afterwards dealing with the dreadful earthquake which took place at Jtva on the, 2Gth of last August. .It was, he said, one of the most terrible recorded in modern history. The island was lifted up and shivered, and then sank and completely disappeared. The sea around was greatly disturbed, and the waters rose into a wave a hundred feet high, which increased the height of 'the tidal wave on the coast of most countries throughout the world. The atmosphere was also disturbed in an extraordinary de- gree, a wave of atmosphere like the wave of water was set in motion, and one authority he had read, steted that it went round the earth three times at least. The lecturer also dwelt op-in the various theories advanced in explana- tion of the beautiful colouring which of late has been ob- served in various quarters of the globe. Votes of thanks Pt ought the proceedings to a close.

" Eh, Jack?' "Except with white lies, which nobody minds, and everybody uses." " White lies ! Ah, Jack, they are often like white light composed of every hue." "And some of them most charming to look at," cried Gentleman Jack, in great glee at the downfall of Stephen's scientific philosophy. But, emrely, I have improved of I late ?" "You certainly have made sacrifices to tell thee truth.' "Oh. I have !—I have! No One knows or games how many !" he replied in seeming emotion, "But always at my cost, and I suppose In expiation of the lies that you tell for your own special benefit.' "Well, but consider," said Gentleman Jack, appealingly. " Absorbed in great objects, who stops to think of. these

petty details? look at our great men. Do they, if they can help it, offer up place, honours, wealth ? Yet was there ever a band of more intrepid martyrs—see how they fraeritice the putlic I" • It was irresistible. Stephen could no longer keep a grave face, or help burstlng out into loud and prolonged laughter. Once more Gentleman Jack had won his way to confidence, and the restoration of the old enjoyable communion, which had caused Stephen to be so indulgent to other parts of Jack's character. . .
And quickly did the latter use his opportunity by saying, in his old conlidential manner— _ . _
4. On my way here I passed year creditor. Baldercomb, talking to a man, who could only be a bailiff." "Are you surer asked Stephen, evidently concerned at the news.

--"Certain. Two minutes after, the bailiff and I were both coming in the direction of this place, and along the edge of a horse pond. Accidentally we jostled, and, would you be- lieve it, he fell right in !" " Really," said Stephen with a laugh. "Really. Dived like a porpoise. Poor fellow, I had a good deal of treuble to help him out, in the course of which he got d,pped again two or three times." But Stephen was no longer able to enjoy Gentleman Jack's sly humour over the discomfiture of the bailiff. This day might be one of the most important in his life, if he rightly understood his mother's message, as relating to some unexpected and new opportunities for renewing his suit to Miss Vandelenr. He knew such events are always in the highest degree unlikely, when an engagement for marriage had been made; and, therefore, was by no means sanguine. Still it was an embarrassing as it was an irritating idea, that of being obliged to run any risk during such a time of being arrested by a vulgar bailiff; with possibly a consequent exposure before all the family. Miss Vandeleur included! So, after a minute's reflection, he saw he must use Jack once more, however unwillingly; an he said to him,— "For special reasons I desire to be undisturbed for the next few hours, so that—" "Say no more," interrupted Gentleman Jack; "I will keep a good watch, trust me !" " Very well. I have not forgotten my promise. In a few days I will see what can be done,for you. By-the•bye, why do you mount a cockade in your hat ?" "As your servant !" "Mina! Am lan officer, Jack ?" "No; but you ought to be. And good servants are bound to think of these things. Besides, I should be taken for what lam, a true gentleman, it I didn't wear somettliog to contradict facts, and truth."

Mr. Thomas Ashton, the High Sheriff of the county, has issued a notice summoning a county court, to be held in the Workman's Institute, Moor-street, Ormskirk, at noon on Monday next, for the election of a coroner for the district of West Derby, in the place of the late Mr. T. Wildman Barker. The nomination of candidates for the office will be made at that hour, and In the event of a poll the polling will take place at a time then to be decided upon. Mr. T. Nash, on benalf of Mr. Robert Halliwell, of Wigan, made an application to the Salford Hundred Quarter Ses- sions, at Manchester, on Tuesday. that the court should, , under the powers of the Coroners' Act, appoint certain 'towns as polling places for use in the forthcoming election of a coroner for the West Derby division of the county of Lancaster. Ormskirk, he said, was the only place at which the votes of the electors could be recorded, although in that town there were only 430 voters, while in Liverpool there were 3,570, in Widnes 790, in Wigan 620, and in St. fleleas 520. It mast be remembered, too, that the voting was taken on the old system, and he urged that not more than 500 votes could be recorded during ' the day if there was only one station, and that station being Ormskirk, if one of the candidates lived there, he could take his supporters early to the poll and block it for the whole day.—A oiscussion ensued, during which it was declared that that was not the proper court at which to make the application, the annual quarter sessions held at Preston being the only court at which such lonsinesa could be transacted. It was further thought by the justices that the application ought to be made to magistrates of the West Derby division of the county, who were acquainted with the circumstances of the case.—The application was refused.

Tau= WILL OUT.—Johnny had come home frem school several times within a month with various braises on his face and body, received in fights with his schoolmates, and on the last occasion his mother threatened him with severe punishment if he ever engaged in a fight again. Only a few days after the small chap appeared with a black eye, and, scared, by the stern maternal greeting, "Well, sir ?" he departed from his usual truthful ways, and stammered "I fell down and hit my head on a stone." "And which got the* worst of it ?" asked his big brother. "Oh, the other fellow, you bet," answered Johnny, briskly. "Re's gone home with two black eyes."

THE STRIKE IN THE 'COTTON TRADE.—ne evil effects of the strike in North-east Lancashire are becoming visible in quarters where' they might have been expected co appear. Shopkeepers and small tradesmen, especially in Blackburn, are suffering heavily from the loss of that custom which the operatives cannot afford to bestow, but are compelled to go on granting some amount of credit by the fear of reprisals when the struggle is ended. A great reduct'on is also noticable in the goods traffic on the railways, which in ordinary times carry to and from the centres of the cotton incluttry enormous quantities of the raw material and finished goods. At Blaekburn, it is stated, eighteen of the goods porters have been discharged on account of the alaclutess of Work. The passenger traffic in that division of of the comity has also very considerably diminiehed.

div.head: CHAPTER DXV.:-A BRIDAL DAY.
div.p: CHAPTER DXV.:-A BRIDAL DAY.

A joyous burst of bells ringing from the neighbouring church stopped their talk. Stephen, turning to look around', then saw the yacht with its gay bunting, as Gentleman Jack called it, and in an instant a dreadful sense of what was intended on the very day of his arrival over- powered him. As he stood half paralysed at the possibility that was now tilling his whole soul with a new sense of his love for Miss Vandeleur, Gentleman Jack saw his state, and guessed the reason. "Surely you know." he said, "that Lord Harlaxton and Miss Vandeleur are to bo married this morning?" Prompt and fierce was tha response: "And if they are, what is that to me? Retire and attend to your watch." When he was alone and could give way to the emotion he felt, his thoughts ran thus: "So dies my one and last hone that my m.ther.ls message was meant to bring me to Miss Vandeleur; a hope that I firmly believe she shared. There was something under all her words and 'behaviour in our interview that revealed to me a consciousness of this kind; though she was too honest, too full of the delicacy if her position, to commit herself or her future husband in any possible manner. "Well, all that is over, and must be detenninedly pushed out of mind, must be forgotten, if only I can find the way.
