FRANCE AND CHINA. TERLIBLE EXPLOSION IN TONQUIN. Intelligence received at Henkong from Hanoi to the 2nd. inst. aniv.,unced that a terrible explosion occurred there on December 28, by which too batteries of French artillery were nearly destroyed. One- artilleryman was killed and three injured. Great destruction was also caused to the houses and barracks in Hanoi. The cause of the explosion was believed to be accidental. On the same day two thousand Annamites attacked a French pest held by fifty Marines and defended by entrenchinents and bamboo palisades. After several hours' fighting the enemy reti,..ed with a loss of one hundred killed and woun Jed.. Colonel Maasun had left with a column of troops to hunt down tne bands of pirates on the banks of the Heltiver,.. and would possibly advance as far as Hunghoa. Womb Brionval had overtaken the Daboc bands in the rroyince of• Namdinh. The enemy were completely surprip,d, and took: refuge in a strongly entrenched position in the neighbouring: village. The fighting continued for several hours, and 15 suited in a decisive success for the Frenr troops. Tbe-, Minister of Marine at Paris has received abs followiux tele- gram from Admiral Courbet, despatched doon on Wednesday, and dated Hanoi from Hongkong at -.December 27th and 31st: " Ts-day, December 27th, a fir a broke out in the artil- lery stores at Hanoi. The loss of onaterial was inconsider- able, and will be replaced within- A fortnight from Saigon by/ the transport Aveyron. Later • And more precise information • gives the enemy's losses dur above 400 killed and 000 we .ng the attack on Sontay as, muted. Liou Yinh Phuve and his lieutenant are among t ne wounded. Several Clkinese officers were killed. Om wounded are generally progressing satisfactorily, the temp erature being favourable to their Pt- coverv, The enem f left in our hands 89 bronze cannon, of which seven ar a rifled, 400 kilogrammes of dynamite,. and 150,000 car' .ridges for Remingtons and Winchesters.

F. om York it is telegraphed that the Park Theatre, at Clevel? -ad, has been burned, the loss being estimated at $200,00' Trr ,11 mADAGAECAB DIM:TM—A despatch from Tama- tav „ d, dated December 260 states that the attempted negotia- ' ,ons between the French and the novas hive failed: The French ships have bombarded the eastern " ports " again. A "political duel" .in Paris has had an unexpected result, one of the combatants being severely wemeded. The duel was fought with swords, which in the experi- enced hands of Parisian journalists are usually as harnaleee as pistols.

SCENE IN A LION'S CAGE- exciting scene is reported to have taken place in a circus at Dijon. Daring an exhi- bition of animals, a lion tamer entered the lions' cage to perform various feats, when he placed his head in the mouth of a lioness. The animal suddenly closed its jaws. The man shrieked, and the spectators were panic-stricken, and fled to the doors. The lioness released the raan, but he 15 severely wounded. THE NIHILIST OUTRAGES IN linsstA.—The statement that the Nihilists have threatened Count Tolstoi with death has been confirmed. M. Orchewski, the Chief of the Gen- darmerie, and the Procurator of the St. Petersburg Criminal Court have also been t‘ warned." Count Tolstoi's body.- ' guard has now been increased to thirty men. Numereoe arrests are being made in connection with the assassination of Colonel Sudeikin.

FILANCH AND MADAGASCAR.—News from Madagascar re- ports the arrival at Tamatave of the Flora. A representative had arrived who full powers to conclude peace, the Mala- gasiesaccepting the French ultimatum, and ceding the north of Madagascar, from Cape Saintardre to Cape Bellone. The settlement of guarantees is to be referred to the Hove Go- vernment, but an agreement is expected, the Malagesies desiring to get rid of the French on any terms short of pro- tectorate.

THE SUEZ CANAL COMPANY' AND THE ENGLISH SHIP. OWNEAS.—The directors of the Suez Canal Company held their monthly meeting, on Tuesday afternoon. Contrary to expectation, the convention with the English shipowners was not discussed. lam informed that the Board will not take the Convention .into consideration until the Millet Government has expressed its views thereon. Sir Rivers Wilson is unwell, and was unable to be present at the meeting. THE FIRE AT A CONTENT: TWENTY-SEVEN LITES LOST. —The Catholic Convent at Belleville, Illinois; which has been destroyed by fire, was.the Convent of the Immaculate Conception. Later particulars state that the fire originated in the basement. The building is now in rains. For ODD hour the operations of the firemen were greatly retarded by the very severe frost prevailing. The inmates consisted of 60 girls, of ages varying from 10 to 20, besides several teachers and servants. Everybody lo2cartte panic-stricken at the outbreak of the fire. Several pupils and teachers jumped from the windows, and were either killed or fatally injured. Many unable to make their escape were burned to death. Twenty-two pupils and five of the sisters, including the mother superior, are known up to the present -to have perished. . . .

TERRIBLE 013TRAGE IN VIENNA.—A brutal murder was committed on Thursday evening at the place of business of a moneychanger named Eisert, in the Mariatiafstret, an important thoroughfare which forms the principal channel of communication between the western suburbs anti the city. Towards six o'clock three men entered Eisert's office on the pretext of desiring to change some roubles, and im- mediately set upon the unfortunate man, whom they wounded very severely. To escape from his assailants be ran into itti adjoining -room, where his children were at their lessons with their governess. The three men, Lowever, followed hitu, and attacked him again with such violeoce that he fell mortally wounded, and they turned upon the children. Eisert's son, a mere lad, was struck down, wounded to death, and a second child was also so terribly injured that recoveryis believed to be hopeless. Thg Rover.. ness fled from the room in terror and escaped unlaurt.

EGYPTIAN AFFAIRS: THE KHEDIVE AND THE ElamNone—On Monday, the ministrypf the Khedive was occe- pied in the consideration of the 'British Note. At eight o'clock at night the Ministers tendered their resignations. An account of two conversations with the Khedive has been forwarded by the Times correspondent at Cairo. As regards abdication, His Highness remarked that he never sought for the Khedivate. The happiest time of hja life was before his acceptance of it. Before accepting he considered first his duty to his father and then his duty to the country. and he considered that he had fulfilled teat duty in following the advice first of the Control and now of England. As to being "unpopular," he continued:—" So far as this terns has any meaning in Egypt the charge is true, and I am. proud of it. The English are unpopular because they seek reforms. The doctors are unpopular who, at the rise of their lives, disinfect houses. The judges are unpopular if th-y punish bribery. An official is unpopular if he refuses ti punish on demand. Every step in the right direction is uaoppular, and will be so for some time; out we must still p- eevere." Referring to the aspect of the Soudan question, H a Highnese said: "No question of abandoning Kordofan or Dar- four arises, for they have abandoned Egypt. A-, regards the Eastern Soudan, on the littoral of the Red Sea, we have no direct interest there, and it costs es money. As we re- ceived it from Turkey, we must fermi ler offer to return it ; but its destiny does not affect Egypt: Khartoum is a more doubtful question. The Ministers think it necessary to hold it. My own opinion I cannot allow you to publish before I have stated it in Council. If the Ministers cannot follow England's advice, they will pro- bably resign. In the actual state of things it would not be difficult to find substitutes for them.' According to a private telegram received, Nnbar Pasha hae accepted the Premiership of a new Egyptian Ministry, and appointed Mr. Edgar Vincent Finance Minieter. The Cairo correspondent of the Pall lifaltGazette laye the corruption and scandalous practices in the interior are incr,ling, and officials are almost certain of impunity—'.hit former masters having been 'rendered impotent, while British in- terference is confined to philanthropic advice. A little earnestness of purpose, he proceeds, and a little irtnnese would go a long way, and the Egyptian official wou;d soon realise on which side his *ad is buttered.—Lateraccounte state :—The new Egyptian Ministry has now been com- pleted, with Nubar Pasba as President of the Council and Minister for Foreign Affairs and of Justice. It is said that Mr. Clifford Lloyd will be appointed Under-Seer-,ary of the Department of the Interior. The projected deepatch of a foe_ce of Black Troops to the Soudan' under the cmonand of Zebebr Pasha, has been abandoned. A Milit..-y Com- mission, under the presidency of Sir Evelyn Wool, will be appointed to devise the means of effecting the evaee it-,en of the Soudan. It is believed that a period of one yeAr will be required to effect the evacuation of the equatorial province!. It is reported from Cairo that the brother-in-law of the hlandi is now a prisoner there. He has been interrogated by Khairy Pasha, and affirms that the Mandi will` net fight Turkish troops; but, on the contrary, will endeavour to his. utmost to make 'common cause with them foe the expulsion of all foreigners. He denies that the Mandi assumes any religious apostleship. He is merely defending his country against exorbitant taxation and the suppression of he slave trade.

SCHOOL THACHEIIS AND ElHALTlL—Children must not hang damp and sometimes soiled over-clothing in a close, unaired room, against other damp or wet garments. Each child's clothing should be kept by itself. The regulation of heating hnd ventilation is .very important; the ther- mometer should guide you as to heat. Air can often be let in though a seive of wire, or between two ti,ubes, with a broad strip beneath the lower one, when a direct draught would be hazrdous. Walls often need whitewashing, kalse' mining or painting, and all woodwork should be frequently and thoroughly washed. Sweeping carefullr under the desks and dusting are important. The condition of the rooms, the distribution of desks according to size of per,soosr light, variation in study and position, exercise, airing Of rooms while empty, moderation of competition, assortment of work to the capacity of the child, and quickness to per- ceive the occasions for temporary variations and adjabtmente are essential in the skilled oversight of the teacher. Tie must feel that he has this charge to keep. It to a joy to get school-work out of a well child, or to help rather than t° oomplicate inability and invalidism. Remember that the kind of day has something to do with the capacity for worki While light gymnastics should be practised daily in schools at stated periods, on rainy or cloudy days Vey= exercises shoal be given, during which tho room me more thoroughly ventilated. Give zest and advice attO out4g-door as well as indoor exercises.

SHOCKING ACCIDENT NEAR WIGAN. FALL OF A RAILWAY..BIgDOE : SEVEN MEN
idi.LE b.

An extraordinary accident, attended with lamentable con- sequences, occurred on Sunday morning, on the London and North-Western Railway, near Coppull station, between Wigan and Preston. Whilst preparations were being made for the demolition of a bridge crossing the line at this spot, the structure fell upon the workmen beneath, killing the inspector and six others, and injuring as many more of the l'ailway servants. The bridge in question carried the high- road over the railway, and stood about a quarter of a mile south of Coppull station. It was constructed entirely ot brick, and the single arch spanning the line was formed of three tiers.of brickwork, the backing extending into the solid clay on each side. The bridge was erected by the old North Union Railway Company as long ago as 1837, and was at the time looked upon as an exceedingly substantial structure for its purpose, the traffic being neither extensive nor heavy. Since the North Union Railway transferred its portion of the great west-coast route to Scotland to the London and North-Western 'Company, not only has the traffic along this road increased, but mining operations have been carried on in the Immediate neighbourhood, and the archway, once strictly elliptical in form, has gradually be- come flattened at the top. The portion of the North-Western Rail way system between Wigan and Preston is being doubled, and the work has reached several miles south of Preston. It could not have proceeded much further without this bridge fuming to be dealt with, but there can be no doubt that the condition of the structure hastened operations in dealing with it, and it was determined'to erect first a tem- porary wooden bridge, preparatory to one being placed there with substantial iron girders. The exigencies of the week- day traffic, which is somewhat throttled at this pint pend- ing the doubling of the lines, as well as the convenience of the public using the bridge, made it desirable that the work should be done on Sttnday and in the least possible time. The usual traffic, both goods and passenger, has ordinarily .- passed this point about half past ten, and eleven o'clock on Sunday morning was fixed for bringing down the arch Early in the morning a special train containing a largo staff of workmen from the engineering department, in charge of Mr. John Hammond, senior bridge inspector for the northern division, left Manchester for Coppull. On arriving there they found that the preliminary work of removing earth from the summit and approaches to the bridge had been accomplished, and as soon as the last passenger train from Wigan had passed active operations were commenced. Part of the workmen were sent on to the bridge to remove the first tier of brickwork,and.ten others, under the personal guidance of Mr. Hammond, who stood in the six-foot, were proceeding with arrangements for placing the supports required for the temporary bridge when, without any noticeable crack or warning whatever, the whole structure fell with a tremendous crash, killing Mr. Hammond and six of his men, inflicting terrible injuries on the others who were on the line, and slighter, but still severe, hurt upon several of the workmen who had been on the bridge itself and had fallen with it. Fortunately there was abundance of help at hand in the re- mainder of the staff which had come from Manchester, as well as by the gangs of labourers which had been formed by the platelayers of the immediate district, and they were soon under the superintendence of Mr. D. B. Worthington, the district engineer, who, having travelled from Manchester by the ordinary train, which was the last to pass under the bridge, had got out at Coppull station and was walking down the line to the scene of the operations when the disas- ter occurred. Mr. A. W. Ditchfield, permanent way in- spector, had entered an adjoining cottage to change his dress when he beard the crash, which he said NUS like a "clap of thunder," and he was quickly on the spot. The engine which had brought the engineering staff from Manchester was forthwith sent to Wigan, five miles distant, for medical aid, and almost at this instant appeared in sight a consider- able number of labourers who were on their way from Eux- ton, the next station north, under instruction to help to clear the main line after the bridge had been pulled down. News of the accident soon spread, and a number of villagers joined in the difficult work of extricating, every- one being able to help in removing the loose bricks. The unfortunate men who had been on the line were com- pletely buried, but those who had been near the sides of the arch had been partially protected by some prejections which remained standing after the main structure, fell, al- though they were badly bruised and injured about the lower parts of the body. Mr. Taberner, the Wigan stationmaster, ' gathered together such medical aid as was available, and in a very short time was able to start for the scene of the' dis- aster with Messrs. Roocroft, William Roocroft, R. P. White, and Bryden, surgeons, and with the ambulance appliances kept at the Wigan station. Mr. W. Brook, district police Inspector, accompanied the party. ' Shortly afterwards another detachment of medical gentlemen' consisting of Messrs. Coombs. Graham, and Cown, arrived from Wigan. The injured as they were extricated were removed to the platelayers' house, a few yards from the bridge, when they were properly attended to. As each of those killed was dis- covered the surgeons examined them. All were terribly distorted, the bodies presenting a shocking appearance. By half-past eleven the last body was recovered, and the traffic on the line was resumed. The inquest on the bodies was opened on Monday by Mr. Milbertson, county coroner. Evidence of the identification was taken, and the if quiry was adjourned until Monday next. On Monday Colonel Rich, one of the inspectors of the Board of Trade, visited Coppull for the purpose of inquiring into the accident. The inspector arrived at Coppull Bridge soon after eight o'clock, and was met by Mr. Worthington, engineer, and several other officials of the London and North-Western Railway Company. After inspecting the re- mains of the fallen bridge, the inspector examined several of the officials as to the accident, returning by noon train to London.
• MINERS' WAGES AND TRADE PROFITS IN LANCASHIRE.

Mr. S. Woods, president of the Lanccshife and Cheshire Miners' Federation, speaking at a meeting at Ashton, near Wigan, on the agitation for an advance of miners' wages, said it was urged that the greatest reason why ployers could not advance wages was that large concerns were paving no dividends, and had not done so for years. This was the\greatest scarecrow that was frequently put up to stifle agitation, but he knew it was scarcely ever believed by anyone outside some of their limited collieries. What he had to say with regard to dividends was, that if these concerns did not pay any they ought to do. There was a greater production now than at any time previously, and consequently greater consumption. Prices were higher now than they had been for years. The demand for fuel was brisk, and if profits were not made under circumstances of this deserip- tion, when could they be made? The truth was profits were made, but they went through such an intricate mani- pulation of divisions nowadays that it would puzzle any- body to understand them. For instance, here was a real sample of how profits were squandered. There was a cer- tain colliery within nine miles of Wigari which a few years ago was sold by the proprietor, after he had made a hand- some fortune, to nine shareholders, who speculated about £50,000 for a colliery which in reality was not worth more than £20,000 in ordinary times, but because there was a cal famine this fabulous sum was given. Now this was one of the non-dividend paying collieries. Let them examine the facts and position of things. These nine directors met every week, or were supposed to do, and they had £5 each per meeting; that was £2,340 per year. Then there was a managing director with a salary of £l,OOO per annum. Again, at a colliery employing 1,000 hands, one under- ground manager was said to be insufficient, and they em- ployed four at £3 per week each, with house and fire. Then they bad a dozen underlookers, where three did the work formerly, at £2 each per week. Then came the ex.officio managers, consisting of director's sons and friends, &n., with about £l,OOO per annum. New, putting these exor- bitant unreasonable salaries together, they found there was the enormous sum of £6,212 to be deducted from the gross proceeds, and then, forsooth, because there was not more than 5 per cent on preferential shares and 3i per cent on the B shares of this most unwise speculatisn of £50,000, they were told that no profits were being made. As to the prospects of the miners getting an advance, ha said the signs were hopeful.

An instance of the extensive traffic in life insurance policies has come to light at an inquest held at Heywood on the body of a labourer who had committed suicide by hang- ing himself. It was proved that the woman with whom the deceased lodged, a Mrs. Corless, had insured his life in two societies, the premiums being regularly paid by her- self. One of the jurymen stated that there was "no one in the town who bad so many persons insured,' as the woman in question. LORD HARTINGTON.—The Daily News says :—The one thing needful to secure Lord liartington authority and popularity equal to that of any Liberal statesman who went before him is that he should take his place openly with the party of movement, and net be content with an influence , that mainly seeks to regulate and control and delay. Per- haps it is only a misapprehension, though a natural misap- prehension, of his own language, which attributes to him a merely regulating and retarding office. Lord ,Hartington has proved himself on more than one occasion a man cap- able of taking a bold and decided step forward. The mem- orable declaration which he made in reference to the land question in the House of Commons some years ago may be said to have marked an epoch in the history of a great social and political movement. A similar declaration defining Lord Hartington's attitude on the great questions of political and suoreie thalreem on, accepting reform, afcreaenpktliytaking his side with the forces that g the position of a power that moves instead of a resistance that is overcome, would be now of great moment—personal and political. A few sentences, a few words, spoken on an important occasion, on any con- spicuous platform' would set all misconception at rest, and would give Lord Hartington an authority in the country and with his party which could not be shaken. The pre- sent time would be most opportune for such an utterance, and it would be a pity indeed if the opportunity were allowed to pass away unused. Ad great career might be marred for lack of appreciation of inch an opportunity. At Westminster Police Court, London, on Tuesday, Frederick Harris was again charged with the murder of Emily Novell, with whom he cohabited, and who was found dead under very mysterious circumstances. As there was no evidence brought against him, the prisoner was dis- charged. • THE PREMIER AND SUNDAY CLOSING. Mr. Caine, M.P., having written to the Premier urging the claim of the supporters of the Sunday Closing Bill fdr facilities in the House of Commons in connection therewith, has re- ceived the following reply from the Premier's secretary : Mr. Gladstone' having received your letter of the 12th ult., desires me to thank you for liming written to him so fully on the subject of Sunday closing, on which you are able to 'bring to bear so much interesting information. You may be sure that your views as to this qnestion have his close attention and will be brought under the notice of his col- leagues, He has always himself believed it to be best to allow a local principal to prevail as to Sunday closing, but he readily admits tire inconvenience which may result from diversity of practice, and the means of escaping from them are full of difficulty. HORRIBLB Smanis.-=-Early on Sunday morning the body of a young wontin, only partially dressed, was found lying across the rails ctutside Shaftsll Station, on the East London branch of tho London and Brighton BA 11 way The . .
body was terriby- in-fared, an engipe ha7,ing evidentli passed orer it. Upon removal to the mortuary the remains were identified as those of Clara Enever, domestic servant at

• Hennis's Coffee House, which is situated close to Shadweli Station and overlooks the line. The supposition is that the girl committed suicide by throwing herself from the roof of the house to the rails, a distance of about one hundred fist. . .

••••-• SUPPOSED MURDER DT CEMETERY.—A prolonged in- quiry took place on Monday at Woking Necropolis, before Mr. Roumieu, county coroner, as to the death of a woman unknown, whose body was found in a retired part of the Cemetery, shot in the head. At first the fatal wound was supposed to have been self-inflicted, but from the careful disposition of the body on the ground, and the manner in which a revolver was found in her lap, suspicions were aroused. These were confirmed by the experience of the coroner and Dr. Shepherd. After the post-mortem examina- tion Dr. Shepherd said that the moment he had examined the deceased's head be became convinced the fatal shot had not been fired by her own hand, and on consideration he felt it was impossible she could have fallen in the position in which she was found. Deputy Chief Constable Barker said he had made every effort to gef the body identified, but was unsuccessful. The woman was dressed very respectably, and was about 45 years old. As there was no direct evi- dence of the murder the jury returned an open verdict, so that the police might pursue their inquiries unfettered.

div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BiARD.

The monthly meeting was held on TueedaY, Air. Tr. H. Gossage presiding. There were also present Dr. O'Keefe, Messrs. 1). Carey, F. H. Panaharst, D. Forster, J. Midwood, J. Houg,hton. E. Martley, S. Sadler, P. Dutton, T. Handley, 0. Wright, .1. T. Allen (clerk), J. Carr (gas engineer), Copeland (sewerage engineer), and Dixon (ouleanse in- spector).

CORRRSPOITDENC The Local Government Board wrote drawing the atten- tion of the siernlArs to the Factory and Werkshope Act and the Sewers Amendment Act It was referred to the com- mittee interested. A letter had been received from the Preston Corporation asking tbe Board to suppoit the hold- ing of the Royal Agricultural Show at Preston rather than at Chester. It had been before the Board on a previous occasion, and no notice was taken of it. It was decided that the letter lie on the table. A letter was also laid on the table fruno the Local Government Board with reference to the dwellings of the labouring classes, and calling atteutiou to the various Acts pasqed on the subject. MORI IN COMMITTERS.

The GAS liulli3a reported to the Lies and Water COM.. rnittee that the gale of the 11th December did considerable. damage to the Stacks Well and Netherby Pumping Stations, it being estimated at £3l. The water in stock, Deceinbar 12th, 1133, 4,624,T07 gAllons. The rainfall for the month has been Per Sas Yard (inns 1,506 inchey} Itema 1,657 Inches. Water pu ped
Cqrrespond- -4 weeks endinz fug period. Dee 12. 1883. 1882. Deereaie Gel i lons. o,ltone. pee cent. etock . Well Inerwt.e 2Z4

c ft. e. ft. Decreaee. G.a made 7,916,000 3.283,000 443 Gas delivered The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 15 94 candles. The Ureneral Purposes committee eppeinted Messrs. Carey and Urossage, the Surveyor, and the Clerk to see Mr. Worthington and the promoters respect- ing the Ship Canal Bill and report. The Highway Com- mittee had received a letter from Messrs. Evans and Lockett respecting the flagging of Derby-road. The committee re- plied that they could not recommend Cie sealing of an agreement to do the work in a shorter term than Lye yeare, unless hoose property be built opposite the unflagged por- tion, when the work would be at once completed. The Clerk was instructed to ask the property owners in the fol- lowing streets to meet the committee on the 10th inst. to consider the advisability of repotting or making the streets: —Hurst-street, James-etrer-t (between Bank and Irwell- streets), Parsonage-road, Welliagton-street, Marsh-street (from Waterloo-road to back passage of Nelson-street), Charlotte-street. Elizabeth-street, Margaret-street, Victoria- street, Dickson-street, Ellison-street, Lea-street, and Fisher- I street. Mr. J. Rimmer offered his services gratuitously during the surveyor's illness. Instructions given to thank Mr. Rimmer, and to inform him that, if necessary, the committee would avail then:selves of his generous offer. The Nuisance Inspector reported to the Health Commit- tee that one death had occurred at James-street, West Bank, from scarlet fever. Small-pox: There have been six patients discharged convalescent, leaving one (almost re- covered) remaining. There was on death at the hospital this month. Two cases—the surveyor, and another in the

, s-ane house—have been reported this month.—A letter re Glycerine Works was read from Messrs. N. Mathi,son and Co. respecting alleged nuisance, which was considered satis- factory.—The Market Superintendent reported that the re- eeipts for the month were £l9 13s 11d, being an increase of .£3 1s Id, as compared with December, 18$2. Seven shops are let; the stalls and fair ground have let well.—The minutes of the various committees were passed.

div.head: TEA IMALLTOX OUTIMMAX.
div.p: TEA IMALLTOX OUTIMMAX.

In moving Ole- adoption of the minutes of tke Health Committee, Mr. Handley said that for three or four Alava the hospital tents ware clear, but he regretted to kave to inform the Board that a fresh case had broken out is Midwood-street. To patient bad been removed to the hospital. He was the only Inmate •1 the hospital now. Mr. Iligginson was convalescent. He hoped he would soon be able to resume his duties. PINANCX. Messrs. R. Davies and Co. wrote to the Finance Com- mittee on the 210th December enclosing Messrs. Part and Co.'s account, £412 13s sd, and thei" own account, £247 15s Bd, re sewer arbitration. The chairman of the com- mittee and the clerk were requiested to attend to tke taxa- tion of the bill. Accounts amounting to nearly £3,00 were recommended for payment.—Mr. HANDLNY moved the con- firmation of the minutes, and also that a cheque be passed for £536 10s, the amount of the arbitrator's award of the 22th August re sewerage.—Mr. WRIGHT seconded, and the I motions were passed.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW PIIELIC OFFICES.
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW PIIELIC OFFICES.
A letter was read from Mr. J. W. Collie, who wrote "As I see from the public papers that some members of your Board have stated that the rent of the offices which you now

bold was LSO wer annum, and this being incorrect, as the rent is only 170 per annum, I will thank you to name the matter to the committee, and as it has been eeveral times expressed by some members of your Board that the rent would be raised at the expiration of pour lease.l beg to state that it is not my intention of doing as, and I am prepared to renew your lease for five years more on the terms of the old . . -

lease, via., s7i9 per year, and still further if you wieh I will let you the room above your Board•roone, and now used as a Workman's Club, for £lO per year, and will give you pos- session in three months time, and you would then be on a rent of 00 per year for the whole." At the conclusion of the ordinary business Mr. Dtvrvort proceeded with the motion of which he had given notice— that the resolution to erect public offices passed on the llth December be rescisded. He did not think it necessary for . .

him to again go ever the reasons why he objected to the building of new offices, because the Board knew pretty well what they were. He had not the remotest desire to excite any acrimonious jealousies on this subject, and he did not wish the Board to think that he was judged by any party motive. He was acting according to the dictates of his own mind,as suggested by the purpose for which the ratepayers sent him. He opposed the resolution in tot°. They did not at present require new public offices, and the original reason assigned for building the offices was entirely removed by the letter of Mr. Carlisle. He contended that the offices, if erected, would cost not £3,500 but £6,000, and protested that a building worthy of the town could not be built for the former sum. He pointed out the utter futility of ob- taining designs for a town hall which they did not intend to erect now, and which a future Board might decline to erect. He produced a letter from Mr. Kershaw, who said he con- curred that it was not requisite to build either new offices or town hall at present. Mr. Kershaw observed Mr. Dutton bad no doubt entirely turned round. He was against him on the last occasion, he was with him that day.—Mr. Mt.- WOOD: He is well able to torn round.—Mr. MARTLEY seconded the motion.—The CHAIRMAN said supposing the Board obtained designs for a town ball it was only to show the bona fides of the transaction. It was their desire that they should not erect anything that would be a burden afterwards, and which a future Board could not incorporate with the town hall without spoiling the beauty of the structure.—Dr. O'Kitatri pointed out thst the proposed offices would really be no expense to the ratepayers, b?cutse the School Board promised to take a large portion of them and pay a large rent. It was also expected that the over- seers and perhaps some of the Government officials would take offices if provision VMS made for them. He referred to the inconvenience of the present offices, and it was neces- sary that they should remove for reasons which some of the members knew, but which it would not be advisable to mea- tion.—At the request of the members the Clerk read Mr. Carlile's letter again.—Mr. SADLER said if Mr. Carlile had said the upper room was an American howling saloon instead of a workman's club he would have been nearer the mark. (Hear, hear.)—Mr H. Dutton's motion was then nut to the meeting and lost —The matter was then referred to the General Purposes Committee.—The meeting then con- eluded.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, when there werii present the Rev. Canon Barclay (who presided), Rev. J. Lockwood, and Messrs. F. Rigby (ex-officio), J. Camphin, J. Highfield, Joseph Stokes, T. Norman, J. Darbyshire, J. G. Hamilton, E. Wallington, Joseph Smith, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. •H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD, in ac- cordance with notice of motion, moved that Mr. Albert Woodvear be appointed school attendance officer for Wes- ton, Halton, Clifton, Stockham, and Norton at a salary of .:435 per annum.—The Rev. CHAIRMAN said be felt bound, in no disrespect to the mover or Mr. Woodyear, as represen- tative of the Attendance Committee at Weston, to move an amendment to the effect that the•district should be divided iato two parts. The district would be a long way round, and therefore be proposed that it be divided, and a a salary of £lO each be given to the school attendance officers* —The CLatti: You can't increase the salary, I think, without giving notice to each Guardian. At present it remains at £l2 103. You propose £2o—The Rev. J. Lomtwooti said the salary in his motion was £l5 per annum. Mr. Wright had 10s, but he did his work in connection with th two at tbe thee. a— re- lieving officer duties—killing two birds with cue at oe Mr. DARRYSHINN thought if they could onldit appoint would same sal iry d 9 they were giving th better caee to go before the Local Government Board. The CLERIC suggested that the district should be divided, and at the next meeting someone should move that an officer be appointed to each.—This was moved by the CHAIRMAN, and seconded by Mr. STOILES.—The amendment was then put to the meet- ing and carried unanimontly.—Accounts amounting to £1,067 12s ld were presented for payment. This consisted of salaries, &c., £525 Is 6d, and contracts, £542 103 7d.— The CLERIC reported that 12 applications had been re- ceived for the post of schoolmaster at the Union, and a committee consisting of the Rev. J. Lockwood, and Messrs. Charles Reynolds (e.r-oficio),Handley, Wallington, and John Ashton was appointed to meet and go through the applica- tions, selecting three to come before the next Board meet- , ing.—lt was stated that the number of vagrants te'ieved in 1882 was 943, against 554 in 1883, a decrease of 330. This was considered highly satisfactory.

, RAILWAY SERVANTS' SUPPER AT WIDNES. The men employed in the traffic department of the Lon- don and North-Western Rally:ay at Widnes station had I their annual supper on Thursday evening, at the Railway Inn, Victoria-road. About 25 persons partook of the excel- . lent repast provided by Mrs. Anderson, and sabs,quently the party adjourned to the parlour, where Mr. Smith, the ' stationmaster, occupied the chair, and Mr. Carter the vice- chair. Amongst those present were Messrs. Warbureon (of the canal department), Turnbull (of the locomotive depart- ment), Ashton (chief clerk), s.t.c.—The Chairman having wished ad present a neppy and prosperous new year, Mr. Ashton proposed the ben il loyal teat of "the Queen and the rest of tue lit -la' family," which was drunk witn musical honours. Mr. Ashton then gave In an appropriate style the toast of the " London and North-Western Railway Co.,' coupled with the name of Mr. Smith. The toast was honoured with enthusitsm.—Mr. Smith, in responding, said this was the second time that he had had the pleasure of meeting those Ipte sent at these pleasant re-unrolls on two occasions. He was gratified to respond to the toast now proposed; in the i' first place not only because the company were their em- provers, but because they strived in the best way possilel e I for the benefit of the working classes in general. Tne Lon- don and North-Western Raiiway Company haa expended thousands of pounds, and the officials had undergone great taxation of brain, in providing for the safety of life p.ud limb. Tne company were the employers of thousands of men throughout the country who would not have been employed fifty years ago. At the time that steam was first introduced as a motive power, it was predicted that the laud would be ruined; but steam had proved a blessiaa, not a curse to the people; and he , therefore looked upon the London and North-Western Rail- I way Company as an enterprising company. He must say they had got some of the best generals, some of the best commanders, and some of the best captains that no other company of the present day possessed. Mr. Smith men- tioned the name of Mr. Carter in connection with the toast, I observing that he was thankful to meet him, and hoped he 1 and all present would be spared to be together next year, and he trusted he should be there to enjoy their company for years to come. (" Hear, hear," and applause.) The next toast was "The Town and Trade of Widnes," which ' was proposed by Mr. Warburton, who expressed the opinion that the trade in the town was improving, and he thought that next year the railway officials would have quite as much work as they could deal with. He honed as employee of the L. and N.-W. Railway Company they would reap their share of the prosperity, whilst at the same time they I did their best for their employers. (Applause.) Mr. Bar- ton, secretary of the engineering department, also re- sponded. He remarked that the pleasure of these annual gatherings would be much enhanced if all the departments could arrange to unite and hold one common meeting.—The Chairman agreed with Mr. Burton, but drew attention to the many claims upon the time of railway officials, and the improbability of them all being at Mowry on one night. He expressed his williagness to endeavour to bring about such an arrangement as suggested by Mr. Burton.—Mr. Ashton then gave the " Health of the donors." Had it not been for the kind generosity of the kind donors, those pleasant meetings could not take place, and they could not do better than wish them "a happy and prosperous New Year." (Applause). The toast was warmly 'honoured, the list being brought to a conclusion by the toast "The health of the host and hostess," proposed by Mr. Ashton. During the evening a musical programme was gone through in a manner which delighted the com- pany, Mr. Sankey ably officiating at the piano. Songs were well rendered by Messrs. Howard, Lambert, Briggs, and Alderson, whilst Mr. Lambert also gave a . recitation in good style.

div.head: DAUSBURY HIGRWAY BOARD.
div.p: DAUSBURY HIGRWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held at the Sessions Hous.., Daresbury, on Thursday afternoen. There were present— Messrs. Joseph Cliffe (in the chair), W. Long, W. C. Jones, Jas. Knowles, A. Kenworthy, Cr. Percivtl, W. Bradford, T. Benmett, J. Parr, H. Houghton, Edward Aaron, Jas. Handley, Jas Cooper, C. T. Whitley, T. S. Burgess, J. Mclntyre, John Mayer. W. Wilkinson, John Rigby, John Baguley, Linaker (clerk), and Darbyshire (surveyor).

div.head: BOARD AND THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE BOARD AND THE SHIP CANAL.

The CLERK said he had received a report and Parliamen- tary notices with reference to the Manchester Ship Canal. They referred to the roads of the district generally, but con- tained some very important matters affacting the Board's district, much more so than did the farmer Bill. The Sur- veyor was instructed eb prepare a report on the matter, and to submit it to a meeting of the Board, which will be con- vened to consider it. _ TIL/3 PROPOSED COGSBILL BRIDGE.

The Clerk had written to ior—d-TeigT:Zng for con- tributions towards erecting the proposed bridge over Cogs. hail Brook, but had received a reply saying that the bridge would affect Lord Leigh's tenauts only in a small degree. If the Board would forward him a tracing of the proposed bridge it would have his consideration. Mr. Smith Barry had been similarly applied to, and had forwarded £25. The trustees of the Behnoute estate had also been applied to, but had replied stating that they did not feel justified in subscribing to the erectioa of the bridge. Mr. Clarke, to whom likewise application had been made, had not yet rc- plied. It was stated that the bridge would cost in round numbers £3OO. The matter was adjourned to the next meeting.

Tinsley, of Grappenhall Lodge, complaining that on the evening of the 29th ult., when driving from Aston Grange to Preston Brook, his trap was nearly upset near to the latter place by some large stones which had Len left in the middle of the road.—The CHAIRMAN : I suppase it is the fault of the roadman.—The SURVEYOR said that the roadman had told him that he had had the " blocks " on the road duting the day, and that he forgot to take them off in the evening. Oakell was the roadman's name.—The CLERK : I have had some narrow escapes in that Oakell's district myself.—The CHAIRMAN: Then he seems to be in the habit of keeping these "blocks" on. Ile appears to be working on the block system. (Laughter.)—The subject then dropped.

The CRAIRmAN intimated that he had a word or two to say respecting what took place in that room on December 12th. They would remember that he opposed the proposi- tion concerning an allowance of beer to the workhouse in- mates at Christmas. He simply opposed the suggestion at the meeting of the committee on principle, and gave no other reason for oppeeing it. He was consequently amazed at reading in the report of the subsequent Board meeting , (which he was unable to attend), that he was coupled with Mr. Derbyshire in the opposition on the:ground of " extrave- gance." He did not know how that came to be said because he had not verbally or by any record in the books stated his reason for opposing the proposition. The chairman re- ferred to a report of the proceedings in which Mr. Harrison was credited with having used the word " contemptible" in reference to the matter. He did not wish to make himself objectionable to any gentleman round the table, but only wished to be put right as he did not think any member would wilfully misrepresent his opiniees.—Mr. HARRISON explained that when he used the word "contemptible" he was not vry fortunate in the selection of a word but he did not mean to say that either the Chairman or Mr. 1 arbyshire were con- temptible. He meant to say that the distinction between the price of coffee and beer was in itself contemptible. Mr. Derbyshire raised ro other issue to the opposition but that of extravagance, and that was a matter to be combated be- cause it was impossible for Mr. Derbyshire or anyone else to sustain such an argumeot. If he had offended the Chairman or Mr. Derbyshire in any way he was exceed- ingly sorry for it.—The Cneeasteet said he was quite attic. fled with the explar tion. THE MINERS' RELIEF QUESTION : A SETTLEMENT: VOTE OF TIZAERS TO THE CLERK. The CLERS said: The correspondence I have had with Messrs. Bradshaw, of Haydockeand Woods, of Wigan, has now te.rminated. Subsequent to the letters I read to your Board on the action of the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Permauent Relief Society in discentinaing the payments to aged injured miners ow the plea of the doctors refusal to Certify that their present debility is the result of injuries received by accident in coal inines, I received an intimation that the subject had been referred to their solicitor, and a proposal was made also that the opinion of counsel be taken. It appeared that emne of the miners had, before my first letter to the secretary, agreed to arbitration, and I suggested that the whole matter should go to the Newton Petty Sessional Court, and that I would attend before the justices in support of my contention that the word and spirit of the rules were alike at variance with the proceed- ings, and with the decision arrived at by the society. We have, as hitherto explained, had to experience the difficulty arising out of the fact that the matter lay entirely outside tee legal jurisdiction of the Guardians, and of my duty as your clerk, notwithstanding that the Inevitable result of the society's proceedings unchallenged or confirmed would be that the present and future maintenance of the old miners, and of other people hereafter similarly dealt with would fell upon the peer rates for the Union. Boards of Guardians can only in- terfere in respect of liabilities to them directly created by Statute, and, save in exceptional Cases so provided for, the law is inapplicable to provident and similar societies. When, therefore, I received, as I did, notice that the subject would be dealt with on December 20th at the offices of the society, Leader's Buildings, Wigan, I deemed it best not to attend. I wrote, however, that consideration be given to my letters and to the views I had argued in favour of the miners' case. I have since 'then received a letter from Mr. Bradehaw, in which he writes " I am in a position to inform von that the decision is in favour of the old men, and we have paid them all the arrears due, which will be as satis- factory to yourself as it is to me." I propose, in couclu- sion, to acknowledge Mr. Braeshaw's communication, and the thanks of your Board for the consideration given to your letter. (Hear, hear)—Mr. APPLETON observed that the matter eras a very important one, and one which was outside Mr. Sutton's dude,' altogether. He thought, how- ever, that the clerk had now entirely carried his point, hav- ing brought the matter before the secretary at Havdock, awl from thence to Wigan, where it was decided in favour of the applicants. The course which had ked been taken had saved the Union a great deal of expense, and he would move that the Board tender -their thanks to Mr. Sutton for the interest he had taken in the question, and for the successfuleresult which he had been instrumental in bringing about. (Hear, hear.)—Mejor CARTWRIGILT : Poor pay. (Laughter.)—. Mr. DARETSEIRE said it was, bat if the Clerk was satisfied with a vote of thanks instead of actual pay be would gladly second the proposition. He thought the Board Red the ratepayers were much indebted to Mr. Sutton for what he had dine, :end the poor people especially should !bank him for having taken up their c ise and brought it to such s satisfactory issue. It was a matter outside the range it Mr. g ot ton's duties officially, and it was only right to acco,d him a cordial rote of thanks for whit he had den 3 in this and other respects. Mr. Sotton bad done many good things for the Board. ID had successfully terminated the question of stamp duties, some years ago he had brought nearly MOO to the Beard in the case of a lunatic named Caldwell, and

country, and they must admit that to a great extent the prosperity of the country was due to the strict observance of the Sabbath and by other such good means. (Hear, hear.) He asked the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton to respond. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON suitably replied. Dr. WHITE proposed "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces," to which Captain Nlcaotsoer responded. He ob- served that undoubtedly great changes had taken place in the service during the past few years, and there was the natural tendency of Englishmen to grumble and object to those changes. The tendency was to criticise the changes and to prophecy evil as arising from them, but they ought to test them first and place a little more trust in the leaders of military affairs in England at the present time. Lord Welseley had been sharply criticised by many people yet on every single occasion when he had come to the front, and which he (Captain Nicholson) did not contri- bute entirely to good luck, Lord Wolseley had shown himself a worthy representative of England and a worthy successor of past history. (Hear, hear.) Mr. ROSE proposed "The Trustees of the Blue Coat School," which he said he did with great pleasure. (Hear, hear.) It was a very encouraging fact that the trustees took such an interest in the society, assisting them not only with their subscriptions, but also with their presence on such occasions as the present. That evening they had among them three trustees of the School. (Applause.) It was likewise a pleasure te know that those who were not I able to be present at the dinner were with them in spirit, and Sympathised with the object they had in view. (Hear, hear.) Personally, he was indebted to the trustees for the kindness and consideration they had shown to him when hescalled upon them for their help in any way, and he was grateful too for the attention they had paid to any sugges- tions which he had from time to time made with reference to the improvement of the school or the welfare of the children. He could assure the "Old Blues " around him that the welfare of their younger brothers and sisters, who were now being educated at the institution, was always upperrr.ost in the minds of the trustees when any improve- ment was being considered by them, and he did not know where they could find a body of gentlemen who would have the interests of the young people more at heart. (Hear, hear.) He only hoped that they might long be spared to carry out the wished of the founders as they did new. (Applause.) Mr. Bracerate, in supporting the toast, observea that he 'could not speak with that elAticity and buoyancy of youth which he once did in that room years ago, yet he hoped they would credit him with being sincere when he said that those feelings, although perhaps net so strongly expressed OP the present occasion, were nevertheless as burning and as Ardent in his heart as ever they were when he was a boy In the school, or when he was one of the younger members of the society. He bad heard the tables ring with acclama- tion when that toast was given. He did not possess the charm of raising those acclamations again, but he was cer- tain that every heart felt now as it always did that there was a debt due to the trustees of the school which Blues could never repay even with all the current coin of the realm_ if it were at their disposal. (Hear, hear.) The best ~return the trustees looked for from himself and from the ' other old scholars was an honest and upright career of enter- prise and energy, and making the most of the opportunities before them so as to prove to the full the benefit of the education they received under their patronage. (Applause.) When he noticed the names of the two gentlemen associated , with that toast be began to think of olden times. His intro- duction to the Blue Coat School wan due to the family of Litton. When 116 was left a kind of waif on the world—parentless and almost friendless_ it was a Mr. Litton who gave him a helping hand and a re- commendation to enter the school. (Applause.) With re- gard to Alderman Davies they all know the original ideas and inventive genious of that gentleman. (Hear, hear.) In the flourishing days for Warrington—which were to come—when it was to be one of the ports in the estuary of the Mersev—(hear, hear, and laughter)—he believed the name of Alderman Davies would be emblazoned on the roll of that enterprise as one of its greatest promoters. (Hear, hear.) He would, however, suggest to him that as he was somewhat interested in the extension of that estuary that he should prevail noon some of their wonderfully capable , engineers to start that estuary somewhere in the neighbOur- , hood of the Blue Coat School instead of at Latchford, and that then their institution might be removed to some better locality. (Hear, hear. and laughter.) He daresay that would be brought about some day, and that they would ex- tend the charity so that instead of having say 40 or 50 children at the school they might have 200. (Applause.) Mr. Birch All next spoke in eulogistic terms of the trustees, to whom he said they should be grateful for having re- ' ceived their education, and whose fostering care had ore- s- eyed the Militarized for their children and their children's children after them. (Applause.) , The to ,et having been received with musical honours, The Cre tIRMAN first responded, and said it was the wish of the trusttes to advance the charity and the scholars ; everything connected with the institution under its present regime was most satisfactory and encouraging, and he thought there was every probability of their being able in
course of.time to have tn:we BC bolArs on the charity. (Ap- plause.)

Alderman DAVIES, in the course of an excellent speech, referred to the foundation of the Warrington Blue Coat School, and the remark-able circumstances "under which John Allen, a native of Warrington, formed the i nucleus of the Blue Coat Society; and spoke at some length on the past masters and benefactors of the charity. They ; deserved, he remarked, to be studied, admired, and imitated at the present day. He did not see many faces there that night he should liked to have seen, and he thought it was a 1 very unwise thing for men who had made money among them to depart from them. There seemed an inclination among some to do so. (Hear, hear.) Passing on to other matters, Alderman Davies said they had heard a great deal of late with regard to how the poor had been housed, or rather not housed, in the exciting words of G. R. Sims, and the earnest words of Sir Richard Cross Lord Salisbury, and many others. He did not wish to stand in the way of those who were competent to look after the interests of the poor, but he would ask those men to consider to some extent those who had to provide the money requ'red for carrying out those noble works. Somebody else was concerned besides the poor. He contended that the poor laws of this country were wonder- fully and admirably conducted, and everything that was possible was done for the good of the poor—and the poor they would always have with them—but there were some classes of the poor which if they were put into better houses would destroy the houses in which they lived. He did not wish to be hard on the poor people, but he wanted the country to understand that there were other peophi to con- sider in those who had to pay money to maintain the poor land maintaining the society of this kingdom. They should consider how money was raised in England. If they took a piece of land, houses, manufactures, collieries, mines, land and building societies, what bad they to do before anything could be done in the shape of earning money or profit for the people who had embarked their capital with them? They bad to support the poor, education, police, hi4hways, and rates of every description, and in this way a man had to pay 63. or 7s. in the £ before he could earn a penny for himself. As he had said before, he did not wish to speak severe,y ror to detract from the miseries of the poor, but they were not to be compared to the anxieties of a man weighed down with the expenses he had spoken of, and only just above the verge of poverty. The question came • how long would such a state of affairs last, and what would be the remedy? He did not want to stand still and say there was nothing to be done for the poor; he said it should be done, but who was to pay for it ? During the last forty years the national wealth of the country had increased 4,596 millions, and where bad that amount gone to? He might tell them that three thousand millions of that money was em- ployed in investments abroad, and in manufactures directly antagonistic to their own. He had nothing to say against Free Trade, but there was the fact that every manu- facture and product made and produced abroad was brought to their own doors free of expense, and the men who owned , three thousand millions abroad possessed all the advan- tages of a necessarily expensive society in this country, but did not subscribe one farthing to the maintenance of the rates. With such great advantages they ought to be called upon for what he would term a foreign investment rate. (Hear, hear.) There was room, he considered, for a formid- able tax upon those who, as he said, were in receipt of all the advantages of a necessarily expensive society, but yet who did not contribute an atom towards it. (Applause.) Mr. PERCIVAL next proposed, in complimentary terms, "The Mayor and Corporation of Warrington," and con- gratulated Alderman Harrison on holding the distiuguished position of Chief Magistrate of the Borough. (Applause.) The toast having been heartily received, The MAYOR suitably responded, pointing out that there was no doubt that the duties of a member of the Council, if properly and conscientiously discharged, were no sinecure, bat on the contrary involved a great amount of labour and trouble. (Hear, hear.) Alderman WEBSTER proposed The Blue Coat Brotherly Society." (Applause.) He said they all knew the society was a very important one. He had seen the rise and fall of a great many societies in Warrington in his time, but during that long period he did not know of one which was more worthy of their support and the support. of all good and benevolent men than that of the Blue Coat Society. (Ap- pliauee.) He coupled with the toast the name of Mr. For- , shew, the hon. secretary. (Applause.) Mr. Foochow, in responding to the toast, said he felt proud of holding the position of hon. sec. tO a society which had done, and was doing, so much good. He sincerely hoped that the society, well founded as it was on the prin- ciples of brotherly love and Christian charity, would go on and prosper in its usefulness. (Hear, bear.) It was very , necessary that some such controlling influence as the society I afforded should increase so as to secure the welfare of the ' Blues after they left school, and especially at that very tryingtime of their lives—the interval between youth and I manhood. (Hear, hear.) Tee committee felt that they had not that general co-operation of old Blues which they ought to have, and he hoped, therefore, the committee would send copies of the report broadcast, so that it might get in the hands of those old Blues who bad not as vet recognised themselves in connection with the society, but who were nevertheless very much indebted to it. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion Mr. Forshaw asked the company to drink cor- dielly the health ef Mr. Percival, and also with feelings of solemnity and respect to the memory of the late Dr. Bowse. (Hear, hear.) The healths having 'aeen drunk, Mr. Was. OWEN proposed briefly "The town and trade of Warrington," to which Mr. PORTER replied. The other toasts were "The Press," proposed by Mr. MORRIS, and responded to by Dr. Mocitte ; "Kindred societies," proposed by Councillor MONKS, and responded to by Mr. TWISS ; "The chairman," proposed by Alderman DAVIES, and received with musical honours. The company shortly afterwards separated.
THE PENKETH DAME'S SCHOOL. CORRESPONDENCE WITH MR. SUTTON AND MR. GASKELL.

At the meeting of the Warrington Union School Atten- dance Committee, held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday, there being present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (in the chair), , Messrs. Darbyshire, Brown, Jolley, and J. Houghton, the CLERK (Mr. J. C. Sutton) read the following correspondence, I which was approved : Weymouth, December 14, 1883.—Dear Sir,—ln ;.e Penkelh Infant Cthol. A. report of the prosecutions of the Union School Attendance Committee hes been forwarded to me. I I gather therefrom that children of such age as thor.e whose parents have been prosecuted will not be allowed to remain at the school. In a letter from my daughter, Mrs. Greg, she says—" Mr Sutton pointed out that they took no proceedings I against children under Vac age of ten years, and he suggested that there should be an arrangement that children should leave at tun." Would you oblige by informing me if the above extrect from my daughter's letter corr.( ctly re- presents what you said, a tOni no such statement in the re- port. jam anxious to avoid similar annoyances in future, and should feel very much obliged if you would kindly infcrm me if no further prosesutlons would be instituted if children leave the school at the 'age of ten years.—l am, yours truly, ROBERT GASKELL —J. C. Sutton. Esq. December 17, 1883. Dear sir,—Penketh Infant Bctr,ol.—No doubt in effect I did ask Mrs. brag, " Will it not be well to !draw a line, as to girls also, say at ten?' I meant all the ques- tion Implies. I know no reason why the school may not be conduced and controlled henceforth as hitherto, if the tutors who instruct and the ladies who inspect ex amine the children Ins the subjects included in the proscribed standards. Free- tie-ally it seemed to be so; anyway, very slight addition to a de- parture from the present procedure is needed if the girls leave the infant school at ten and attend the certified school, and the committee would not then interfere. It is, however, the duty of the committee to know that every child in their district of school age attends school regularly. !Their officers have to prove to them at each meeting that the law is duly observed in that respect within their several die. teicts. Probably the objection to official interference prompted refusal of perusal of the school register to the Attendance Officer I feel sure you will relieve the committee of this diffi- culty. and, the officer on his part will fall in with any reason- able desire as to periods for inspection. I have confined my reply to the subject of your letter. lam without instruction, but feel sure the two letters may be viewed as the basis of a simple and equitable arrangement to act upon.—Yours truly, JAMES C. StrrTon.—Robert Gasket!, Esq., Weymouth. In re Penketh Infant School. Weymouth, December 21st, 1883.—Dear sir,—Allow me to thank you for your letter of I December 17th, a copy of which I have sent to Miss Sankey, as also of this and mine, dal A December 14th. The examina- tion of the children by ladles visiting the school may be desir- able, but it is much more Fatisfactory 1.1 me that the Govern- merit Inspector something more than two years ago (I cannot exactly tlx the time) c:sually entered the school, and at Miss , Sankey's r luest kindly examined the czildren, and after do- ing so said that the acquirements of the children were quite equal to those of children of similar age In the Government in- spected schools. I have reason to believe the school is now even more efficient. Ido not see any objection to the inspection of the school register by the attendance officer. Mrs. Gaskoll has periodic reports of the attendance, and from what I have heard the average attendance compares favourably with schools in th neighbourhood. Schools in the Warrington Union may be better attended, of this I am ignorant.-1 am, yours truly, ROBERT GASKELL.—J. C. Sutton, Esq.

GOOD TEMPLARS MEETING AT EARLESTOWII. The weekly meeting of the members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Template was held in the lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening last. Bro. John Taylor, W.C.T., presided. One new member was initiated and another candidate for membership proposed. A report on the New Year's Eve tea party was read by the W.C.T. The report was considered very eati'sfactory as a balance re- mained in hand after *the payment .of expenses. The evening's programme was headed "Enigmas and Conun- drums" and a number of the members submitted an in- teresting and specially-chosen lot. AN ARTILLERYMAN IN TROUBLE AT ST. HELENS.—On Friday, at the St. Helens Police Couit, John Donoghue, a private in the Royal Artillery, was charged under remand with assaulting P.C. Cottam whilst in the execution of his duty; and further with having been convicted of a similar offence within two years from this date. Prisoner pleaded !guilty to both charges.—P.C. Cottam having proved the assault, Superintendent Johnston said the prisoner had en- listed under an assumed name, and be had reason to believe he had been " drummed " out of another rer,iment. A few • months since prisoner was trazetted a deserter, but, in reply t; his t the superinteisclen t's) letter of inquiry, the command- ing officer stated that the prisoner had been an absentee since the 31st tilt. He had been six times convicted of as- saulting the police, fifteen times for being drunk and dis- orderly, three times for being drunk on licensed /premises, four times for breaches of the peace, and four times for other offences—thirty-two times in all.—A sentence of four montias with hard labour wse imposed.
CHARGES AGAINST WARRINGTON
PUBLICANS.

Yesterday, at Wartington Police Court, John Mather, landlord of the Rose and Crown, Bridge-street, was sum- moned for suffering gaining to take place on his licensed premises.—kr. Brown, of Stockport, appeared for the defen- dant.—Sergeant Bowen said that about eight o'clock on Saturday evening he and P.C2Pennington visited the defendant's house, and in the taproom saw five men. On the table was a pack of cards "cat," A man named Wm, Cook took up one half of the cards, and another named potter took up the other. Witness took possession of the cards, and Cook said that they belonged to him, and added that he had been playing them and that the next time he would play them at the police station. There were eight or nine glasses of beer on the mantleplece, the tables being clear. Ile asked the defendant's son where his father was, and he replied that he was away from home. When he was taking the men's names. one, who gave his name as Daley— but whose name he believed was Dooley—took up a six- pence from the table. The defendant's son, in reply to a question, said he did not know that the men in the taproom had been playing at cards.—P.C. Pennington corroborated. —William Cook, of Glum-yard, Naylor-street was summoned as a witness by the police. but when he was put into the witness box he answered the questions put to him in a very reticent and disrespectful manner. The effect of his evidence was that the cards belonged to him, that he pulled them out of his pocket while getting out a pipe of tobacco, and that the men did not play with thena.—There being no other evi- dence the case was dismissed Thomas Archer, landlord of the Royal Exchange, Market-place, was summoned for keeping his house open doling prohibited hours; and Wm. James Barrie, Thomas M. Thorne, Percy Randalls, and Ed- ward Birchall were summoned for being on the said premises during such prohibited hours. Mr. Moore, junr., appeared for the defendants. Sergeant Spinks stated that on Tuesday night, after 11 o'clock, he heard some men in the defendant's house, and on looking through the keyhole he could see a faint light in one of the rooms. He went to the window, and could hear a noise like the shuffling of dominoes and heard one man say, " This is either six or eight." An- other said, "It is sixpennyworth each." As he could not get in he waited until Mr. Archer let the men out, which was about 20 minutes to one, and .then got their names. On going into the house he found six glasses containing beer. Mr. Archer said that the men had come straight from the theatre, and had been having a quiet glass; that they had not paid for anything; and that they were his guests. —Sergeant Cox corroborated.—Mr. Archer was sworn, and said that the men were his private guests, that he asked them in the afternoon to spend a few hours with him after leaving the theatre, and that they certainly paid for nothing. —The Chief-Constable said that Mr. Archer bad never been reported before, and that there was no complaint against the house; but he remarked that it was the custom for land- lords when intending to entertain their friends to intimate the same to the police. Mr. Archer had not done 90 in this case, and the police were perfectly justified in the action they had taken.—The case was dismissed.

BURNED TO DEATH AT ST. lIELENS.-011 Tuesday after- noen an inquest was held by Mr. T. B. Edge, coroner, at the Finger Post Hotel, Parr, touching the death of a collier named Daniel Swift, who lived at 13, Bishop-street. Swift, it seemed was aliout 40 years of age, and during the last seven years had not done any work owing to his being sub- ject to fits. On Monday night his wife went out for a short time, and some time after Mr. Lee, the owner of the house in which they lived, heard a moaning in Mr. Swift's room, and on looking in saw him lying on the floor, his clothes being on fire. Lee at once drew him out, and Dr. Knowles was at once sent for, but the decsased did not live long. It was stated that a chair was lying up against the fire grate, .and it was supposed that the deceased had taken a fit and fallen upon the fire. A verdict of Accidental death' was returned.

SUDDEN DEATH AT Sr. HELENS.—OH Tuesday after- noon, an inquest was held at Catham Arms. St. Helens, by Mr. J. B. Edge, as to the death of a young man named John Cummins, a bricklayer's labourer.—lt seemed that , the deceased, who lived with his parents in Claughton- street, bad been employed at the St. Helens chemical works at the relaying of a caustic pot on Saturday morning, when he suddenly fell down and died almest immediately. Tme deceased, it appe:,red, had been at work 48 hours previous to his death, and as it was supposed that death might have been caused by over-exertion, a post-mortem examination bad been made by Dr. McNicoll.—Dr. McNicol I was, how- ever, of opinion that deceased had had a severe attack of congestion of the lungs owing to the cold and exposure, and this resulted in a sort of fatal syncope. He did not think the fames from the caustic pots had contributed to the death.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

A HOSPITAL BURNED DONYN.—AdriCeS from St. Lucia to the 3rd inst. report the destruction of the Colonial Hespitil iu that island. EGYPTIAN DISTURDANCES QUELLED —The disturbances which broke out in the provinces of Benisuef and Fayourn have been quelled. THE PRIZE FIGHT AT BARNET : THE SENTENCE. —At the Central Criminal Court, London, yesterday, 11 men were found guilty of taking part as principals or accessories in the prize fight at Barnet, and were each fined .£5. THE NORTHERN IRON TRADE.—A Micicileborounh cor- respondent telegraphs that in consequence of rumoured in- tention of Cleveland iron masters to restrict output of pig iron, price for pig iron advanced yesterday sixpence per tou.

• An extraordinary instance of the mildness of the season has just occurred at Bedworth. A brown linnet's nest , containing six eggs, has been found by a man while walk- ; in the Bedworth Woodland, and on looking further in the ; same locality he discovered the newly-built nest of a black- ! bird. DREADFUL WIFE MURDER THROUGH JEALOUSY.— ! Martha Lloyd, who was so dangerously stabbed by her husband in a fit of jealousy, on Saturday night, whilst in bed at her husband's house, Devon-street, Birmingham, nag died from th effects of the injuries. The 'husband now stands remanded on a cbargv of wilful murder. Ins MINERS' STRIKE IN SOUTH STAFFORDSHIRE.—The strike of miners at Old Hill, South Staffordshire, partially terminated yesterday, when all the men employed by Messrs. Harper and Moore resumed work, the dispute having been settled. Efforts are being made to compro- mise the dispute with the other miners on strike in the district.

FATAL OurRAGE ON A WIFE.—At Hull, yesterday, a man, named Rowland was remanded, charged with murdering his wile by kicking her. The woman was rendered unconscious, and was taken to the Infirmary, where she lingered several days, and erysipelas having set in she died on Thursday night. The prisoner was thereupon charged on the graver count. Six SUICIDES IN ONE FAMlLY.—Yesterday Mr. Moles- worth held an inquest at Birch on the body of Reuben Booth, 64, who hanged himself on the Bth inst. The de- ceased was a tailor, and afraid that his wife might die first. It was stated in evidence that the deceased's father, son, brother, and two uncles had committed suicide. The jury returned a verdict of suicide whilst of unsound mind. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A HUNTING PARTY.—Whilst the Fitzwilliam hounds were out in Huntingdonshire yesterday they crossed the main line of the Great Northern Railway in full cry in front of an express train, which dashed into their midst, injuring some of the dogs. About the same time Lady Elane Gordon, sister of the Marquis of Huntley, was thrown violently from her horse and sustained a severe shock.

A PARIS TRAGEDY : ATTEMPTED MURDER Sy A Dts- CARDED MISTRESS—Marie Feral, a former mistress of a man-cook named Courtois, in the employment of a wineshop keeper of the Rue Cade!, Paris, went into his kitchen on ThursdAv morning, and, after a violent scene of recrimina- tion, fired two shots of a revolver pointblank at him. He was removed to the hospital in a dying state, and the woman was arrested.

DEFIANT ORANGE PROCLAMATION. - The following placards have been posted throughout Cavan —"To: the Orangemen of Fermanah. Brethren, this so-called National League has called a meeting on Wednesday, the 16th inst., at Blacklion, on the border of our county. If the Govern- ment, regardless of the lamentable result at Dromore, fail to prohibit this meeting, let us arise in defence of our homes, our country, and our Bible, and assemble in our thousands to show that Orangemen will never consent to Home Rule or separation."

THE RECENT DROMORE HIOTS.—The remains of Giffin, the young Orangeman, who died from a bayonet wound re- ceived in Dromore riots, were yesterday accorded at Porta- down, what is described as the largest public funeral ever witnessed in the North of Ireland. Thousands of Orange- men from neighbouring towns took part in the procession, which was headed by three bands, accompanied the corpse to the cemetery. The funeral cortege also comprised some thousands of factory and mill operatives, and many local clergymen, magistrates, and other notables. A Frcnrions Co:um/ay.—Yesterday, George Dunn, 40, merchant, Weaman.street, Birmingham, was remanded for a week for obtaining by "long firm " frauds money and goods from various persons in Manchester, Leeds. London, Liverpool, Glasgow, Dumfries, Huddersfield, and various other places. Inspector Heiden stated that the prisoner car- oled on "The Manufacturing Supply Association, Regis- tered," but which was not registered. The prisoner pre- tended to be the manager of the fictitfous company, and thus obtained SLIM of money for articles which he professed to supply, but did not. The room in which the business of the " company " was carried on was rented at 33. 6d. per week. An application for bail was refused. THE TRANSVAAL DELEGATES were entertained at lun- cheon, at Brighton, yesterday. President Kruger, speaking in Dutch, Mr. Du Tort translating, regretted his inability to speak in English as he knew that differences in language and die cons:quent inability to understand one another had been cne of the causes of misunderstanding between the Transvaal and England. He hoped, however. that now the English language was being taught in the Transvaal schools this great drawback would before long be a thing of the past. lie was glad to find that many people in England trusted them, and he hoped they would not dis- appoint their friends. The delegates were the guests of Mr. Hall, and the preceedings had no official character.
